# The Minute Between

When my aunt died, she left me a shop full of clocks and a letter that said, among other things, not to trust the grandfather clock beside the stove.

“It gains time when the room is cold,” she wrote. “People do much the same.”

The shop stood at the narrow end of Bell Street, where the pavement gave up and became steps leading down to the river. Above its door hung a wooden sign shaped like a pocket watch. Rain had erased most of the lettering, but you could still read REPAIRS if you knew what to look for.

I had not visited in eleven years.

This was not because we had quarreled. A quarrel would have given our silence a shape. Instead, I had moved away, found work, changed jobs, moved again, and developed the habit of believing that a telephone call postponed was merely a telephone call stored for later.

There is no warehouse large enough for all the things we mean to do later.

I arrived on a Thursday with one suitcase and a folder of documents. The solicitor had explained that selling the building should be straightforward. A developer wanted the adjoining properties. Mine would complete the row.

“You needn’t make any decisions immediately,” he said, with the careful tone of someone who expected me to make them immediately.

Inside, the shop smelled of brass, dust, and the faint medicinal sweetness of furniture polish. Clocks covered the walls. Clocks crowded the shelves. A clock shaped like a cathedral stood beside one shaped like a cheerful cow. Some ticked. Some hummed. Most were silent.

Together, the working ones sounded like rain beginning in several different places.

I found the light switch behind the door. A fluorescent tube blinked overhead, reconsidered, and came on.

My aunt’s workbench occupied the back of the room. There was a green-shaded lamp, a magnifying glass on a jointed arm, and six shallow dishes containing screws so small they resembled pepper. Her cardigan hung from the chair.

I touched its sleeve before I could stop myself.

On the bench lay an open watch, its hands removed, its tiny interior exposed. I had the uneasy sensation of having interrupted an operation.

The letter waited beneath a jar of pencils.

Most of it was practical. The stopcock was behind the stove. The upstairs window stuck in wet weather. Mr. Vale collected the scrap metal and should not be allowed to pretend it was a favor.

Then came the sentence about the grandfather clock.

At the bottom she had written, “There is one job outstanding. You’ll know it when you see it.”

I turned the page over, expecting an explanation.

There was none.

That evening I began making an inventory. I worked in a spreadsheet, assigning each object a number, a description, and a provisional value. This was the kind of activity at which I excelled: converting uncertainty into columns.

At item forty-three, someone knocked.

A boy stood outside, perhaps twelve years old, holding a cardboard box with both hands. He wore a school uniform under an enormous yellow raincoat. The hood framed his face like a badly drawn sun.

“Is she in?” he asked.

I told him she had died.

He looked down at the box.

“Oh.”

For several seconds we listened to the clocks.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“Thank you.”

“She was fixing this.”

He lifted the lid. Inside lay a kitchen clock with a blue plastic rim. One hand pointed at four; the other had fallen loose beneath the glass.

“She said Thursday.”

His voice had no accusation in it. That made the sentence harder to bear.

“I don’t repair clocks,” I said.

The boy considered this.

“Are you going to learn?”

The sensible answer was no. I had a job in another city, although I was currently on leave. I had a flat with a leaking shower. I had a buyer who might offer more if I moved quickly.

“I don’t know,” I said.

He nodded, accepting this as the sort of uncertainty adults were entitled to have.

“It’s my grandad’s. He likes that one because the numbers are big.”

I took his name and telephone number. His name was Eli. He wrote it carefully in my aunt’s order book, directly beneath three pages of her handwriting.

After he left, I carried the clock to the workbench.

The loose hand was simply a loose hand. Even I could see that much. But I did not know how to open the casing without breaking it, and this ignorance seemed suddenly representative of my entire life.

I could lead a meeting about operational resilience. I could not restore a minute hand to its rightful place.

The next morning, I bought a screwdriver.

It was the wrong screwdriver.

At the hardware shop, a woman named June examined it and asked what I was trying to dismantle.

“A clock.”

“One of Martha’s?”

“Yes.”

She put the screwdriver back on its hook.

“You’ll want these. And don’t force anything.”

This, I discovered, was the first principle of clock repair and possibly the first principle of many other useful things.

The blue clock opened with four small screws. I worked beneath the magnifying glass, feeling enormous and clumsy. The hand pressed back onto its shaft. A fresh battery started the mechanism.

I watched it for an hour, certain that something more complicated must be wrong.

Nothing was.

At noon, I called Eli’s mother.

She thanked me as though I had done something substantial. I nearly explained that I had not, but stopped. My aunt, I remembered, had never corrected people’s gratitude. She had simply accepted it and gone on working.

Word traveled quickly.

By Monday, three people had come in asking about repairs. A woman brought a carriage clock that had belonged to her mother. A man wanted a new battery in a watch he insisted was waterproof, although it contained visible river sand. Someone telephoned about the church clock.

I told them all I was not a clockmaker.

They seemed to regard this as a temporary inconvenience.

Meanwhile, the developer’s representative sent an email with a proposed timetable. It was brisk and courteous. The word “opportunity” appeared four times.

I placed the email beside my inventory and spent the afternoon opening drawers.

My aunt had labeled everything. SPRINGS. GLASS. GOOD HANDS. HANDS, UNCERTAIN. There was a drawer marked THINGS THAT WILL COME IN USEFUL, which contained, among other objects, a brass curtain ring, three foreign coins, and a tiny porcelain dog.

In the lowest drawer I found a photograph of my father at seventeen, standing beside my aunt on the river steps.

He was holding a fish. She was laughing at something outside the frame.

My father had been dead for twenty years. I knew him mostly through photographs in which he looked serious or startled. Here he looked pleased with himself in a way I recognized, unwillingly, from mirrors.

Behind the photograph was a notebook.

The first page said: STATION CLOCK.

Below that, in my aunt’s handwriting: Not broken. That is the trouble.

The station had closed before I was born. Its building remained at the edge of town, beyond the old grain warehouse, serving occasionally as a polling place and more often as a place nobody quite knew what to do with.

I walked there that afternoon.

The clock still hung above the platform entrance. Its face was white, its hands black, its numbers plain. It read twelve minutes past three.

My phone said eleven minutes past three.

I waited.

The minute hand moved.

Inside, a caretaker sat beside an electric heater, reading a newspaper so thoroughly folded that it looked like a private document.

“Clock?” he said when I asked.

“Yes.”

“Martha was always on about that clock.”

“What was wrong with it?”

“Nothing, according to everybody else.”

He introduced himself as Leon and took me upstairs.

The mechanism occupied a cupboard beneath the roof. It had been converted to electricity decades earlier, but some of the old machinery remained: wheels, shafts, a large weight suspended uselessly in a wooden channel.

Leon pointed to a small control unit.

“They set it from the radio. Never misses a beat.”

“Was it always a minute fast?”

His expression changed.

“Not fast,” he said. “Early.”

Apparently this distinction mattered.

The notebook explained why.

When passenger trains still stopped in town, the station clock had been kept one minute ahead of the railway’s official time. The stationmaster believed people required a small allowance for human weakness: untied boots, misplaced tickets, reluctant goodbyes.

The clock encouraged haste. The train provided mercy.

My aunt had copied this from an interview with the stationmaster’s daughter. Beneath it she had written:

A useful lie, while the trains ran.

After the line closed, the clock remained early. Over the years, newer systems replaced older ones. Technicians faithfully preserved the discrepancy, believing it to be intentional, which it was, though no longer for any reason they understood.

The notebook contained diagrams and measurements. There were notes about the clock’s ownership, its maintenance contract, the access ladder. There was also a list of people who thought it should be corrected.

The list was short.

A much longer list contained people who thought it should not.

I recognized several names, including June from the hardware shop and the solicitor who had urged me not to decide immediately.

At the bottom of the final page, my aunt had written: Ask them why.

So I did.

June said the clock had been that way when she was a child and she saw no reason to start improving everything now.

The solicitor said changing it might create liability, though he could not specify for what.

Leon said an accurate clock on a closed railway station struck him as a waste of accuracy.

The woman with the carriage clock said her husband had proposed beneath it.

“Was he a minute early?” I asked.

“No. Twenty minutes late. But I married him.”

Eli’s grandfather said he had missed the last train out of town in 1968 because he stopped to buy a meat pie.

“The clock couldn’t save me,” he said. “Nothing could.”

These conversations should have been irritating. I had come to settle an estate, not conduct a survey on municipal timekeeping. Yet each afternoon I found myself walking into another shop or knocking on another door.

People invited me in.

They made tea. They brought out photographs. They told me things I had not asked and sometimes things they had evidently waited years to tell anyone.

The clock was seldom the real subject.

On Wednesday, the developer’s representative called.

He was passing through town and wondered whether we might meet.

We sat in a café that had once been a butcher’s. The old hooks remained above the counter, painted white and used to hang plants.

He was younger than I expected, with tired eyes and a careful suit. His name was Daniel. He showed me drawings of what the row of shops could become: apartments above, commercial units below, larger windows, improved access.

The drawings were not monstrous. This disappointed me. I had begun preparing myself for a villain.

“What happens to the sign?” I asked.

“The watch sign? We could incorporate it.”

“And the steps?”

“Public access would remain.”

He answered every question reasonably.

When he left, I realized that selling was still sensible.

The building needed expensive work. I did not know the trade. Affection did not mend roofs, and inheriting a room full of someone else’s purpose did not mean I had inherited the purpose itself.

That night I dreamed of the shop with all its clocks removed. Pale circles marked the walls.

The following morning, I found another note tucked into the station notebook.

It was not addressed to me.

“Changing a thing because it is wrong is easy,” my aunt had written. “Leaving it because it is familiar is easy too. The difficult part is finding out what it is doing.”

I read it several times.

Then I phoned Leon.

“Can we stop the station clock?”

“For what?”

“One minute.”

He was quiet.

“You’d better speak to the council.”

The council, surprisingly, had no policy concerning the removal of a historical minute. They did have policies concerning work at height, electrical systems, and public notices.

I was not permitted to touch the mechanism.

A qualified technician could do it.

The technician charged enough to make the minute seem extravagant.

I paid.

Before the appointment, I put a notice in the shop window.

**ON SATURDAY AT NOON, THE STATION CLOCK WILL BE STOPPED FOR ONE MINUTE SO THAT IT CAN BE SET TO THE CORRECT TIME.**

Underneath, after some hesitation, I added:

**ANYONE WISHING TO SAY GOODBYE TO THE EXTRA MINUTE IS WELCOME.**

June came in carrying the notice, which she had apparently removed from the window.

“This is ridiculous,” she said.

“I know.”

“What will happen to the minute?”

“It won’t actually go anywhere.”

“Then why say goodbye?”

I had no satisfactory answer.

She studied me, then put the notice back.

On Saturday, twenty-three people came to the station.

Some had come to object. Some had come because they were curious. Eli came with his grandfather, who brought a folding chair. Daniel came too, unexpectedly, wearing walking shoes instead of his careful suit.

“I saw the notice,” he said.

Above us, the clock approached noon.

The technician waited in the roof cupboard with Leon. We had agreed that when the station clock reached twelve, its hands would stop. The rest of the town, and the rest of the world, would catch up.

I had imagined saying something. Now that people were watching me, every possible speech seemed unbearably grand.

So I said only, “My aunt wanted to do this.”

June folded her arms.

“She wanted a lot of things.”

“Yes,” I said.

The hands reached twelve.

They stopped.

At first, nothing happened.

A van passed on the road. Somewhere behind the warehouse, someone dropped a metal sheet with a tremendous crash. Eli’s grandfather adjusted his chair.

Then people began talking.

Not about time. About whether the rain would hold off. About a daughter visiting next weekend. About the old ticket office and the terrible coffee they used to sell there.

June told Daniel the new plans needed somewhere to sit that did not require buying anything. He took out his phone and made a note.

I stood beside the platform wall, listening.

For months I had thought of grief as a task I was failing to complete. Standing there, I missed my aunt sharply, particularly her ability to look perfectly comfortable among people who were annoyed with her.

The minute ended.

The clock moved.

No one applauded.

Leon emerged from the station and announced that everything had gone properly. Then Eli asked whether there would be another minute next year.

“Probably not,” I said.

“That’s a shame.”

By autumn, I had made a decision about the shop.

I sold the building, but not immediately, and not without conditions. Daniel’s company restored the watch sign and kept the river steps open. June got her bench.

I rented a smaller room two streets away, where I worked three days a week repairing simple clocks while a patient man from the next town taught me how much I did not know.

I kept my other job, reduced my hours, and discovered that an imperfect arrangement could sustain a life.

My aunt’s cardigan still hangs behind the workbench. I wear it when the room is cold.

The grandfather clock is there too.

It gains time in winter.

For now, I let it.

# The Department of Lost Afternoons

The Department of Lost Afternoons occupied the fourth floor of a building that had only three floors when viewed from the street.

This was not its most unusual feature.

The lift reached it only when someone pressed the button marked CLOSE DOOR twice, then apologized. The windows looked out on weather that had already happened. And the receptionist, who was a tortoise named Mrs. Bell, could tell whether a visitor had genuinely lost an afternoon or merely spent one badly.

“Regret,” she often said, “is not a filing category.”

Mara discovered the department on a Thursday, between a dental appointment and a meeting she had already decided to dislike.

She had entered the building to escape the rain. It was a narrow municipal building, the kind people generally walked past without noticing unless they owed money. Inside, a directory listed Licenses, Drainage, Archives, and a fourth entry that seemed to appear only when she looked away:

**LOST AFTERNOONS: ENQUIRIES AND RESTORATION**

Mara had been having trouble with afternoons.

They vanished while she answered messages. They disappeared between the purchase of groceries and the putting away of groceries. Sometimes she sat down at her kitchen table in daylight, opened her laptop, and looked up to find her reflection hovering in a black window.

She was forty-three, worked in procurement, and had become excellent at obtaining things nobody loved.

After making the lift’s acquaintance, she arrived in a room that smelled of paper, oranges, and warm electrical wiring.

Mrs. Bell sat behind a desk, wearing half-moon spectacles.

“Name?”

“Mara Vale.”

“Nature of loss?”

“I’m not sure.”

“That is common.”

“Is this a council office?”

“Not anymore.”

“Who runs it?”

Mrs. Bell considered the question.

“Continuity.”

Behind her, shelves climbed toward a ceiling too high to belong to the building. The shelves held glass jars, envelopes, biscuit tins, shoe boxes, and a surprisingly large number of rolled-up rugs. Each bore a label.

**AUGUST 19, AGE ELEVEN: WAITING FOR THE ICE-CREAM VAN**

**THE AFTERNOON AFTER THE LETTER**

**FOUR HOURS IN A GARDEN, OWNER UNKNOWN**

From somewhere beyond the shelves came the distant sound of children arguing about the rules of a game.

Mara looked back toward the lift. Its doors had closed.

“I have a meeting at three.”

“You may still attend it.”

“What time is it?”

“Here?”

“Yes.”

“Thursday.”

Mrs. Bell slid a form across the desk.

It asked for a name, an address, an approximate age, and the last known location of the missing afternoon. Beneath that was a box marked:

**DESCRIBE THE LIGHT.**

Mara uncapped the pen chained to the desk.

“I don’t know which afternoon I’m looking for.”

“Then begin with the light.”

She nearly wrote *normal*.

Instead, after a moment, she wrote: *Yellow. Through leaves. There was a table outside.*

The nib paused.

*Someone was cutting a pear.*

Mrs. Bell raised her head.

“Ah.”

“What?”

“A recoverable loss, perhaps.”

She took the form gently, though Mara had written only two lines.

“Please follow me.”

They passed into the stacks.

The room expanded as they walked. Corridors opened between shelves that Mara was certain had not been there a moment earlier. Some jars glowed faintly. One contained rain falling onto a red bicycle. Another held a woman laughing with her head tipped back.

A tin labeled **TUESDAY, MOSTLY IRONING** rattled as they passed.

“Are those memories?” Mara asked.

“Not precisely. Memories are what people carry away. These are the afternoons themselves.”

“Why would an afternoon end up here?”

“Sometimes someone mislays it during a move. Sometimes grief puts it somewhere difficult to reach. And sometimes a person gives it so little attention that it slips out of their possession altogether.”

“Can you get them back?”

“Occasionally.”

Mrs. Bell stopped beside a shelf of ordinary cardboard boxes.

“Usually they are looking for something they once knew how to do.”

“What sort of thing?”

“Sit still. Be absorbed. Enjoy another person’s company without considering what else they ought to be doing.”

She drew out a flat box and brushed dust from its lid.

**SEPTEMBER 6. ORCHARD TABLE. M. VALE.**

Mara knew the handwriting.

Her father had written labels that way: capital letters, widely spaced, as though each needed a little room to stand.

He had been dead for nine years.

“No,” she said.

Mrs. Bell did not open the box.

“You needn’t claim it.”

Mara touched the cardboard. It was warm.

The orchard belonged to her grandmother, although by then her grandmother had been too old to walk among the trees. Mara had gone there with her father near the end of a summer she remembered mostly as an interval between jobs.

She remembered the train journey.

She remembered being irritated that the village had no reliable phone signal.

She remembered her father wearing a shirt with one cuff repaired in slightly different fabric.

She did not remember the table.

“Can I see it?”

“Of course.”

Inside the box lay a folded afternoon.

It resembled a square of pale cloth, but its surface moved. Leaves cast shadows across it. A wasp entered one corner and vanished at the other. Mara heard the scrape of a knife against a plate.

Then her father said, very clearly, “These are better if you don’t hurry them.”

She caught the edge of a shelf.

Mrs. Bell waited beside her.

Mara had saved three voice messages from her father after he died. She had transferred them through several phones and two computers. In all three he sounded brisk and practical.

*Call me when you get this.*

*I’ve found the number you wanted.*

*No need to bring anything.*

She had forgotten that his voice could be lazy.

“Is he in there?”

“Your father was in that afternoon.”

“Can I go back?”

“For a visit.”

“For how long?”

Mrs. Bell looked at the cloth.

“As long as it lasts.”

Mara swallowed.

“What does it cost?”

“We don’t charge money.”

“Then what?”

“A present afternoon.”

Mrs. Bell led her to a reading room furnished with mismatched chairs. A kettle sat on a hot plate. Through the windows Mara could see a snowstorm, although outside the building the rain had been warm.

“Restoration requires time,” Mrs. Bell said. “Not clock time. A clock will pass through an afternoon whether anyone is there or not.”

“I have annual leave.”

“That is a matter between you and your employer.”

“I could give you Sunday.”

“Possibly. What were you planning to do?”

“Laundry. Finish a report. Order a new lamp.”

“And would you be willing to let all that wait?”

“The laundry wouldn’t complain.”

“Would you?”

Mara looked down at the little square of orchard light.

“What would I have to do instead?”

“We can arrange a placement.”

Mrs. Bell set out three envelopes.

The first was labeled **A MAN WHO WOULD LIKE COMPANY WHILE HE SORTS HIS WIFE’S BOOKS**.

The second read **A GIRL LEARNING TO RIDE WITHOUT STABILIZERS**.

The third said **A WOMAN WAITING FOR THE TIDE**.

“Are these tests?”

“No. These people requested company.”

“Why didn’t they ask someone they know?”

“You could ask them.”

Mara turned over the third envelope. There was an address near the coast, a date, and a time.

“What’s she waiting for?”

“The tide, according to her form.”

“That’s all?”

“She wrote that she would explain when you arrived.”

Mara chose the third envelope.

She was given a train ticket, directions to a beach, and a paper bag containing two pears.

“Do I take the afternoon home afterward?” she asked.

“You may return for it when you’re ready.”

“And if I do this wrong?”

Mrs. Bell took off her spectacles.

“There are no marks, Miss Vale. But you must stay until the woman says she is ready to leave.”

On Sunday, Mara went to the sea.

She nearly canceled.

Her report was unfinished. Rain was forecast. The journey required two trains and a bus. At seven in the morning she stood in her kitchen, looking at the pears and composing a sensible explanation.

Then she put the pears in her bag and left.

The beach lay below a village of pale houses and narrow streets. At low tide it was enormous, a plain of wet sand interrupted by shallow channels. Far out, the sea lay beneath the sky like a second, darker horizon.

A woman in a green coat sat on a folding chair above the waterline.

Beside her was an empty chair.

“You must be Mara.”

“Yes.”

“I’m June.”

She offered no explanation.

Mara sat.

For several minutes they watched gulls walk around a stranded buoy. One pecked experimentally at a length of rope.

“Do you live here?” Mara asked.

“Forty years.”

“It’s lovely.”

“It can be.”

Mara reached for her phone.

June glanced at it without comment. Mara put it back.

“I’ve brought pears.”

“How thoughtful.”

“They gave them to me.”

“Still thoughtful to bring them.”

June produced a pocketknife and cut one into quarters.

Mara watched the blade move.

June handed her a piece.

They ate without speaking. The pear was harder than it looked. Mara put her remaining quarter on the paper bag and rested it on her knee.

“My husband died in March,” June said.

“I’m sorry.”

“He used to sit here when the tide came in. Not every day. Often enough that people thought he was eccentric.”

“What did he like about it?”

“He said he could see things changing here. That helped him when he was having a bad week.”

A small wave broke far out on the sand.

June folded the knife.

“I tried coming alone. The first time, I lasted ten minutes. The second time, twenty.”

“How long have you been here today?”

“Since half past eleven.”

Mara looked at her watch.

It was nearly one.

“Did you always come together?”

“No. Usually he came by himself. I preferred swimming, or walking. I used to leave him sitting here and meet him afterward for lunch.”

June adjusted the collar of her coat.

“I don’t want you to think I’m trying to pretend you’re him.”

“I didn’t.”

“Good.”

A dog raced through a shallow channel, throwing up silver water. Its owner called it back with diminishing confidence.

Mara began to tell June about the department, then stopped.

June noticed.

“Yes,” she said. “I know where you came from.”

“How did you find it?”

“I lost an afternoon in a hospital waiting room. They helped me retrieve it.”

“Why would you want it?”

“My daughter was there. We had quite a good talk before the doctor came.”

Mara looked toward the advancing water.

“I’m trying to get one back with my father.”

June nodded.

“Was it a happy one?”

“I think so. I hardly remember it.”

“Then you’ll have something to look forward to.”

The tide reached the stranded buoy.

It lifted once, settled, then lifted again. The rope loosened and began moving in the water.

Mara felt the familiar impulse to leave. She had been sitting for more than an hour. She could imagine the report waiting on her laptop, the laundry in its basket, Monday morning arriving before she had prepared for it.

She shifted in the chair.

June was watching the buoy.

Mara stayed.

After a while June told her about a neighbor who fed every cat in the village except her own, because her own was on a special diet. Mara told June about a colleague who used the phrase *going forward* even when discussing a broken office printer.

They laughed.

Then they fell quiet again.

The water erased a child’s sand fort, entered the channels, and gathered around a rock Mara had thought was part of the beach. A ferry appeared on the horizon.

June ate the last piece of pear.

“I think that will do,” she said.

They folded the chairs. Mara carried both up the steps to the promenade.

At the bus stop, June took her hand.

“Thank you for staying.”

“I’m glad I came.”

She was surprised to discover that this was true.

Mara returned to the department the following Wednesday.

She had begun the report on Sunday evening. It was less polished than she had intended, but no one appeared to notice. The laundry had dried across the backs of chairs.

Mrs. Bell recognized her.

“How was the sea?”

“Cold. June said she might go again next week.”

“Good.”

“Will I forget that afternoon?”

“I couldn’t say.”

“I’d like not to.”

Mrs. Bell led her to a small room containing the orchard box and a single chair.

“What happens when I open it?”

“You’ll be there.”

“Can I change anything?”

“You may attend to it differently. The events themselves are already settled.”

Mara sat down.

She held the folded afternoon in both hands.

The room smelled briefly of oranges. Then the walls receded.

She was twenty-six.

Her father sat opposite her at a wooden table, cutting a pear with his old penknife. His repaired cuff rested against the plate. Behind him, leaves stirred in a breeze she could feel against her cheek.

Her phone lay beside her hand.

She remembered it now. She had been waiting for a message about a job.

She turned it face down.

Her father glanced up.

“These are better if you don’t hurry them.”

“I know,” she said.

He passed her a slice.

For a while they ate. A wasp hovered over the plate and he moved it gently away with the back of his hand.

“Your grandmother wants to know whether you’re staying for supper.”

“I can.”

“She’ll be pleased.”

He began telling her about a branch that had come down during a storm. Mara listened closely. She asked which tree. He pointed, then told her about climbing it when he was a boy.

She wanted to tell him what lay ahead. She wanted to ask questions she had not thought of until years after his death.

Instead she let him finish.

Then she said, “Tell me another.”

He smiled, a little puzzled, and did.

The afternoon lasted until the light thinned and her grandmother called from the house.

When Mara returned to the chair, the box was empty.

She remained there for some time before finding Mrs. Bell.

“Can I come back?”

“If you lose something.”

“What if I don’t?”

“Then I hope you have a pleasant afternoon.”

Outside, it was Wednesday. A delivery driver was eating lunch in his van. Two schoolchildren were arguing over an umbrella. Mara stood on the pavement and watched a woman carefully steer a pram around a puddle.

Her meeting began in twenty minutes.

She went to it.

But on Friday she bought pears, and on Saturday she took them to her sister’s house. They sat at the kitchen table while her nephew built something complicated on the floor.

Mara put her phone in her coat pocket.

Her sister asked whether she had much time.

“Yes,” Mara said, and reached for a plate.

samples.result:
# The Museum of Almost Nothing

The museum occupied the ground floor of a building that had once been a bank. You could tell by the doors, which were too heavy for anything as harmless as a museum, and by the marble counter where a teller had probably spent forty years sliding money toward people who immediately wished they had more. Above the entrance, someone had mounted brass letters spelling THE MUSEUM OF ALMOST NOTHING. The word ALMOST was slightly crooked. The curator insisted this was intentional, though nobody believed him.

Mara first entered because it was raining. She had missed a tram, stepped into a puddle, and discovered that the job interview she was going to had been canceled twelve minutes earlier. The message on her phone said the company was moving in another direction. It did not specify which direction, but apparently it was one without her. She stood dripping onto the museum’s tiled floor while an elderly man behind the counter looked up from repairing a cardboard box with blue thread.

“Admission is free,” he said. “But you have to choose something before you leave.”

“Choose something to buy?”

“Choose something to notice.”

This seemed like the sort of answer people gave when they had stopped worrying about rent. Mara considered leaving, but the rain had become theatrical. She walked into the exhibition room. It contained eleven glass cases, three chairs, a coat stand, and a window overlooking a brick wall. In the first case lay a small gray stone. Its label read: STONE FOUND IN A SHOE AFTER A LONG WALK. Beneath that, in smaller letters: The walk is no longer remembered.

The second case held an envelope that had never been sealed. The third contained a wooden button, a length of green string, and a key identified only as NO LONGER REQUIRED. There was a shopping list with everything crossed out except pears. A cracked saucer. A matchbox containing no matches. Mara moved from case to case with the growing suspicion that she had entered either a joke or the private headquarters of someone’s grief. Finally she stopped before a glass shelf holding a folded paper bird.

“Who made this?” she asked.

“A boy waiting for his mother to finish work,” the man said. He had followed her at a distance, carrying his box. “He made seven. That was the only one that remained airborne.”

“Airborne?”

“For three seconds.”

“And that gets it into a museum?”

“Three seconds is longer than some things get.”

His name was Elias. He offered her tea in a mug with a faded picture of a lighthouse. She accepted because her socks were wet and because nobody had offered her anything uncomplicated in several months.

Elias had been curator for twenty-eight years. Before that he had repaired watches, and before that he had done something involving freight trains which he declined to explain because, he said, the explanation made it sound more interesting than it had been. He received no salary from the museum. A small trust paid the rent and electricity. Visitors left coins in a bowl, though the bowl was labeled FOR THE ROOF, and the museum had no access to its roof. Mara asked whether this was misleading.

“The building has a roof,” he said. “I feel we benefit.”

She laughed despite herself. It was the first laugh of the day that had not required some preliminary work. Elias asked what she did, and she told him she was between jobs. She had previously arranged schedules for a company that delivered office furniture. Before that she had answered complaints about subscriptions. She was good at managing things nobody noticed unless they went wrong. Elias nodded as though she had named a rare and useful profession.

“Would you like a temporary job?”

“Doing what?”

“Helping me decide what belongs here.”

He needed to close the museum for a week in October while he went to see his sister. Mara would open the doors, make tea, keep the donation bowl from disappearing, and accept objects brought by visitors. Nothing larger than a suitcase. Nothing alive. Nothing stolen, unless it had been stolen so long ago that restitution had become impractical. She agreed before asking the pay, which was unlike her. When he told her, she nearly withdrew. Then he added that she could bring a chair of her own.

During training, Elias explained that significance was not the same as importance. Important objects usually arrived with certificates, security arrangements, and people arguing about insurance. Significant objects tended to turn up wrapped in dish towels. An important object might change the history of a country. A significant one could change the temperature of a room. Mara wrote this down, then crossed it out because it sounded foolish on paper. Elias noticed. “Most true things do,” he said. “Paper is a very demanding audience.”

On her first morning alone, a woman brought in a teaspoon. It was ordinary stainless steel, bent slightly at the tip. The woman said her husband had used it to tap the side of his cup when he wanted more hot water. He had died nine years earlier. She had kept the spoon because she liked it, not because she believed it contained him. Now she was moving into a smaller flat, and she wanted someone else to keep it for a while.

Mara asked whether the woman wanted her husband’s name on the label.

“No,” the woman said. “He would have hated that.”

“Then what should it say?”

The woman thought for a moment. “He always asked nicely.”

After she left, Mara placed the spoon on a square of dark cloth. She typed the words, cut out the label, and stood it beside the spoon. The effect was embarrassing and then, without anything visibly changing, not embarrassing at all. She found herself looking at the small bend in the metal.

By Wednesday, she had accepted a bus ticket, a chess pawn, and a packet of seeds whose contents had been replaced with tiny screws. She rejected a television, three boxes of unpaid invoices, and a stuffed fox because its owner had admitted, after questioning, that he simply wanted it gone. A girl of about eight brought a dead battery. “It was in my torch,” she explained. “We used it when the lights went out. My dad made shadows on the ceiling.”

“Do you want to keep it?” Mara asked.

The girl shook her head.

“Will you want it back later?”

“Maybe.”

Mara found a card and wrote TEMPORARY LOAN in large letters. The girl signed her name carefully and asked whether the battery needed food. Mara said no. The girl appeared relieved. Afterward, Mara sat behind the marble counter and looked at the battery lying in its shallow dish. She could hear traffic outside, the pipes knocking in the wall, and somebody upstairs practicing the same five piano notes badly.

On Thursday afternoon, a city official arrived carrying a folder and wearing shoes that had never met uncertainty. His name was Doran. He inspected the room without removing his coat, then asked about annual attendance, educational programming, fire safety, and measurable community value. Mara answered what she could. Attendance was recorded in a notebook. Educational programming consisted mainly of questions. The fire extinguisher had been serviced in March. As for measurable community value, she suggested he might ask the woman whose spoon was in case four.

Doran did not smile. The building belonged to the city, he explained, and its lease was being reviewed. There was interest in turning the ground floor into something with wider public benefit. He mentioned a visitor information center, a digital experience hub, and a flexible commercial space. Mara wondered what an inflexible commercial space would be. Doran left a form for Elias and a deadline for submitting evidence that the museum deserved to remain. He was courteous throughout, which somehow made the visit harder.

That evening, Mara called Elias. He listened without interrupting while his sister could be heard in the background asking where he had put the good scissors. When Mara finished, he said the review had happened before, though never quite so formally.

“What did you do last time?”

“Made tea for the people who came.”

“That’s not a strategy.”

“No.”

“Do you want to keep the museum?”

He was quiet long enough that she checked whether the call had dropped. Then he said, “Yes. I think I do.”

She spent Friday going through the attendance books. Some years had careful totals. Others had sketches, recipes, or entries such as THREE PEOPLE, ONE DOG, DOG UNINTERESTED. There were letters from visitors thanking Elias, but almost none explained precisely what they were thanking him for. A man wrote that he had stayed forty minutes and was glad he had. A woman enclosed a photograph of a doorway. Someone had sent a postcard consisting entirely of the words IT WAS GOOD TO SIT DOWN.

Mara knew how to arrange evidence. She had done it for managers who wanted late deliveries to look less late and customer complaints to appear unusually isolated. She opened a spreadsheet and entered attendance figures, donations, loans, opening hours. She estimated the cost per visit and immediately wished she had not. Then she made a second document listing schools, community groups, and local businesses that might be willing to say the museum was useful. There were no schools. One community group had visited accidentally.

On Saturday, she put a sign in the window: THE MUSEUM MAY CLOSE. PLEASE TELL US WHAT, IF ANYTHING, WOULD BE LOST. Elias, back from his sister’s house, read it twice. He said he disliked the word “may,” but could not suggest a better one. By lunchtime, eleven people had come in. Two were annoyed about the possible closure. Three had never noticed the museum before. One asked whether the glass cases would be for sale. The others stayed to look.

Over the next week, the counter filled with notes. Some were sentimental. Some were angry. One proposed a café, another a children’s workshop, and a third suggested that Elias improve the lighting before asking the city for anything. Mara kept that one. A nurse wrote that she sometimes came after a night shift because nobody required her to be cheerful. A teenager said it was the only place in town where being alone did not feel conspicuous. Several visitors admitted they had come just once.

The public hearing took place in a room above the library. Doran sat beside two council members and a woman from the property department. Mara had brought the spreadsheet, a folder of letters, and photographs of every object in the museum. Elias wore a suit that fit him badly and carried nothing. The first speaker described the proposed digital experience hub. It would offer interactive local history displays, visitor services, and opportunities for partnership. The presentation had attractive colors and no visible uncertainties.

When Mara stood up, she realized she could not remember the opening sentence she had rehearsed. She looked at her notes, found it, and decided not to use it. Instead, she gave the attendance figures. They were modest. She explained the running costs. Those were modest too. Then she read the nurse’s letter and the teenager’s note. She described the girl who had lent them a battery and had returned twice to check on it. She showed a photograph of the spoon.

One council member asked whether a selection of the objects could simply be displayed in the new hub. Mara said perhaps they could. She had thought about this and knew it was possible. But someone would still have to listen when people brought things in, decide what to write beside them, and remember which child wanted something back. The display cases were not the expensive part. Doran asked whether she was proposing a funded staff position. She looked at Elias, then answered yes.

Outside, Elias thanked her. He did not say she had saved the museum. Neither of them knew what would happen, and Mara was grateful not to have to pretend otherwise. They walked back through streets glossy with recent rain. At the corner, Elias stopped to retie a shoelace. Mara waited beside a shop window displaying kitchen appliances. For the first time, she wondered how many people had brought him objects he had refused, and how carefully he had managed those refusals.

The decision arrived three weeks later. The museum could stay for eighteen months under a revised lease. There would be a small grant for staffing, provided it extended its opening hours and submitted quarterly reports. The lighting also needed improvement. Mara read the letter aloud behind the counter while Elias cleaned the lighthouse mug. He seemed pleased by the reports, which surprised her until he asked whether she would be willing to write them. She said she would, if she could choose the chair.

Nothing dramatic happened after that. Attendance rose briefly, then settled. Mara took another part-time job and spent three days a week at the museum. Elias began going home earlier. They replaced two bulbs and bought a kettle that switched itself off. The girl reclaimed her battery because she wanted to put it in a box with other things from that year. They returned it without a ceremony. Mara liked the empty space it left, though she filled it the following morning.

One afternoon, a young man brought in a strip of wallpaper from his childhood bedroom. While Mara wrote down his story, Elias struggled with the printer, which had swallowed a label. The kettle clicked off. Rain began against the window. The young man stopped talking and looked around, apparently reconsidering the whole enterprise. Mara waited. At last he asked whether his scrap of paper was too ordinary. She glanced at the cases, then back at him. “No,” she said. “But tell me about the room.”

# The Museum of Unfinished Things

The museum stood between a locksmith and a bakery on a street that most maps had stopped naming. Its sign was small enough to miss: THE MUSEUM OF UNFINISHED THINGS, painted in blue letters that grew progressively fainter toward the end. Whether this was an artistic decision or a problem with the painter’s supply of paint, I never learned. I arrived on a Thursday carrying a wooden bird in a shoebox. My father had carved its body twenty-three years earlier. He had meant to add wings. Instead, he developed an interest in astronomy, then tomatoes, then silence.

The woman at the admission desk was repairing a cardigan with green thread. The cardigan was purple.

“Is that a donation?” she asked.

“I don’t know.”

“That’s how most of them begin.”

She set down the needle and took the box from me with the care generally reserved for injured animals. Inside, the bird lay on a bed of old receipts. Its body was smooth except around the shoulders, where my father had left two rough knobs of wood. There were pencil marks indicating the future arrangement of feathers. One eye had been drilled. The other remained a dot.

“Lovely,” she said.

“It isn’t finished.”

“No,” she said. “I can see that.”

***

I had found the bird while clearing my father’s house. There were four boxes labeled MISCELLANEOUS, three labeled IMPORTANT, and one labeled DO NOT THROW AWAY, which contained instruction manuals for appliances he no longer owned. The bird was in a kitchen drawer beneath rubber bands, expired coupons, and a small screwdriver with a red handle. I recognized it immediately, though I had not thought about it in years. When I was eight, he had promised it would perch on my windowsill. Every morning, I would wake and discover what kind of bird he had decided it was.

At first, he said it might be a kingfisher. Then he considered a swallow. He had a book of birds propped open beside his workbench, and the pages acquired thumbprints of sawdust and oil. I watched him carve on winter evenings while the kitchen radio announced distant weather. He would hold the unfinished shape against the light and turn it slightly, as though a bird were hidden inside and he was trying to find the angle from which it could escape. Eventually, he placed it in the drawer. I assumed this was temporary. Children have no reason to distrust that word.

***

The woman introduced herself as Miriam. She gave me a paper ticket with no number on it.

“Do you charge admission?” I asked.

“Not today.”

“What happens today?”

“People come in.”

The first gallery contained unfinished sentences. They were displayed in frames, on scraps of paper, along the edges of napkins. Some had been abandoned accidentally. Others had stopped at places where the writer could not bear to continue. A letter began, *I have been meaning to tell you why I left.* Below it, the page was blank. Nearby, a grocery list ended after *bread, onions, something for*. That one troubled me more.

“Why keep a grocery list?” I asked.

“Someone had a use for the words when they wrote them,” Miriam said.

I wondered whether there was a category of object too ordinary for the museum. Miriam considered the question seriously.

“We once received half a peeled orange.”

“What did you do with it?”

“Composted it. We’re a museum, not a miracle.”

There were rules, then. I found that reassuring. The building did not preserve everything indiscriminately. It had made choices.

I looked again at the grocery list. The handwriting leaned forward with impatient energy. Whoever wrote it had probably remembered what they wanted and simply gone to the shop. I hoped so.

***

In the next room stood a staircase that rose six steps and stopped. A brass plaque read: *Constructed by Elias Venn, carpenter, for a house never built. Pine. 1974–1976.* The steps were polished in the middle, though they had apparently never led anywhere. Beside them hung a photograph of a field under snow. A square of stakes marked the intended foundation. I imagined a couple visiting that field, discussing windows, bedrooms, where the light would fall in the afternoon. At some point the stakes must have come out. The carpenter had kept the staircase.

“Can people climb it?”

“They do.”

I climbed to the sixth step. From there, I could see into a neighboring gallery, where a long table held chessboards with games suspended midway through. Some positions were tense and crowded. Others looked almost peaceful. A white king stood alone beside a black rook. The players’ names were written on cards, along with the date of the last move. One game had paused in 1911. Another had stopped the previous Tuesday.

“Do you know who was going to win?” I called down.

“In a few cases. We don’t put that on the labels.”

***

Miriam led me through a room of garments missing sleeves, books without endings, and an enormous quilt composed of seven completed squares and thirty-two pinned arrangements of fabric. A sign requested that visitors not straighten the pins. Near the quilt, a glass case held a jar labeled STARTER. Inside was a grayish residue.

“Bread?” I asked.

“Yes. Someone became ambitious during a difficult winter.”

“Did they ever bake anything?”

“Three loaves. They were disappointed in all three.”

The museum was quieter than I expected. There were no explanatory videos, no recordings of machinery or voices. From the bakery next door came the dull sound of metal trays being stacked. Once, I heard a bus kneel at the curb outside. It seemed possible to spend an afternoon here listening to things being accomplished elsewhere.

I thought of my father’s house again. I had been sorting it into categories: sell, keep, donate, discard. The work required speed. A person could become trapped inside every teaspoon if they allowed themselves to wonder who had last held it. I had learned to make decisions quickly and sometimes cruelly.

***

“Was your father a woodworker?” Miriam asked.

“Occasionally.”

“Did he make other birds?”

“No.”

She nodded, without seeming disappointed.

“He made shelves,” I added. “A spice rack. A little gate for the garden.”

“Useful things.”

“Mostly.”

The gate had worked for nearly twenty years. It sagged in wet weather, and its latch had to be lifted rather than turned, but it kept the dog out of the vegetable beds. I had sold the house without thinking to remove it. Now the gate belonged to someone who might replace it by summer. I found myself wanting to explain its latch to them.

My father’s death had not been sudden, but the administrative consequences had. For months, we had occupied the slow time of illness: appointments, medication schedules, afternoons measured by naps. Then he died, and the world immediately requested certificates, signatures, cancellations. His life, which had taken seventy-nine years to accumulate, became a series of tasks I could complete before lunch. I was efficient. People praised me for it. Only the bird resisted. I could not decide whether it was a toy, a piece of wood, an artwork, or evidence of a promise. The shoebox kept moving from one pile to another.

***

We entered a narrow room containing a single violin. It had a neck, a back, and one carefully shaped side. Its front lay separately on a velvet pad. The maker had penciled measurements on the pale wood, some crossed out, some circled.

“This is our most frequently misunderstood exhibit,” Miriam said.

“Why?”

“People ask whether we can finish it.”

“Could you?”

“Probably. We know a luthier.”

“Then why don’t you?”

“We would have to make decisions the maker hadn’t made. And it belongs to his daughter.”

She pointed to the card. *Loaned by Ruth Bell, who remembers being instructed not to touch the wood because it was still deciding what it wanted to sound like.*

“Her father talked that way,” Miriam said. “According to Ruth, he was usually less poetic. He also left her a garage full of broken lawnmowers.”

I laughed, and she looked pleased.

***

There were visitors elsewhere in the building. An elderly man sat before an unfinished oil painting of a harbor. All the boats were present, but the water beneath them had only been sketched. A teenager photographed a page of music. In an alcove, a woman held a child on her lap while they examined a dollhouse with no roof. The child wanted to know whether rain could get inside.

“It’s indoors,” the woman said.

“But if it went outdoors?”

“Then yes.”

“Would they get wet?”

“There aren’t any people in it.”

The child leaned closer to check.

I remembered sitting on the floor beside my father’s workbench, making roads in the sawdust with one finger. I had not cared whether the bird resembled a kingfisher or a swallow. I wanted him to finish so we could carry it upstairs together. But I also liked those evenings in the kitchen, and I had forgotten that part.

***

“Where would you put it?” I asked Miriam.

“The bird?”

“Yes.”

“If you donate it, we’d probably start in the small objects room. We haven’t had a carving for a while.”

“You make it sound as though it might have preferences.”

“I make that mistake sometimes.”

She opened a door marked STAFF ONLY. Inside were shelves, a kettle, and two desks. This ordinary room relieved me more than any exhibit. There were invoices here. A leaking ceiling had left a brown stain over the filing cabinet. Someone had pinned up a calendar and neglected to turn it from March to April. Even a museum of incompletion needed a plumber.

***

Miriam poured tea into two mugs that did not match. She asked whether I knew when my father had stopped carving the bird.

“Not exactly. I remember noticing it wasn’t on the bench anymore.”

“Did you ask him about it?”

“Probably.”

“What did he say?”

“I can’t remember.”

This bothered me. I had brought the object, but not the information that would make it suitable for a label. There should have been a reason: a shortage of wood, a damaged tool, some private discouragement. I could offer none.

“He took up a lot of hobbies,” I said. “Sometimes he went back to them.”

“Then we can write that.”

I looked at the shoebox between us.

***

“Could I finish it?” I asked.

“Do you know how?”

“No.”

“You could learn.”

It was a practical answer, almost disappointingly so. I imagined buying tools, choosing wood for the wings, consulting videos made by cheerful men in immaculate workshops. I imagined ruining one wing, improving the second, discovering that neither fitted the body. I could see myself putting the whole thing in a drawer.

“What if I make it worse?”

“That’s a possibility.”

“You’re supposed to discourage that.”

“I don’t know you well enough to say whether you should carve a bird.”

I drank my tea. It was too hot. Miriam waited while I put the mug down.

***

She brought out a ledger so thick that its spine had been repaired with cloth. Each donation had a page. There were descriptions, names, dimensions, histories. Some histories occupied several pages. Others were one sentence: *Found in grandmother’s shed. Nobody knows.*

“We keep the uncertainty,” Miriam said. “People sometimes give us three different explanations in the same conversation. We write them down.”

She showed me an entry for a knitted sock. Its owner had said she abandoned it after falling in love, then corrected herself: she had stopped because the pattern was difficult. Later, she telephoned to report that both statements were true.

“Did she make the other sock?”

“No. We asked.”

***

I thought about taking the bird home and setting it on my windowsill exactly as it was. I had been avoiding that possibility because it felt like agreeing that my father would never finish it. The house sale, the certificates, even the funeral had somehow left a little room for error. The bird was more exacting. Its bare shoulders waited for two wings.

Miriam turned the ledger toward me.

“You don’t have to decide today. People bring things in and take them away again.”

“How often?”

“Often enough that we keep spare boxes.”

For the first time since entering the museum, I felt that I could leave.

***

We returned through a gallery I had not noticed before. It contained unfinished maps. One depicted a coastline with meticulous bays and promontories, then dissolved into faint pencil marks. Another mapped a city with streets named after flowers. The streets grew increasingly tangled toward the eastern edge, where the cartographer had apparently lost patience and written HERE BE SHOPS. My favorite was a child’s map of a bedroom. It marked the bed, the wardrobe, the window, and a region under the bed labeled UNKNOWN. There was a small expedition route leading toward it. The route stopped halfway.

I told Miriam my father had bought a telescope.

“Did he use it?”

“For a while. He tried to show me Saturn, but I couldn’t see anything.”

“Were you disappointed?”

“He was. I said I could see it.”

“Could you?”

“No. I was looking at a streetlamp.”

She smiled, but did not ask me what the telescope meant. I was grateful.

***

At the desk, Miriam returned the bird to its shoebox. She folded a sheet of tissue paper around it, replacing the receipts.

“We can keep those too,” she said.

“No, that’s all right.”

One receipt was from a hardware store that had closed twelve years earlier. Another recorded the purchase of milk, apples, and batteries. I put them in my coat pocket anyway.

Outside, the baker was turning the sign in his window from OPEN to CLOSED, though warm air still escaped each time the door moved. A woman hurried past carrying flowers wrapped in newspaper. For a moment, I stood without choosing a direction.

***

I took the bus home. The shoebox occupied the seat beside me until the bus became crowded, and then I held it on my lap. At a red light, I lifted the lid. The bird’s single drilled eye seemed larger in the afternoon light. A tiny curl of wood remained lodged in the hole. I removed it with my fingernail and placed it in the box.

At home, I put the bird on the kitchen table. I did not search for carving lessons. I did not place it on the windowsill. Instead, I washed the dishes that had been waiting since morning.

***

The following Sunday, I bought a small sheet of sandpaper from the hardware shop near my flat. I spent a long time choosing it, though there were only three suitable kinds. Back home, I spread newspaper over the table and sanded the roughest edge beneath the bird’s body. It had always caught against the receipts, and I wanted it to sit without wobbling.

After a few minutes, I stopped. The pale patch I had made was conspicuous. I rubbed it with my thumb, then set the bird upright.

It stood slightly crooked, but it stood.

I left the wings alone.

# The Department of Unfinished Things

On the oldest map of the city, the Department of Unfinished Things appeared as a small blue rectangle between the municipal baths and a street that no longer existed. On newer maps it did not appear at all. Nevertheless, every morning at eight thirty, Mara unlocked its front door, shook the rain from her umbrella, and went inside. The building smelled of pencil shavings, wet wool, and the particular dust that gathers inside closed pianos. There were seven floors, although only six could be reached by the stairs. Nobody had discovered how to reach the seventh. This was considered appropriate.

Mara worked in Intake. Her job was to receive whatever people had begun and could not finish, determine whether it was still alive, and assign it a shelf. Most things arrived in ordinary containers: cardboard boxes, envelopes, biscuit tins. Novels came tied with string. Apologies arrived in little bottles, cloudy and warm. Unfulfilled promises were heavier than they looked and had to be handled with both hands. Once, a woman brought in a language she had invented with her sister when they were children. It escaped its jar and hid behind the radiator, whispering names for colors nobody else could see.

There were rules. An unfinished thing had to be surrendered voluntarily. It could not be stolen from someone’s desk or removed from a drawer by a helpful spouse. The department accepted abandoned ambitions but not ordinary laziness, though distinguishing between the two sometimes required a committee. It did not accept living children, unfinished meals, or arguments that had merely paused for breath. Most importantly, it did not promise completion. This was printed on the receipt in large, reassuring letters. People often looked disappointed when Mara explained it. They had imagined a government office that could finally do something useful.

On a Tuesday in November, a boy came carrying a lighthouse.

It was no bigger than a milk jug, built from driftwood, white paint, and the brass workings of an alarm clock. He held it against his chest with such care that Mara assumed it contained something breakable.

“What’s unfinished?” she asked.

“The light,” he said.

She waited.

“My grandfather said we’d put it in last. Everything else works.”

He turned a tiny handle. Somewhere inside the tower, gears clicked. A little door opened at the base, and a wooden keeper stepped out with a lantern that did not shine.

Mara took out the green form, the one for projects interrupted by death. She had learned not to ask certain questions. Grief disliked being made to repeat itself for administrative purposes.

“What’s your name?”

“Eli.”

“And your grandfather’s?”

The boy gave it. Mara wrote carefully.

“You can leave it here,” she said. “Or you can take it home and decide later. There isn’t a deadline.”

Eli looked around at the shelves behind her. A paper moon hung above a half-knitted sleeve. Beneath the counter, something tapped patiently from inside a shoebox.

“Will you finish it?”

“No,” she said. “We’ll keep it safe.”

“What’s the difference?”

Mara could have recited the department’s official answer. Instead, she said, “Sometimes keeping something safe gives a person enough time to know what they want to do with it.”

The boy considered this. Then he placed the lighthouse on the counter.

“He said the lamp needed to be strong enough to bring somebody home.”

Mara issued the receipt and watched him leave. Afterward, she carried the lighthouse to the third floor, where objects associated with the sea were stored. There were unfinished boats, maps ending in blank water, and a sailor’s letter that had been waiting eighty-one years for its final sentence. She put the lighthouse beside a ship in a bottle whose stern remained outside the glass. For a moment, the little wooden keeper seemed to turn his head toward her.

That evening, Mara did something she had not done in nine years. She opened the bottom drawer of her own desk.

Inside was a brown envelope, a train ticket, and a photograph of her father standing in front of a house without a roof.

The house had been his project. He had bought a narrow plot outside the city, near the marshes, and spent weekends building what he called their summer place, although they had never owned a winter place worth mentioning. He was a bus mechanic with enormous hands. When he measured timber, he held the pencil between two fingers as delicately as a conductor holding a baton.

“We’ll see the sky from here,” he used to tell her, standing where the kitchen would be.

As a child, Mara loved the unfinished house. Its rooms were suggestions. You could walk through walls that would later stop you. Rain pooled in the future hallway, and swallows flew through the space intended for her bedroom. Her father would point to a patch of air and say, “Window,” and for an instant she could see it: curtains, afternoon light, a glass of water on a sill. Then the vision vanished, leaving posts, nails, and the smell of cut wood.

When she was nineteen, he asked her to spend one Saturday helping him lift the roof beams. She had an exam on Monday and a boyfriend who was leaving for another city. She told him she could not.

He said, “There’ll be other Saturdays.”

There were three.

After his funeral, the house became a burden too shapeless to carry and too substantial to ignore. Mara paid the taxes, answered occasional letters from the council, and never visited. The brown envelope contained the plans. The train ticket was unused. She had brought both to work, intending to surrender them, but had never filled out the form. It embarrassed her to be custodian of so many abandoned things while unable to place her own on a shelf. She closed the drawer.

The next morning, the department received an order to empty the building.

It arrived in a yellow envelope marked URGENT, accompanied by a man whose shoes squeaked with newness. His name was Mr. Vale, and he represented the Office of Practical Renewal. The city needed storage for emergency equipment. A survey had identified this building as underused. Its contents were to be catalogued, assessed, and disposed of within thirty days.

“Disposed of how?” Mara asked.

“According to category.”

“These things don’t have those kinds of categories.”

Mr. Vale consulted a tablet.

“Combustible. Recyclable. Hazardous. Other.”

From somewhere upstairs came a prolonged, offended chord.

Mr. Vale looked at the ceiling.

“Is someone playing an instrument?”

“Not yet,” Mara said.

The department’s director, Mrs. Saye, had worked there for forty-three years. She wore a silver brooch shaped like a closed eye and carried keys to cupboards that had been demolished before Mara was born. When she read the order, she sat very still.

“Perhaps we can appeal,” Mara said.

“We can.”

“Will that work?”

“Probably not.”

For the first time, Mara noticed how old her director’s hands were.

“What happens if we burn them?”

Mrs. Saye looked toward the shelves.

“Some will burn. Some will not.”

“And the ones that don’t?”

“They’ll have nowhere to go.”

The staff began making an inventory. There were six of them, not counting the porter, who insisted he had retired fifteen years earlier but continued to arrive because no one else knew how to persuade the lift to work. They found a wedding dress with one sleeve, seventeen nearly identical inventions for peeling oranges, a treaty never signed, and a box labelled THE REST OF THE SUMMER. When opened, it released the smell of hot pavement and caused everyone nearby to remember a different childhood. Mr. Vale classified it as mixed materials. Mara put it aside.

On the fifth floor, behind a cupboard of unfinished jokes, she discovered a ledger bound in green cloth. It recorded withdrawals. People had returned for their things more often than she realized. A man reclaimed a violin concerto after twenty-six years. A woman retrieved an application to medical school at sixty-eight. Someone collected an apology and brought the empty bottle back the following afternoon. Others took things away only to return them later, changed or smaller or no closer to completion. In the margins, former clerks had written brief remarks: *Needed another winter.* *Found a collaborator.* *Decided against it.* *Kept the useful pages.*

Mara read until the winter light faded from the windows.

The next day, she asked Mrs. Saye for permission to contact the owners.

“All of them?”

“As many as we can.”

“The records are incomplete.”

“So is everything else.”

Mrs. Saye smiled, then pulled a telephone directory from beneath her desk.

They wrote letters. They made calls. They followed addresses through demolished neighborhoods and changed surnames. A clerk named Tomas persuaded the local radio station to broadcast an announcement. It sounded ridiculous when read between the weather and a report on roadworks: *If you have deposited an unfinished thing with the municipal department, please contact us urgently.* Nevertheless, the telephone began ringing before the bulletin ended. Some callers thought it was a joke. Others had forgotten what they had left. One woman started crying as soon as Mara answered.

For a week, hardly anyone came. Then the waiting room filled.

People arrived carrying receipts softened by years of handling, or nothing at all except a memory of what they had surrendered. A retired baker reclaimed a book of drawings. Two brothers came for a conversation they had abandoned after an argument about their mother’s care. They took it outside, where it unfolded between them like a gray scarf. A woman collected the language she had invented with her sister. The radiator went quiet. In the lobby, she opened the jar and spoke a word that made every blue object in the room briefly smell of rain.

Not everyone took their things.

Some stood before their boxes for a long time, then shook their heads.

“I’m not that person anymore,” one man said, looking at the model railway he had once intended to build across an entire attic.

Mara asked whether he wanted to keep any part of it. He chose a small red station and put it in his coat pocket. Another woman, who had left a stack of handwritten poems, asked permission to read them before deciding. She spent the afternoon by the window. At closing time, she kept three and asked Mara to recycle the rest.

Eli returned on the seventeenth day.

Mara brought down the lighthouse. The boy inspected it, turning the little handle and watching the keeper emerge.

“Are you really closing?”

“It looks that way.”

He rubbed a thumb over a patch of chipped paint.

“I don’t know how to make the light.”

“We could find someone who does.”

“But then they’d finish it. Not him.”

Mara sat beside him on the waiting-room bench. Beyond the window, people hurried through a cold rain.

“Yes,” she said.

For a while they listened to the gears slowing inside the tower.

Then Eli asked, “Could I leave the lamp part unfinished and finish something else?”

“What else?”

“The keeper needs a dog.”

Mara found him a piece of scrap wood.

News of the closure spread. People who had never deposited anything came to see the shelves. At first Mara resented the visitors, who treated the department as an exhibition of charming failures. Then a carpenter offered to repair damaged boxes. An electrician repaired the lobby lights and asked whether any of the objects needed wiring. A schoolteacher brought students to help sort old addresses. Several visitors found things they wanted to try, though Mara insisted on obtaining the owners’ permission wherever possible. The orange-peeling inventions attracted an unexpectedly fierce discussion.

Mr. Vale returned with revised disposal instructions and found the lobby full of people sharing tools.

“This is not in the plan,” he said.

“No,” Mara agreed.

He watched an elderly woman explain a knitting pattern to a teenage boy. Beside them, the inventor of three orange peelers was taking apart the fourth, which belonged to somebody else.

“Who’s responsible if something gets damaged?”

“We’re recording every transfer.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

Mara handed him a clipboard. It contained consent forms, contact details, and a list of volunteers. He read it twice, looking disappointed to find the headings sensible.

That night, Mara took the train ticket from her drawer. It had expired years earlier, so she bought another.

The house stood beyond a field of reeds, smaller than she remembered. Rain had darkened the timber. Part of the back wall had collapsed, and weeds grew through the kitchen floor. She stepped inside carefully. There was the place where her father had promised a window. There was the doorway where she had once measured herself against a chalk mark. Above her, the missing roof exposed a pale winter sky. She waited for some strong feeling to tell her what to do. Instead, she noticed that the remaining floorboards were slippery and that a blackbird had nested in the chimney.

She spent an hour walking around the house. Then she sat on the foundation wall and unfolded her father’s plans. His handwriting crowded the margins: prices, measurements, reminders to borrow tools. Beside the kitchen window he had written, *Mara says wider.* She did not remember saying it. She remembered arguments about money, the smell of his work jacket, the embarrassing jokes he told her friends. Here was evidence of an ordinary afternoon she had lost: herself pointing, him listening, a pencil moving across paper. She folded the plans carefully and went home.

The following week, she telephoned a builder. The house, he said after inspecting it, could be made safe, but completing the original design would cost more than she could afford. Mara asked what could be kept. He showed her which timbers were sound and which foundations would hold a smaller structure. Together they drew a single room with broad windows and a covered porch. She disliked it at first. Then she could imagine sitting there. She asked him to leave the chimney intact until the blackbirds had gone.

At the department, Mrs. Saye submitted a proposal. The building would still hold emergency equipment on its ground floor. The upper rooms would become a public workshop and archive, supported by a modest municipal grant and volunteers. Unclaimed objects would be reviewed individually rather than emptied into skips. Mr. Vale objected to several costs, corrected two tables, and quietly supplied a form no one had known they needed. Approval arrived four days before the deadline. The staff celebrated with tea in paper cups because all the proper cups were packed.

Eli finished the dog in February. It was lopsided and had ears too large for its head. The electrician helped him install a small amber bulb in the lighthouse, with a switch concealed beneath the base. When Eli turned the handle, the keeper came out, the dog followed, and the lamp glowed. He watched the sequence several times.

“I think he would have made a better dog,” he said.

“Probably,” Mara said.

Eli laughed. Then he asked to take it home.

That spring, Mara helped paint her smaller house. On the first warm Saturday, she carried a chair onto the porch and sat beneath the finished roof. The marshes stirred beyond the field. She had brought her father’s plans in a protective folder, but left them inside while she drank her tea. There was plenty still to do: a shelf, the garden, a stubborn door. She wrote a short list on the back of an envelope. When the light began to fade, she went indoors, leaving the chair where it was.
