# The Department of Small Repairs

On the morning the city announced it would be removing the benches, Mara found a teaspoon in her shoe. This was not unprecedented. Her apartment had reached the stage of disorder at which objects migrated without explanation, like birds following magnetic fields. Still, the spoon seemed deliberate. It lay bowl-up inside her left boot, holding a single bead of water. She tipped the water into the sink, put the spoon beside the kettle, and went downstairs to argue with someone.

The notice was attached to the nearest bench with three plastic ties. MUNICIPAL SEATING RATIONALIZATION PROGRAM, it said. Beneath this came a diagram showing the bench replaced by a smooth rectangle of pavement. The projected benefits included improved pedestrian flow, reduced maintenance costs, and fewer undesirable gatherings. A person had underlined “undesirable” in blue ink and written WHO? The bench itself held a sleeping delivery rider, two pigeons, and a woman eating an orange with the concentration of a surgeon.

Mara photographed the notice. Then she sat beside the woman, who offered her a segment of orange without asking whether she wanted one. Across the street, a bakery was raising its shutters. The delivery rider woke, checked his phone, and went back to sleep. “They’re taking it away,” Mara said. The woman nodded toward the notice. “They said that last year.” “Did they?” “They took the other one.” She pointed to a rectangle of newer pavement beside the bus stop.

Mara worked in the Department of Small Repairs, which occupied the third floor of a building nobody could find on their first visit. The entrance faced an alley, though the official address belonged to the street. Its sign had faded until it read DEPARTMENT OF SMALL REPAI S. She had submitted a repair request for the sign twice. The second request was returned because the department was not authorized to repair its own signage without approval from Municipal Identity.

Her duties involved things considered too minor for emergency crews and too public for private responsibility: a handrail loose on three steps, a drinking fountain that sprayed sideways, a pedestrian button that worked only when pressed hard. She liked the work. A repair had an agreeable clarity. Before, the gate scraped the ground. After, it opened. Nobody needed a consultation period to establish whether a gate should open, although recently a consultant had suggested one.

Her supervisor, Mr. Venn, was standing beside the office printer, watching it produce blank pages. “It’s printing,” he said when she arrived. “That’s an improvement.” Mara put the photograph of the bench notice in front of him. He examined it and pushed his glasses higher on his nose. “Public Realm Strategy,” he said. “Not us.” “The bench isn’t broken.” “Then it’s definitely not us.” The printer released another page. He caught it before it joined the white heap on the floor.

Mara asked how a perfectly usable bench could be designated for removal. Mr. Venn opened the shared calendar, as if the answer might be scheduled there. The program had been discussed in February. Small Repairs had not attended; the invitation had gone to a defunct mailbox. “You can ask Strategy,” he said. “But don’t take it personally.” He handed her the morning’s assignments: a tilted litter bin, a broken latch, and a complaint about a mysterious clicking sound near the canal.

The litter bin required two bolts. The latch required oil and patience. The clicking sound came from a man feeding dried peas into the spokes of his bicycle. He said it kept sparrows away from his sandwich. Mara asked whether it worked. He looked at the sparrow standing on his knee and admitted the results were mixed. By lunchtime she had completed her official work and found the seating program online. Forty-seven benches were marked for removal. Her bench was number nineteen.

The assessment gave each bench a score based on surface condition, location, observed usage, and maintenance burden. Number nineteen had received a usage score of zero. Mara looked back at the photograph she had taken that morning. Three people were sitting on it. She scrolled to the assessor’s visit: Tuesday, January 16, 6:10 a.m. That had been the morning of freezing rain, when even the buses stopped on the hills. She printed the page, then wrote a polite email requesting another assessment.

The reply arrived almost immediately. Her message had been received and assigned a reference number. Further correspondence should quote that number. At the bottom, in smaller type, she was advised that submission of correspondence did not constitute grounds for delaying implementation. She read this twice, ate the sandwich she had brought from home, and called the number on the website. A recorded voice thanked her for contributing to a more efficient city. Then the call disconnected.

After work she returned to the bench with a notebook. The orange woman was there again, this time holding a pharmacy bag. Her name was Inez. She lived above the locksmith and came down each afternoon because the staircase tired her and the bench made the walk worthwhile. Mara asked whether she could record how long Inez sat there. “Are you charging?” Inez asked. When Mara explained, she agreed, provided Mara did not describe her as elderly. “Write retired,” she said.

For the next four days, Mara spent her lunch breaks and evenings counting people. A schoolboy tied his shoelaces. A cleaner waited for a lift. Two sisters ate chips from separate paper cones and argued about their father’s birthday. A man in a dark suit sat for eight minutes with his face in his hands, then straightened his tie and left. Mara recorded times but not names. Some people wanted to know what she was doing. Others seemed relieved when she did not ask.

On Friday, rain drove her under the bakery awning. The baker came out carrying a tray of rolls that had split crookedly in the oven. He gave her one and asked about the notebook. When she explained, he fetched a chair from inside. “You can watch from here,” he said. His name was Tomas. He claimed not to care about the bench, but he remembered who had sat on it every morning that week. He also supplied coffee after Mara’s thermos ran out.

She sent her count to Public Realm Strategy: one hundred and thirty-two separate uses over sixteen hours of observation. She attached photographs showing the cracked foot of the bench, which she could repair cheaply, and the bus stop beyond it, which had no seating. This time a person answered. An officer named Calder thanked her for the additional information. Unfortunately, usage was only one component of the evaluation framework. Removal remained scheduled for the following Thursday. Mara asked for the other scores.

Calder sent a spreadsheet. The bench’s principal failing was that it did not match the street’s proposed visual scheme. New seating would be installed at the civic square, seven hundred metres away. Mara walked there during lunch. The square had pale stone paving, six young trees tied to stakes, and a fountain that ran on alternate days. The new seats were attractive. She sat on one and watched an office worker carefully arrange a folded jacket between his back and the metal support.

She returned to her office and asked Mr. Venn whether replacing a cracked bench foot required permission from Strategy. “Ordinarily, no,” he said. “But you know it’s coming out.” “Until it comes out, it’s a public asset with a reported defect.” He looked at her for a while, then requested the photograph. The crack was real, and the repair was within their budget. He signed the work order. “No speeches,” he said. “Repair it, photograph it, close the job.”

On Monday morning Mara arrived with a toolbox, a steel brace, and two bags of quick-setting concrete. Her colleague Dev came with her. He had offered to help without asking why she was so interested in this particular bench. They lifted one end, cleaned the damaged foot, and bolted on the brace. Inez watched from the bakery chair. The delivery rider, whose name was Leon, held a spirit level against the seat. By ten, the bench stood squarely for the first time in years.

While the concrete cured, Tomas put a handwritten sign on it: PLEASE DO NOT SIT UNTIL NOON. Someone crossed out NOON and wrote FREE. Someone else added a smile. Mara removed the altered sign and made another. She had no wish to submit a photograph of a repaired public asset apparently advertising free sitting. Dev laughed, but he helped her clean the old paint drips off the slats. Underneath, they found initials, a date, and a shallow groove where somebody had worked patiently with a key.

At noon they took away the barrier. Inez sat first. She tested the bench by shifting her weight, then pronounced it better. Mara photographed the repaired foot and returned to the office to close the job. Before she did, she sent the photograph to Calder, along with the new maintenance cost: forty-three pounds and twenty pence. Calder replied that the repair was appreciated but had no bearing on the removal decision. Mara stared at “appreciated” until Mr. Venn asked whether she was going home.

On Tuesday, Inez brought an envelope containing seven signatures from her building. Tomas had collected twenty-three from customers. Leon sent Mara a message from a rider’s group, where nine people said they used the bench between deliveries. Mara had not asked any of them to do this. She spent the evening putting their comments into one document, keeping the spelling as written. At midnight she removed a paragraph of her own explaining why benches mattered. The comments were more useful.

On Wednesday Calder called. The residents’ submission had been forwarded by two councillors and needed a response. He could meet Mara at the site at three. She asked whether the removal would be paused. He could not promise that. At three he arrived wearing a coat too light for the weather, carrying a folder under one arm. He was younger than Mara expected and looked tired. For a moment they both stood beside the bench, uncertain how to begin without sounding hostile.

Inez settled the matter by asking Calder to sit down. He did. She described the journey from her flat to the pharmacy: thirty-one stairs, a crossing, a stretch without shop doorways where she could rest. The civic square was in the wrong direction. Calder took notes. Leon arrived and explained that the nearest café required a purchase and closed before his last shift. Tomas brought coffee, including one for Calder, who accepted it with both hands. Mara stayed standing. She had already said plenty.

Calder opened his folder. The removal contract covered all forty-seven benches, and changing it would incur a charge. The visual scheme had been approved. There were complaints about late-night noise at several locations. “Here?” Mara asked. He checked. Not here. The assessment had grouped benches by street rather than by site. He looked at the repaired foot, then asked for a copy of the work order. Mara emailed it while he watched. He said he would make a recommendation, but the crew might still arrive tomorrow.

They did, at eight fifteen. Mara was there because she had slept badly and left home early. A flatbed truck stopped beside the curb. Two workers got out and checked a tablet. One laid a socket wrench on the bench while the other photographed it. Mara introduced herself, gave her department, and asked whether they had received a revised instruction. They had not. The older worker, Bell, showed her the screen. Bench nineteen, removal authorized. He was friendly but clearly expected an argument.

Mara called Calder. No answer. She called his office and was transferred twice, eventually reaching someone who said he was in a briefing. Behind her, the bakery shutter rose. Inez appeared at her doorway in slippers, saw the truck, and went back inside for shoes. Bell waited while Mara called Mr. Venn. “I can’t stop their job,” Venn said. “Send me the contract reference.” She did. He told her not to stand in front of the truck. She had not considered it until then.

By eight thirty, seven people had gathered. Nobody shouted. Tomas brought a tray of coffee and asked the crew whether they wanted breakfast. The younger worker accepted; Bell checked his watch. They had another eleven removals to complete. Inez sat on the bench and opened her newspaper. Leon arrived carrying a bicycle wheel that needed replacing. He leaned it against the repaired foot. It was a small, awkward assembly, with no banner and no clear plan beyond making the removal take longer.

At eight forty-two, Bell’s phone rang. He listened, looked at the bench, and asked the caller to repeat the instruction. Then he picked up his wrench. “Leave this one pending review,” he said to his colleague. Mara felt so relieved she almost thanked him for something he had not decided. Instead, she thanked both workers for waiting. Bell drank his coffee standing up. Before getting into the truck, he told Inez she could close her newspaper now. She said she had been reading it.

The review lasted six weeks. During that time Mara learned more about procurement than she had ever wanted to know. Retaining one bench required a revised asset record, a small contract adjustment, and an exception to the visual scheme. Calder asked her department to confirm responsibility for future maintenance. Mr. Venn agreed, then sent Mara a private message: This is not an invitation to adopt all forty-seven. She promised nothing. There were eleven other benches whose usage scores looked suspiciously low.

Bench nineteen stayed. Three others stayed too, after residents challenged their assessments. Twenty-nine were removed, seven were relocated, and seven received another review. Mara could not call the outcome a victory without thinking of the places she had not visited. Nor was it nothing. On the morning the final decision arrived, she took her usual route downstairs and found Inez sharing the bench with a boy whose schoolbag occupied almost as much space as he did. They moved the bag so Mara could sit.

Autumn brought smaller jobs. A door closer needed adjusting at the library. The canal path acquired a loose railing. Someone reported that the repaired bench had a splinter on the backrest. Mara sanded it down and sealed the patch before rain could get into the wood. Leon passed while she worked and stopped to tell her he had found a better delivery route. Tomas tapped on his window to ask whether she wanted coffee. She held up one finger: a minute.

That evening she cleaned her apartment. Under the bed she found two socks, a receipt from the winter, and the missing cap from a jar of cumin. The teaspoon was still beside the kettle. She washed it and put it in the drawer, where it fitted among the others. Then she made tea and sat by the open window. Downstairs, somebody laughed. A bus stopped, lowered itself toward the curb, and waited while a passenger boarded. Mara drank her tea before it cooled.

# The Museum of Unfinished Things

The museum opened on a Tuesday because nobody could agree on a date.

For nearly three years, its trustees had debated whether an institution devoted to unfinished things ought to have an opening ceremony at all. A ceremony implied completion. So did a ribbon, which would have to be cut, producing two finished lengths of ribbon where previously there had been one unfinished obstacle.

Eventually, the caretaker unlocked the front door to let in a plumber, and a woman carrying a wet umbrella followed him inside.

“Are you open?” she asked.

The caretaker considered the puddle forming around her shoes.

“Apparently,” he said.

By noon, there were seven visitors. By Friday, there was a review in the local paper. The reviewer called the museum “a quietly devastating indictment of modern ambition,” although he had stayed only twenty minutes and spent eight of them asking whether the café would serve lunch.

The café never opened.

It became the museum’s most popular exhibit.

Behind its glass doors stood four tables, sixteen chairs, an espresso machine still wrapped in protective plastic, and a chalkboard reading:

**TODAY’S SPECIAL:**

People photographed it constantly.

***

Mara began working there in November.

She was thirty-eight, recently divorced, and qualified for very little that could be explained in a box on an application form. She had once edited technical manuals for agricultural machinery. Before that, she had studied architecture for two years. Before that, she had wanted to restore paintings, but the course required chemistry, and chemistry had seemed at seventeen like a personal insult.

The museum’s vacancy notice asked for someone with “an orderly temperament and a tolerance for ambiguity.”

At the interview, the director asked whether she had ever failed to finish anything important.

“Yes,” Mara said.

He waited.

She waited.

“You don’t wish to elaborate?”

“Not particularly.”

“Excellent,” he said. “Some applicants arrive with photographs.”

The director’s name was Bell. He wore inexpensive suits with beautifully repaired cuffs. His office contained a filing cabinet, a kettle, and an oil painting of a harbor in which the ships were fully rendered but the sea remained a broad brown undercoat.

Mara looked at it during the interview.

“My grandmother’s,” Bell said. “She could never get the water right.”

“Was she a painter?”

“She was a dentist. But she was a very serious dentist.”

He hired Mara to catalogue new acquisitions.

On her first morning, he gave her a pair of cotton gloves and a warning.

“Do not confuse unfinished with unsuccessful. We are not a museum of mistakes.”

“What’s the distinction?”

“If I knew that,” Bell said, “we could simplify our paperwork considerably.”

***

The collection occupied a former municipal library.

Its tall windows admitted a pale, noncommittal light. There were radiators that clicked as if considering an announcement. The reading room had become the main gallery, though the old sign above the door still requested silence.

Mara’s first assignment was a sweater.

It was moss green and knitted for a child, with one sleeve completed and the other extending only three inches from the shoulder. Two needles remained lodged in the wool. A loose strand curled across the tissue paper like a route on a map.

The donor’s form read:

*Begun for my son in 1987. Stopped because he grew.*

Mara entered the dimensions, materials, date, and condition into the catalogue.

Under “Reason for noncompletion,” she typed the donor’s sentence.

Then she deleted it and typed:

*Recipient exceeded anticipated size.*

Then she deleted that too.

By lunchtime, she had catalogued nothing.

Bell found her looking at the sweater.

“First one?”

She nodded.

“It passes,” he said.

“What does?”

“The need to improve the explanation.”

After he left, she restored the donor’s original words.

***

Some objects announced themselves.

A violin lacked its neck. A globe displayed Europe and half of Africa, while the rest of the world remained blank cream plaster. A chess set contained all the white pieces and seven black pawns.

Others required explanation.

There was a sealed envelope addressed but never stamped. A pair of train tickets for a journey interrupted by fog. A notebook containing seventeen pages of a novel and, on the eighteenth, a shopping list.

The museum held a wedding speech that had been abandoned halfway through when the speaker began crying, and a doctoral thesis left unfinished because its author inherited a bakery.

Mara liked that one.

The label read:

*Discontinuation voluntary. Subsequent career reportedly satisfying.*

In the west corridor stood a grandfather clock whose maker had completed the cabinet, dial, and hands, but never installed a mechanism. It always said eleven minutes past four.

Children loved it. Adults checked their watches.

There was also a large abstract painting with a small card beside it:

*The artist considers this finished. The donor disagrees.*

Bell refused to resolve the dispute.

***

Every afternoon at three, an elderly man in a charcoal coat visited the same display case.

It contained a model sailing ship.

The hull was complete, and two masts stood upright, but the third lay beside it. Threads hung loose from the rigging. Several miniature barrels waited in a shallow cardboard tray.

The man would stand with his hands behind his back for about twelve minutes. Then he would nod once and leave.

After two weeks, Mara approached him.

“Did you make it?”

“My brother.”

“Is he—”

“Dead? No. In Bournemouth.”

Mara looked at the ship.

“Does he know it’s here?”

“He donated it.”

“And you come to see it?”

The man considered this.

“We started it together.”

His name was Mr. Venn. He and his brother had received the kit one Christmas when they were boys. They worked on it through winter afternoons, arguing about instructions and borrowing their mother’s sewing scissors.

Then they grew older and discovered other ways to quarrel.

Their brotherhood did not break in a single dramatic moment. It wore thin around money, a house, the care of their mother, and remarks repeated by relatives who claimed they disliked getting involved.

“Last year he sent it here,” Mr. Venn said. “My daughter spotted it in the paper.”

“Have you spoken to him?”

“No.”

Mara almost asked why.

Instead, she said, “The barrels are very good.”

“I did those.”

He bent closer to the glass.

“I remember thinking they were terrible.”

***

Winter settled around the building.

Visitors shook rain from their coats. The windows darkened before closing time. In the unfinished café, someone placed a jar of instant coffee beside the wrapped machine, and the staff began making drinks with water from Bell’s kettle.

Mara learned the rhythms of the museum.

People moved quickly through the first room, smiling at the oddity of it. In the second, they slowed down. By the third, they were often thinking about something that was not on display.

Couples sometimes argued in whispers.

A man once stood before an incomplete family tree and said, “Well, she could have asked.”

A woman answered, “She did.”

They left separately, although only for a minute. He waited for her on the steps.

Schoolchildren were less solemn.

“Can you just donate homework?” one boy asked.

“Only if it has historical significance,” Mara said.

“It’s about the Romans.”

“That helps.”

A little girl studied the unfinished globe for a long time, then asked whether anyone had tried to paint the missing countries.

“No,” Mara said.

“Would they be allowed?”

“I don’t think so.”

The girl frowned.

“That seems mean to the countries.”

***

In January, a parcel arrived without a donor form.

It was wrapped in brown paper and tied with blue string. Mara opened it on the worktable.

Inside lay a wooden box.

The box contained a fountain pen, three photographs, and a letter in her father’s handwriting.

For a moment, she thought the museum had made a mistake so large it had become supernatural.

Then she found the note from her sister.

*You said they take this sort of thing. I couldn’t keep moving it from cupboard to cupboard. If you don’t want it there, send it back.*

Her father had died six years earlier. Her sister had dealt with his papers because Mara had been abroad when he became ill, and remained abroad for nine days longer than she should have.

The letter was addressed to Mara.

Not in an envelope. Just her name at the top.

She recognized the heavy pressure of the pen, the narrow letters, the way he crossed his t’s as if putting lids on jars.

*Mara,*

*Your sister tells me you think I didn’t want you to leave. That isn’t quite right.*

Then half a page about the weather, a neighbor’s dog, and trouble with the kitchen tap.

Finally:

*What I should have said at the station was*

Nothing followed.

***

She took the letter home.

Her flat was small and pleasantly anonymous, furnished with objects selected because they had no history. A blue sofa. A square table. Plates that could be replaced individually.

She laid the letter beside her supper.

At the station, eighteen years earlier, her father had carried her suitcase to the train. He had complained about the price of coffee and told her to keep her passport somewhere sensible.

When the doors began to close, she had hugged him awkwardly.

“Don’t waste this,” he said.

For years, she had heard that sentence as an accusation delivered in advance.

She had wasted things, of course. Everyone had. Time, money, opportunities, affection. She had stayed in a marriage after kindness became administrative. She had abandoned courses, postponed visits, failed to answer messages until answering required an apology.

Her father’s sentence had accompanied all of it.

Now there was this other sentence.

*What I should have said at the station was*

She tried endings.

*I’m proud of you.*

*Come home whenever you need to.*

*I wish I were brave enough to go.*

Each felt plausible. Each felt stolen.

She turned the page over, although she had already checked it at work.

Blank.

***

The next morning, Mara asked Bell whether the museum ever completed anything.

He was repairing the handle of a drawer with a screwdriver so small it looked ceremonial.

“Objects?”

“Anything.”

“We pay invoices.”

“You know what I mean.”

Bell set down the screwdriver.

“Sometimes donors request it. A musician wanted us to commission someone to finish her mother’s composition.”

“Did you?”

“No. We returned it.”

“Why?”

“Because she wanted music, not an exhibit.”

Mara told him about the letter.

He listened without rearranging his face into sympathy.

“Would you like it accessioned?”

“I don’t know.”

“Then don’t.”

“But it belongs here.”

“Possibly.”

“It’s unfinished.”

“So is your relationship with it.”

That annoyed her, mostly because she could not think of anything useful to say in response.

Bell picked up the screwdriver again.

“Leave it in a drawer for a while,” he said. “Drawers are good at waiting.”

***

In February, the museum’s funding was reviewed.

A council representative arrived carrying a tablet and a face composed for reasonable disappointment.

She toured the galleries with Bell and Mara, asking about visitor numbers, educational outcomes, and opportunities for commercial partnerships.

At the café, she brightened.

“This could generate revenue.”

“It does,” Bell said. “People buy postcards of it.”

“But as a café.”

“Then it would no longer be this.”

She looked through the glass doors.

“What exactly is this?”

Bell did not answer immediately.

Mara noticed a dead fly on the windowsill. She made a mental note to remove it.

The representative proposed an interactive room where visitors could finish replicas of selected objects. Complete the painting. Assemble the ship. Write the end of the letter.

“No original materials would be affected,” she said.

Mara looked at her sharply.

“Which letter?”

“Oh, any letter. You must have several.”

The idea was sensible. It was engaging. It offered measurable participation.

Bell asked for the proposal in writing.

After the representative left, Mara said, “You can’t let people do that.”

“Why not?”

“Because they’ll think they’ve solved something.”

“Perhaps some of them will.”

“You don’t believe that.”

Bell stood beside the unfinished globe.

“I believe we need to repair the roof.”

***

That afternoon, Mr. Venn arrived with an envelope.

He handed it to Mara.

“If my brother comes in, would you give him this?”

“Are you expecting him?”

“I’ve written to ask him.”

She glanced toward the ship.

“Would you rather we sent it?”

“No. I might change my mind before he gets here.”

He smiled without much conviction.

Mara placed the envelope in a drawer beneath the reception desk.

“What did you say?”

“Not enough.”

“Could you add something?”

“Probably.”

He looked tired.

“But I’ve posted the other one now.”

***

Mara began noticing how often people finished things badly merely to be rid of them.

Reports acquired conclusions unsupported by their contents. Conversations ended with “fine.” Buildings were handed over with buckets beneath leaks.

She had done it herself. The final technical manual she edited contained a sentence that troubled her:

*When the warning indicator ceases to illuminate, normal operation may be resumed.*

She had queried it twice. Nobody answered. Eventually, she approved the page.

She still did not know whether the light going out meant the machine was safe or the bulb was broken.

Completion could conceal neglect as easily as accomplishment.

But incompletion had its vanities too.

The novel never finished could remain brilliant. The apology never offered could remain perfectly worded. The journey never taken could remain life-changing.

Anything attempted had to endure being actual.

At her table one night, Mara unfolded her father’s letter again.

This time she read the parts about the dog and the kitchen tap slowly.

The dog had learned to open a garden gate. Her father had bought the wrong washer twice.

There he was: irritated, amused, alive.

She had been treating half a page of his life as packaging for one missing sentence.

***

In March, two men in charcoal coats stood before the model ship.

Mara saw them from reception.

Mr. Venn’s brother was shorter, with a hearing aid and a shopping bag from a pharmacy.

They did not embrace.

For a while they pointed at things.

One of them laughed. The other shook his head.

Mara remained at the desk, watching the entrance instead.

Eventually, Mr. Venn approached her.

“Could we have it back?”

“The ship?”

“He says he still has the instructions.”

His brother stood a little behind him.

“Most of them,” he said.

Bell authorized the return that afternoon.

The ship was packed in a box much larger than necessary, surrounded by tissue paper and supports cut from foam.

Mara brought out the envelope from the reception drawer.

Mr. Venn looked at it, then at his brother.

“You can give me that later,” his brother said. “There’s a bus in six minutes.”

They carried the box between them.

The empty display case remained for a week while Mara prepared another object.

Visitors examined it with great seriousness.

One asked whether it represented an abandoned ambition.

“For now,” Mara said, “it represents a ship we gave back.”

***

The interactive room was approved, but not quite as proposed.

Bell found funding for the roof elsewhere. Mara suspected he had called in favors, though he claimed only to have written several tedious letters.

The new room contained paper, pencils, wool, wood scraps, and simple tools.

Visitors could begin something.

They could also finish it.

If they wished, they could leave it for someone else.

There were no instructions beyond those.

Within days, the room contained a scarf, several poems, a small crooked shelf, and a drawing of the museum with a enormous café attached.

Someone began a list titled **THINGS I OWE PEOPLE**.

Someone else added **£12**.

A child constructed a boat that floated briefly in a sink, then sank with unmistakable completeness.

Mara called her sister from the workroom one evening. They talked about the parcel, then about their father, then about a dishwasher her sister was trying to have repaired.

The conversation lasted forty minutes.

Afterward, Mara put his letter back in its box. She kept it at home.

There was still no ending to the sentence.

In April, the museum acquired a new clock.

It was unfinished too, but it worked.

Its maker had installed the mechanism in a plain wooden case, intending eventually to carve leaves and birds around the face. Arthritis had stopped him.

The clock was mounted opposite the one that always said eleven minutes past four.

Now, through the west corridor, one clock kept time.

The other kept something else.

# The Museum of Unfinished Things

The museum occupied a building that had once been a railway station, though no train had stopped there for forty-three years. Its clocks showed different times. Its platforms ended in nettles. Above the entrance, the original sign still read ARRIVALS, which people sometimes mistook for a joke.

I became its caretaker because I answered an advertisement in a newspaper.

**Wanted: someone comfortable with incompletion. Some lifting required.**

At the interview, a woman named Mrs. Vale asked whether I had ever abandoned anything important.

“A degree,” I said. “A marriage. Several attempts at learning Italian.”

She nodded, but not approvingly. More as though I had confirmed that I possessed elbows.

“Abandonment isn’t always the same as incompletion,” she said. “Can you tell the difference?”

I told her I wasn’t sure.

“That will do.”

The salary was modest. There was an apartment upstairs, with a bath deep enough to drown a small ambition. My duties included opening the doors, cataloguing donations, dusting exhibits, and making sure visitors did not finish anything.

This last rule was printed on every ticket.

**PLEASE LEAVE THE WORK AS YOU FOUND IT.**

On my first morning, Mrs. Vale handed me a ring of keys and a feather duster.

“What exactly do we collect?” I asked.

She considered this.

“Evidence,” she said, “that people began.”

Then she put on her coat and left. I assumed she would return after lunch. It took me three weeks to understand that she had retired.

---

The first gallery contained objects that could be identified immediately.

There was a sweater with one sleeve, a violin lacking its varnish, and a jigsaw puzzle assembled around an empty rectangle of blue sky. A wooden chair had three legs and the beginnings of a fourth. In a glass case lay a manuscript that ended halfway through the sentence, *When he opened the door, he saw—*

I disliked that manuscript at first. It seemed to exert a small, deliberate pressure on the mind.

Nearby stood a model ship whose maker had completed every detail except the sails. Tiny sailors waited on its decks, painted with expressions too small to read.

The labels were brief.

**DINING CHAIR. Beech. Maker unknown.**

**NOVEL. Forty-seven pages. Donated by the author’s daughter.**

**SHIP. Intended name: Perseverance.**

In the second gallery, the exhibits became harder to classify.

An architect had donated plans for a hospital that was never built. A woman had given us a box of postcards addressed but not sent. There was an engagement ring still in its tissue paper, accompanied by a note requesting that no story be attached to it.

We honored that request.

The museum did not arrange objects according to why they had been left unfinished. Sometimes we knew. More often, families arrived carrying things they could not bear to keep and could not bear to throw away.

I learned to accept a parcel without immediately asking for an explanation. People usually gave one anyway, but it mattered that they could choose not to.

---

Our visitors were not the people I expected.

I had imagined aspiring artists, perhaps, or melancholy students looking for a handsome place to feel misunderstood. We received some of those. Mostly we received people on their lunch breaks, couples who had run out of errands, and children brought by adults who hoped the museum might be educational.

Children were often offended.

“Why didn’t somebody just finish the chair?” a boy asked me.

“Perhaps they couldn’t.”

“I could.”

He was eight, and probably correct.

An older woman visited every Thursday to look at the postcards. She never asked to read them. A bus driver spent twenty minutes in front of the hospital plans, then said, “That would have been near my old route.”

Once, a man stood before the unfinished novel and laughed so hard that he had to sit down. When I brought him water, he apologized.

“My father used to tell stories like that,” he said. “He’d get distracted. We never found out what happened to anybody.”

“Did you ask him?”

“All the time.”

“And?”

“He’d start another story.”

School groups presented a practical problem. Teachers wanted a lesson. They asked whether the museum encouraged perseverance.

“Sometimes,” I said.

“What else does it encourage?”

I looked toward the chair, visible through the doorway.

“Careful storage?”

The teacher did not smile. After that, I made a leaflet suggesting questions children might ask about the objects. I avoided supplying answers, which made it surprisingly difficult to fill both sides of the paper.

---

In November, a woman arrived carrying a bridge.

It was a model, about four feet long, wrapped in a blanket and held against her chest. One tower had been completed. The other ended in exposed dowels. Between them, thin wires hung slack over a river painted on plywood.

“My brother made it,” she said.

I cleared a space on the receiving table.

“Was he an engineer?”

“An accountant.”

She removed the blanket carefully. Small flecks of paint fell onto the floor.

“He worked on it every Sunday. For eleven years.”

I waited.

“He died in August.”

We filled out the donation form. Under *Reason for incompletion*, she wrote *Death*, then crossed it out.

“He stopped working on it before that,” she said. “Nearly a year before.”

“Do you know why?”

“No. He said he was thinking.”

She stood with one hand resting on the finished tower.

“I used to tease him. Eleven years, and still no bridge. I’d bring him newspaper pictures of bridges that had gone up in eighteen months.”

“What did he say?”

“That those people had funding.”

She smiled for the first time.

When I asked what name should appear on the label, she gave me his full name, then his profession, then the dates of his life. Before leaving, she asked if she could change one word.

The label we eventually printed read:

**BRIDGE MODEL. Wood, wire, paint. Made on Sundays by Daniel Mercer, accountant.**

She came back the next month with photographs of him working on it. In every photograph, he wore the same blue cardigan.

---

There was one room I kept locked for the first winter.

Its key had a red thread tied through the bow. Mrs. Vale’s inventory called it the Room of Things That Should Not Be Finished.

Inside stood a cabinet of abandoned devices, several sealed boxes, and a table covered with papers. Unlike the other galleries, this room had curtains drawn across its windows.

A proposed housing development would have required demolishing a neighborhood of inexpensive flats. The planning documents included photographs of the residents’ washing hanging behind their homes. Beside them lay a map on which those homes had become gray blocks.

There were drawings for a machine intended to monitor employees’ bathroom breaks.

There was an incomplete pamphlet arguing that certain people should not be allowed to vote.

On a shelf sat a mechanical bird designed to sing whenever its owner clapped. According to the donation letter, its inventor had dismantled the mechanism after his wife complained that she could no longer clap at concerts without expecting it.

That one seemed less sinister than irritating, but I understood its inclusion.

For weeks, I thought the room contradicted the museum. Then I noticed how many visitors treated finishing as a duty. They looked at the abandoned hospital and the half-written novel with the same regret.

I opened the room in January.

Some visitors hurried through it. Others stayed longer than anywhere else. One woman examined the housing plans and said, “My uncle lived there.”

“Did they build it?”

“No,” she said. “Thank God.”

---

My own unfinished object was a letter.

It lived in the drawer beside my bed, folded once, though I had never put it in an envelope. I had begun it after my sister called to say that our father had died.

We had not spoken properly for almost six years.

Our disagreement had started with his care and widened until it included money, childhood, and accusations neither of us could withdraw gracefully. She had lived near him. I had lived far away. Each of us believed the other misunderstood the weight of that arrangement.

The letter began, *Dear Anna, I’ve been trying to work out what to say.*

Below that were three paragraphs explaining why I had not come home more often.

Each time I read them, I added a qualification. Each qualification required another explanation. Eventually the letter occupied five pages and said almost nothing I wanted her to hear.

One night, I carried it downstairs.

I put it on the receiving table and took out a donation form. It was absurdly easy to imagine the exhibit: paper, ink, brother, cowardice.

But the museum could not be allowed to become my excuse.

I returned the letter to its drawer.

For several days afterward, I was impatient with the visitors. I caught myself wishing they would stop studying their choices and make one. This was unfair, especially in a place that sold them tickets to do precisely the opposite.

I took two days off. On the second, I bought an envelope. I did not use it.

---

The storm arrived in March.

Rain struck the station roof with the persistence of a bill collector. By midnight, water was entering the west gallery through three separate cracks. I set out buckets, then bowls, then the large soup pot from my kitchen.

At two in the morning, a section of ceiling fell above the model ship.

I called the emergency number on the insurance folder. A recorded voice told me that unusually high call volumes had increased waiting times.

While a cheerful tune played, I moved everything I could lift.

The novel went upstairs. The postcards went into the ticket office. I dragged the three-legged chair away from the wall, where it immediately fell over. I carried Daniel Mercer’s bridge last, because its wires caught on my sleeves.

By dawn, the west gallery smelled of wet plaster and old wood.

The damage was not catastrophic, but it was expensive. The insurer required estimates. The estimates required inspections. The inspections required a survey of the roof, which revealed a structural problem that no amount of strategically placed soup pots would address.

We closed for six weeks.

Visitors left notes through the letterbox. Some enclosed money. A child sent a drawing of a roof with enormous red gutters.

I phoned Mrs. Vale.

“I thought you’d know what to do,” I said.

“I usually asked somebody.”

“Who?”

“Whoever seemed to know.”

It was the first time I had heard her sound tired. I had been treating her as though retirement had merely made her wisdom available by telephone.

---

The town held a meeting about the museum in the library basement.

There were eighteen people, or nineteen if we counted the infant asleep against the bus driver’s shoulder. I explained the repairs and the cost. A council member asked whether the museum could increase its revenue.

“People enjoy interactive experiences,” she said.

I imagined visitors completing the puzzle, attaching the chair leg, writing an ending to the novel. The idea made me protective in a way I had not expected.

“We could offer workshops,” suggested a local carpenter.

“To finish things?”

“To fix them. Different business.”

The woman who visited the postcards proposed a room where people could work on projects they had brought from home.

This caused an argument.

If we helped people finish their work, would that undermine the museum? If we refused, were we making incompletion into something precious and untouchable?

The bus driver shifted the sleeping child onto his other shoulder.

“You’ve got a lot of tables,” he said. “And that room nobody uses.”

He meant the old parcels office.

We applied for a repair grant, organized a sale of donated books, and opened the parcels office on Saturday afternoons. People brought sewing, tax forms, broken lamps, and one screenplay.

There was no requirement to finish.

The carpenter volunteered twice a month. A retired librarian helped with paperwork. I made tea and watched a woman spend three Saturdays repairing a coat she later decided she no longer liked.

She donated it to a charity shop. Nobody regarded this as a failure.

---

In May, Daniel Mercer’s sister came to see the repaired gallery.

She stood before the bridge for a long time. We had placed his photographs nearby, in a narrow case. The blue cardigan had faded almost to gray in one of them.

“I found something else,” she said.

From her bag she took a small cardboard box. Inside were tiny lamps, railings, and two painted figures.

“He’d finished these. I didn’t know.”

We examined them at the receiving table. One figure wore a hat. The other carried what might have been a suitcase or a toolbox.

“Should they go on the bridge?” she asked.

I nearly quoted the rule on the tickets.

Instead, I asked whether she knew where he had intended to put them.

“There are pencil marks.”

There were. We found them near the completed tower: small crosses almost hidden beneath the paint.

For half an hour, we placed the pieces without attaching them. Then we returned them to their box. Neither of us wanted to make the decision that afternoon.

Before she left, she asked whether there was anything of mine in the museum.

“No.”

“Nothing unfinished?”

“Plenty. Nothing here.”

That evening, I took out the letter to Anna. I read it once and put it in the stove.

On a fresh sheet, I wrote that I was sorry she had carried so much alone. I said I understood if she did not want to answer. I asked whether she still had the photograph of us sitting in the wheelbarrow.

I posted it before breakfast.

---

Anna answered three weeks later.

Her letter contained no photograph. She said she knew the one I meant, but it was somewhere in the boxes from our father’s house. She had not sorted them yet.

She also said she was still angry.

I read those sentences several times. Then I read the rest.

Her eldest had started secondary school. The kitchen window needed replacing. She had planted beans too early and lost the first seedlings to frost. She asked whether I was still living above the museum.

We wrote cautiously that summer. There were matters we approached and then left alone. Sometimes an ordinary detail—the price of a window, the behavior of beans—carried more between us than a direct apology could manage.

The museum reopened fully in June.

On Saturdays, the parcels office filled with people and the uneven sounds of work. Upstairs, the exhibits remained as they were. Daniel Mercer’s little lamps stayed in their box beside the bridge, with a note explaining that their placement had not been decided.

Mrs. Vale visited in September. She examined the roof, drank tea, and complained that we had moved her favorite chair.

“It was getting wet,” I said.

“Good reason.”

Before closing, I walked her to the entrance. The old ARRIVALS sign was lit by the last of the afternoon.

“Are you comfortable here?” she asked.

“Mostly.”

She nodded, as she had at my interview.

After she left, I checked the windows and emptied the bins. In the parcels office, someone had forgotten a knitting bag. A row of green stitches rested on a needle, waiting for next Saturday.

# The World Is Held Together by Small Things

## 1. The Door That Sticks

Imagine a door that sticks in wet weather.

It belongs to a house on an ordinary street, and nobody remembers when it began resisting. Perhaps the frame settled. Perhaps the wood swelled one winter and never entirely recovered. To open it, you lift the handle slightly while pushing with your shoulder. Visitors do not know this. They push, pause, and look back at whoever invited them.

“Lift it a little,” someone says.

Every inhabited place accumulates instructions like that. The second burner runs hot. The window closes if you press the upper corner. The dog barks at hats but settles once you take yours off. The upstairs light requires patience: one flick, a moment of darkness, then another.

These details rarely appear in the official description of a home. A property listing counts bedrooms, measures floors, and mentions sunlight. It does not mention the knowledge needed to live there.

Yet that knowledge can become part of affection. Someone learns how much force the drawer can tolerate. Someone knows which mug has a cracked handle and quietly stops giving it to guests.

Of course, not every inconvenience deserves preservation. A dangerous staircase needs fixing. A leaking roof is not charming when you cannot afford repairs.

Still, the sticking door offers a useful distinction. There is the world as designed, and there is the world as encountered. Between them stands a person, lifting the handle slightly.

Much of daily life takes place in that adjustment, so familiar that it scarcely feels like knowledge.

## 2. The Spoon

A spoon is a modest technology.

It does not announce itself as an invention. It waits in a drawer, usually among others shaped almost like it. Its purpose seems so obvious that it disappears into the action it enables. You notice the soup, not the instrument that carries it.

But take a spoon seriously for a minute.

Its bowl must hold enough without becoming awkward. Its handle must balance reach against control. Its edge should meet the mouth comfortably. It needs to survive heat, washing, pressure, distraction, and being dropped behind the stove. It must work for someone who is hungry, sleepy, ill, hurried, very young, or very old.

A good spoon contains answers to questions most people never have to ask.

Everyday objects can be unusually instructive that way. Their success often consists in not drawing attention. They make room for something else: eating, writing, opening a window, getting safely downstairs.

A poorly designed object recruits its user into constant troubleshooting. A good one returns attention to the task.

At the scale of a civilization, that returned attention matters. How many hours have been saved by readable signs, reliable hinges, clear instructions, comfortable handles, and forms that ask understandable questions? How many have been lost to their opposites?

We celebrate spectacular inventions, reasonably enough. But there should also be some quiet honor for the person who made a kettle pour without dripping.

Their achievement enters kitchens every morning. Nobody gives a speech. The tea simply reaches the cup, and breakfast continues.

## 3. The Bench

A public bench makes a small but consequential claim: you may remain here without buying anything.

In places where nearly every comfortable seat belongs to a business, this is generous. A bench permits rest without requiring an explanation. You can be tired, early, lonely, content, lost, or merely unwilling to stand.

The same wooden slats support many versions of a day.

A teenager waits for a friend and checks the time repeatedly. An older person pauses halfway through a familiar walk. A delivery worker eats from a paper container. Two people sit at opposite ends until one asks whether the other is waiting for the bus.

Public space does not guarantee community. A crowded square can be hostile, and a neighborhood can display its hospitality selectively. Still, the physical invitation matters. A place to sit changes what bodies are allowed to do.

Design sometimes reveals suspicion more clearly than policy does. Dividers, spikes, uncomfortable slopes, and absent shade can communicate who is welcome and for how long.

A bench cannot solve housing insecurity or loneliness. We should not ask furniture to accomplish what institutions refuse to attempt. But furniture can participate in either welcome or exclusion.

Imagine judging a city partly by what it offers someone with no money to spend that afternoon.

Can they drink water? Find a toilet? Sit down? Read? Shelter from rain?

The answers reveal something that a skyline photograph cannot. They show how the city treats a person whose presence produces no sale and requires no celebration.

## 4. The Library

A library is one of the few institutions where taking something away can be the intended result of entering.

You arrive empty-handed and leave carrying borrowed worlds. The transaction is organized around trust: this belongs to everyone, and for a while it may travel with you.

That arrangement remains remarkable even when the building is shabby and the printer is temperamental.

Inside a library, many different needs share a roof. Someone researches a family name. Someone studies for an exam. Someone reads a newspaper slowly because the room is warm. Someone asks how to attach a document to an email.

The books matter, but so does the permission to linger among them.

There is a particular freedom in browsing without knowing what you want. Search systems reward a formulated question. Shelves allow the question to emerge late. You look for gardening advice and find a history of pigments. You investigate a local river and become interested in bridges.

Such accidents are not opposed to knowledge. Sometimes they are how knowledge begins.

A library also offers a useful answer to the fear of not understanding. Here is a room built on the assumption that nobody arrives knowing everything.

You may ask where something is. You may mispronounce a name. You may begin with the wrong book and return it.

At its best, the institution makes ignorance ordinary rather than shameful. The catalog, the desk, and the borrowing card all provide ways forward. A question that felt embarrassing outside can become manageable here, among other people looking things up.

## 5. The Repair

A repaired object carries evidence that somebody chose it twice.

The first choice was to acquire it. The second was to keep it when keeping required effort.

A patched coat, a resoled boot, a lamp with a replaced switch: each records a negotiation between convenience, cost, affection, and skill. Sometimes repair is necessary because replacement is unaffordable. Sometimes it is satisfying because the object already fits the life around it.

There is dignity in both reasons.

Modern commerce often makes replacement easier than understanding. An object fails, and the available response is to buy another. The broken thing becomes opaque, almost embarrassing, as though failure has erased its right to remain useful.

Repair begins by refusing that erasure.

What has actually gone wrong? Is the damage local? Can the worn part be replaced? Is there someone who knows how?

These questions encourage a more accurate relationship with things. Instead of treating an object as either perfect or worthless, they ask how it works and what it needs.

But repair has limits. Some things are unsafe. Some efforts consume more resources than replacement. Some relationships, institutions, and habits should end.

The value lies less in always preserving than in examining before discarding.

To mend something well, you must first look closely. You turn the coat inside out. You follow the loose wire. You find the point where the seam began to separate.

Then, if the work is possible, you make a change small enough to leave most of the object intact. The lamp lights again. The boot goes back outside.

## 6. The Rain

Rain changes the social geometry of a street.

People who were walking independently gather beneath the same awning. Distances shrink. Strangers negotiate inches of dry pavement with small movements of shoulders and bags. Someone checks the sky as though it might be persuaded.

Water makes neglected details visible. A blocked drain becomes a lake. The pavement reveals its slope. A roof demonstrates whether it was maintained. Shoes disclose the difference between looking waterproof and being waterproof.

Weather is often discussed as if everyone experiences the same event. In a meteorological sense, they may. In a human sense, rain is distributed through circumstance.

For one person, it is a pleasant reason to stay indoors. For another, it means lost wages, a dangerous commute, soaked bedding, or a roof that cannot be trusted.

This does not forbid delight in rain. It gives that delight context.

There is real pleasure in the sound of water against a window, in the smell rising from dry ground, in watching leaves tremble under drops. Pleasure need not disappear because someone else is uncomfortable. But awareness can turn pleasure outward.

You might make room beneath the awning. You might offer a dry place to wait. You might notice that the person arriving late has spent twenty minutes crossing the weather you watched from a warm room.

Rain supplies these encounters without arranging their outcome.

Then it eases. People step back onto the pavement, sometimes exchanging a nod, and resume journeys that briefly occupied the same few square feet.

## 7. The Map

A map is useful because it leaves things out.

If it included every leaf, crack, conversation, smell, and parked bicycle, it would become as difficult to navigate as the territory itself. Clarity depends on omission.

This is obvious with maps and easier to forget elsewhere.

A résumé is a map of a working life. A medical chart is a map of a body in time. A news article maps an event. A financial statement maps an organization. Each can be accurate and still incomplete.

Trouble begins when usefulness hardens into total authority.

The street exists beyond its name and width. The employee exists beyond the list of roles. The patient exists beyond the measurements. Knowing which details a document excludes is part of knowing how to use it.

Even a familiar route changes when traveled for another purpose. Walking to work, you notice crossings and delays. Walking with a child, you notice dogs, low walls, and unusually shaped stones. Walking with someone who uses a wheelchair, you notice gradients and broken surfaces.

The place has not become different in every respect. Your attention has acquired another obligation.

A practical way to understand a place, then, is to ask how someone else moves through it.

Where do they pause? What do they avoid? Which supposedly minor detail controls their whole journey?

No one can hold every possible view at once. We still need simplified accounts. But we can compare them, correct them, and occasionally put them aside long enough to walk the route ourselves.

## 8. The Seed

A seed is an unusually compact expression of possibility.

It is not a promise that growth will occur. Seeds fail. They dry out, rot, fall on unsuitable ground, or become food. Their future depends on conditions they cannot supply alone.

That limitation makes them more interesting, not less.

People often speak about potential as though it belongs entirely to the individual. A talented child, a promising researcher, a gifted musician: the language points inward, toward qualities waiting to unfold.

But unfolding requires a world.

Time, nutrition, safety, instruction, equipment, encouragement, luck, and freedom from constant crisis all affect what becomes possible. A seed does not demonstrate poor character by failing on concrete.

The metaphor has limits. People are not plants, and human agency matters enormously. Still, it corrects the habit of crediting success only to the person who succeeds.

Growth is both personal and environmental.

Gardeners understand this practically. They do not lecture a struggling seedling about ambition. They check the light, the soil, the water, and the roots. They ask whether their own intervention has helped or harmed.

Institutions might benefit from a little of that patience.

When someone falters, the first question need not be whether they possess sufficient determination. It might be whether the conditions make determination usable.

This is not an argument for lowering every expectation. Gardens require work. It is an argument for directing some of that work toward the surroundings, rather than placing all responsibility on the thing we hope will grow.

## 9. The Silence

There are silences that comfort and silences that punish.

The difference is not measurable in decibels.

A comfortable silence leaves room. Two people can sit together without needing to prove that the relationship continues. Each can look out the window, read, or think. Speech remains available without being compulsory.

A punitive silence withdraws that availability. It makes the other person guess, fear, pursue, or apologize without knowing for what.

From outside, the scenes may look identical.

This is one reason human life resists purely visible interpretation. A photograph can show two people sitting apart. It cannot tell you whether the space between them is restful or unbearable.

Silence also has public forms.

A meeting goes quiet because people are considering an idea. Another goes quiet because everyone knows disagreement will be punished. A classroom falls silent from concentration, confusion, boredom, or fear.

Good leadership requires distinguishing these states rather than praising quietness automatically.

So does good friendship.

Sometimes the most helpful question is simple: “Do you want company, or would you rather have some space?”

It gives the other person a way to make the silence legible. Asking does not guarantee an honest or immediate answer, but it can remove some of the guesswork.

We often admire eloquence, and rightly. Yet there is another skill in knowing when language should stop. Not every pause needs filling. Not every difficult feeling is ready to become a story. Sometimes companionship means remaining nearby without demanding a report, while keeping the possibility of conversation open.

## 10. Tomorrow Morning

Most of what sustains a life will happen again tomorrow.

The kettle will need filling. The bus will arrive, perhaps late. Someone will unlock a building before anyone thanks them. Someone will wipe a table, answer a question, check a dosage, carry a bag, replace a bulb.

Repetition can make labor invisible.

We tend to notice beginnings and endings: openings, launches, breakthroughs, collapses. Maintenance occupies the long middle, where things continue because people keep attending to them.

A clean hallway is not a permanent achievement. Neither is a functioning relationship, a reliable bridge, or a fair institution. Each depends on recurring acts that are easy to overlook precisely because they work.

You can see some of those acts early in the morning, before a place becomes busy. A cleaner checks the corners. A baker moves trays. A driver inspects a vehicle. The finished scene will look effortless to most of the people entering it.

Tomorrow will bring damage as well as care. Something will break. Someone will be careless. A plan will fail. The work will not produce a final, flawless version of the world.

It can still produce a usable morning.

The door can open. The spoon can carry breakfast. The bench can offer rest. The book can travel home. The repaired lamp can illuminate a page.

None of these things resolves every difficulty. But together they give people somewhere to begin.

And in the morning, among all the larger matters still unsettled, someone will lift the handle slightly.

samples.result:
# The Department of Small Repairs

The first thing Mara repaired was a silence.

It arrived on a Tuesday in a cardboard box with airholes punched through the lid. The woman carrying it wore a green raincoat, though the morning was clear. She set the box on Mara’s counter and rested both hands beside it, as if preventing something from escaping.

“It’s the silence after my son calls,” she said.

Mara looked at the box.

“What’s wrong with it?”

“It used to be peaceful.”

From inside came the faint sound of a refrigerator humming in an empty kitchen.

Mara had worked for the Department of Small Repairs for eleven years. She fixed umbrella springs, loose spectacle arms, kettle switches, the wooden handles of knives. Occasionally she repaired something less straightforward: a recurring dream with a stuck door, a promise that had developed a wobble, the particular blue of a childhood swimming pool.

Silences were uncommon, but not unheard of.

She took the box into the workshop.

***

The Department occupied a narrow building between a pharmacy and a shop that sold expensive soap shaped like fruit. Its sign had once read MUNICIPAL DEPARTMENT OF SMALL REPAIRS. Weather had removed MUNICIPAL and most of SMALL, leaving DEPARTMENT OF REPAIRS, which sounded grander than anyone inside felt.

There were three employees.

Mr. Vale repaired objects with moving parts. He could coax another decade from a toaster and had no patience for bicycles.

Juno handled fabric, paper, and delicate misunderstandings. She was twenty-six and wore a different silver ring on every finger. When concentrating, she hummed songs nobody recognized.

Mara took whatever remained.

They were funded through a line in the city budget called Miscellaneous Continuity. Every spring a council member proposed eliminating it. Every summer someone’s wedding photograph faded from the edges inward, or a public fountain forgot the sound of water, and the proposal quietly disappeared.

The department charged according to difficulty and means. A replacement screw cost twenty cents. A repaired childhood smell cost whatever the customer could comfortably spare.

Some people paid in cash. Some brought oranges. Once, an elderly man paid with directions to a bench from which the sunset looked unusually generous.

Mara still went there sometimes.

***

The silence in the box was cold.

She opened the lid and felt it settle across her wrists. Inside lay a small, translucent sheet, folded into quarters. One edge had frayed. Another bore a pale stain shaped like a thumb.

She spread it on the workbench.

The refrigerator sound stopped.

Now she heard a woman saying, “Of course. No, I understand.”

Then nothing.

Mara inspected the fraying under a lamp. Silences damaged by loneliness usually thinned in the middle. This one had been stretched at the corners, pulled repeatedly toward something it could not reach.

Juno came over holding a paperback whose last page had detached itself from its ending.

“What is it?”

“A telephone silence.”

“Bad?”

“Not ruined.”

Juno leaned closer. “You’ll need a little ordinary sound.”

“I know.”

“Not radio.”

“I know.”

“And definitely not advice.”

Mara gave her a look.

Juno returned to the paperback.

From a drawer, Mara selected a spool labeled SPOON AGAINST CUP, another labeled NEIGHBOR WATERING PLANTS, and a short length of FOOTSTEPS THAT DO NOT LEAVE.

She threaded a needle.

***

At noon, Mr. Vale burned his toast.

This happened most days despite his professional expertise.

“The machine is temperamental,” he said.

“You set it to seven,” Juno replied.

“Seven exists for a reason.”

“Arson exists for a reason too. Usually insurance.”

They ate in the courtyard behind the building, where a fig tree grew from a square of soil barely larger than a bathtub. Nobody knew who had planted it. Its fruit was poor, but its shade was excellent.

Mara had brought a cheese sandwich wrapped in wax paper. Juno ate noodles from a chipped bowl. Mr. Vale scraped his toast with a pocketknife.

Beyond the wall, traffic moved through the city in surges.

“Did you see the notice?” Juno asked.

Mara shook her head.

Mr. Vale stopped scraping.

“They’re reviewing us again,” he said.

“That’s all they ever do.”

“This time they’ve hired consultants.”

Juno made a small, theatrical gasp.

Consultants had visited once before. They wore identical visitor badges and asked how many units of regret the department processed annually.

Mara had said regret was generally outside their remit.

They had asked whether it could be brought inside.

“What do they want?” she asked.

“Evidence of impact,” said Mr. Vale.

The three sat quietly.

A fig fell from the tree and struck the table.

Juno picked it up.

“Put that in the report.”

***

Mara finished the silence shortly before closing.

The woman in the green raincoat returned with a shopping bag pressed beneath her arm.

“Will it be different?”

“A little,” Mara said. “It won’t make him call more often.”

“I didn’t ask that.”

“No.”

The woman looked away, then back.

“I almost did.”

Mara folded the silence into the box. The repaired edge held a faint warmth.

“You may notice things you were overlooking,” she said. “The cup in your hand. Someone moving upstairs. It should help the room remain a room.”

The woman lifted the lid.

For a moment, the shop smelled of tea.

Her shoulders lowered.

“How much?”

“Three pounds.”

The woman took out five.

Mara gave her two back.

After she left, Mara stood behind the counter longer than necessary. Then she put on her coat and walked home.

Her own telephone had not rung in nineteen days.

She knew because she had stopped counting after eighteen, and then counted once more.

***

Her father lived thirty miles away, in the house where she had grown up.

He was eighty-one and increasingly suspicious of things that asked to be updated. He refused a new television because the old one already knew what channels he liked. He kept a paper road atlas under the passenger seat of his car, though he no longer drove.

Their last conversation had concerned a cracked garden wall.

“You should have someone look at it,” Mara had said.

“I’m someone.”

“Someone qualified.”

“I built it.”

“Forty years ago.”

“That doesn’t make it someone else’s wall.”

The conversation had ended there, though neither had actually hung up for several seconds.

Afterward, Mara had waited for him to call.

This was a habit they shared: waiting with sufficient determination that it began to resemble a principle.

Her mother had once handled the distance between them. She would phone Mara and say, “Your father wants to know whether your boiler is behaving,” or tell him, “Mara mentioned the apple tree.”

Since her death, six years earlier, messages had accumulated on both sides without a courier.

Mara boiled water, made soup, and put her phone on the kitchen table.

It remained a phone.

***

The consultants arrived on Thursday.

There were two of them, a tall man and a short woman, neither unpleasant. This made them harder to dislike.

They admired the workshop. They photographed the drawers. They asked whether the department had considered a digital booking system.

“We have,” said Mr. Vale.

“And?”

“We stopped considering it.”

The woman smiled professionally.

Mara showed them the intake ledger. Beside ordinary entries—WATCH STRAP, BLUE; TABLE LAMP; CHILD’S MUSIC BOX—were others:

CONFIDENCE IN A FAMILIAR STAIRCASE.

LAST FIVE MINUTES OF A HOLIDAY.

ABILITY TO HEAR ONE’S OWN NAME WITHOUT FLINCHING.

The tall man tapped that final line.

“How do you quantify the outcome?”

“The customer came back for her scarf,” Mara said.

“I’m sorry?”

“She’d forgotten it. Before the repair, she wouldn’t come back anywhere once she’d left.”

He wrote something down.

At the end of the visit, the woman asked what would happen if the department closed.

“People would manage,” Mara said.

The consultants seemed relieved.

“Mostly,” she added.

***

On Friday, a boy brought in a bus timetable.

He was perhaps twelve, with wet hair and a schoolbag dragging one shoulder lower than the other.

“It’s wrong,” he said.

Mara examined it.

The timetable was printed on ordinary paper. Route 18. Six stops. Weekday service every twenty minutes.

“Which part?”

“The waiting.”

She looked up.

The boy rubbed his nose with his sleeve.

“My dad used to meet me at the stop. Now my aunt does. But when I’m there, it still feels like he might come.”

Mara did not touch the paper again.

Behind her, Mr. Vale carefully set down a screwdriver.

“Is your father away?” she asked.

“He died in January.”

“I’m sorry.”

The boy nodded impatiently. He had heard that often enough to know it did not lead anywhere useful.

“Can you fix it?”

Mara considered the timetable.

There were repairs that could be made and repairs that should not be. The distinction was rarely printed on the object.

“I can look,” she said.

“Will it take long?”

“Come back tomorrow.”

He left the timetable on the counter.

His name, written in the ledger, was Eli Ward.

***

That evening, Mara missed her usual bus and found herself waiting beneath the shelter outside the library.

The rain had stopped. Cars passed with their lights reflected in the road.

A man beside her held flowers wrapped in supermarket plastic. Across the street, a restaurant worker emptied a bucket into the gutter.

She thought about the boy.

Then she thought about her father sitting in his kitchen, perhaps waiting for her call with exactly the stubborn attention she was giving his.

She took out her phone.

His number was still listed under Home.

She pressed it before she could decide otherwise.

He answered after seven rings.

“Yes?”

“It’s me.”

“I know.”

A pause.

“How’s the wall?”

“Still there.”

“Good.”

Another pause.

Then he said, “There’s a crack in the mortar near the gate.”

Mara closed her eyes.

“Has it got bigger?”

“A bit.”

“Shall I come Sunday?”

“You don’t have to.”

“I know.”

A bus approached.

Her father cleared his throat.

“There’s soup in the freezer.”

She let the bus pass.

***

On Saturday morning, Mara examined Eli’s timetable under magnification.

The printed times were sound. So were the route numbers and the little symbol indicating wheelchair access.

The trouble lay in the blank spaces.

Between 15:40 and 16:00, something had lodged itself: not a memory exactly, but a repeated expectation. A tall figure turning the corner. A familiar coat. A hand lifted before the face became clear.

Mara could remove it.

She had the tools.

In the back cabinet was a bottle of clean forgetting, rarely used. A single drop would loosen the expectation from the paper. Two would remove its stain.

She fetched the bottle, placed it on the bench, and waited.

Juno came to stand beside her.

“No?” she asked.

“I don’t know.”

“What does he want gone?”

“The moment before he remembers.”

Juno watched the timetable.

“That’s a hard moment.”

“Yes.”

Outside, someone laughed. The sound crossed the shop and disappeared into the shelves.

Mara returned the bottle to the cabinet.

Instead, she took out tracing paper, a brass ruler, and a pencil worn almost to its ferrule.

***

Eli arrived at eleven.

Mara showed him the timetable.

She had not changed any of the times.

In the margin beside the stop where he waited, she had drawn a small square. Within it were three faint lines.

“What’s that?”

“A place to put something else.”

He frowned.

“Like what?”

“Whatever is actually there. A dog. A funny sign. Someone’s shoes. You can write it down while you wait.”

“That’s not fixing it.”

“No,” Mara said. “Not the way you asked.”

He looked at her for a long time.

“Can you?”

“Yes.”

His fingers tightened around the paper.

“But I’m not sure I should.”

“That’s stupid.”

“It might be.”

He stared at the little square.

“If you took it away,” he said, “would I forget him?”

“Not all of him.”

“Which bit?”

“I can’t promise exactly.”

The workshop was quiet.

Finally he folded the timetable along its old creases.

“I don’t want that.”

“All right.”

“Do I still have to pay?”

“No.”

At the door, he stopped.

“What if there’s nothing interesting?”

“You can write that.”

He nodded once, as if accepting a rule he intended to test.

***

On Sunday, Mara found her father beside the garden gate wearing a coat held closed with one large button.

“You’re late,” he said.

“By four minutes.”

“I didn’t say how late.”

The crack in the wall was worse than he had admitted. Ivy had entered the mortar, and water had done the rest.

Mara pressed gently against the brickwork.

Her father watched.

“Well?”

“It needs work.”

“That’s what I said.”

She almost reminded him what he had actually said. Instead, she knelt and scraped loose mortar into her palm.

They spent the afternoon removing ivy.

Her father could no longer kneel comfortably, so he sat on an upturned bucket and sorted usable bricks from damaged ones. He complained about the bucket, the weather, and the inferior quality of modern gloves.

At three, they went inside.

He heated soup.

The kitchen was much as it had been when her mother was alive, except for the small absences Mara still encountered unexpectedly: no glasses beside the crossword, no cardigan over the spare chair.

Her father placed two bowls on the table.

“I kept meaning to ring,” he said.

“So did I.”

He nodded.

They ate.

Later, she wrote a builder’s number on a piece of paper.

He put it beside the telephone rather than in a drawer.

***

The department’s funding decision came in June.

They would remain open for another year, subject to quarterly reporting and improvements in public visibility.

Juno proposed a sign that said WE FIX SOME THINGS.

Mr. Vale objected that this undersold their expertise.

His alternative, COMPETENT REPAIRS WITH REASONABLE LIMITATIONS, received no support.

They compromised on repairing the existing sign.

On the first warm evening of summer, the three of them stood outside while Juno touched white paint into the missing letters. People passed carrying groceries, gym bags, takeaway dinners.

A woman stopped to ask whether they fixed zippers.

“Yes,” Mara said.

“My mother’s coat. It catches halfway up.”

“Bring it in.”

The woman promised she would.

Across the street, a bus pulled away from its stop.

Eli stood beneath the shelter with his aunt. He saw Mara and lifted a folded piece of paper.

She raised her hand.

Later, when the paint was drying and Mr. Vale had gone inside to rescue his toast, Mara’s phone rang.

Home.

She answered.

Her father wanted to know whether the builder’s estimate seemed reasonable. Then he wanted to tell her about a blackbird nesting in the ivy they had left.

Mara leaned against the newly painted doorframe and listened while Juno rinsed the brush.
