samples.result:
At the end of our street stood a shop that repaired things nobody knew were broken.

Its window contained a brass telescope, three empty picture frames, a shoe with a bird’s nest in it, and a sign:

**PLEASE BRING ALL THE PIECES.**

I passed it every morning on my way to work. Every evening, too, though by then the window reflected the traffic and I mostly saw myself.

One Thursday, my kettle stopped boiling.

This was the sort of problem I understood. There would be a fuse, a wire, a small component with a name. I put the kettle in a shopping bag and went to the shop.

A bell rang when I opened the door, then rang again after I had closed it, as though reconsidering.

Behind the counter sat a woman knitting something long and gray. The room smelled of sawdust and oranges.

“What seems to be the trouble?” she asked.

“It won’t boil.”

“That is certainly a trouble.”

She took the kettle out of the bag, plugged it in, and flicked the switch. Nothing happened.

“Could be the element,” I said.

“Could be.”

She opened a drawer, selected a tiny screwdriver, and removed the base. I watched her set each screw in a saucer.

“When did it last work?”

“Yesterday.”

“And what were you doing?”

“Making tea.”

She looked up.

“Before that?”

I thought. “Talking to my mother.”

“Ah.”

“My mother lives in Bristol.”

“That doesn’t rule anything out.”

She peered into the kettle’s underside.

“You ended the call quickly.”

“I had things to do.”

“Of course.”

“She calls at inconvenient times.”

“Most people do.”

The woman reached in with tweezers and pulled out a small blue thread. It kept coming: six inches, a foot, a yard. She wound it around her finger.

“What is that?”

“Something caught in the mechanism.”

“It’s an electric kettle.”

“Yes,” she said. “They’re surprisingly vulnerable.”

When she finished, she had a blue ball of thread the size of a plum. She placed it beside the screws and fitted the base back on.

The kettle began to hiss.

“How much?”

“Call your mother.”

“I mean for the repair.”

“So do I.”

***

I didn’t call that night.

Instead I inspected the kettle, turning it upside down under the kitchen light. There was a scratch near the switch that I couldn’t remember seeing before. I wondered whether she had simply cleaned a contact.

On Friday morning I called my mother while the water boiled.

She told me the fox had returned to her garden. She told me someone had stolen a planter from outside the library. She asked whether I was eating properly.

I said yes.

There was a pause.

“What?” I asked.

“Nothing. I’m pleased you called.”

I leaned against the counter. The kettle clicked off. Neither of us said anything for a little while, and then she asked if I remembered the blue coat I had worn to school.

“The one with the enormous buttons?”

“You insisted on sleeping in it.”

“I don’t remember that.”

“You were very determined.”

Afterward, I made tea with water that had already begun to cool.

***

The following week I brought the woman a wristwatch.

It kept excellent time, but I hated looking at it.

She turned it over in her palm.

“A gift?”

“From my father.”

“Is he alive?”

“Yes.”

“Then this should be straightforward.”

It wasn’t. She worked for nearly an hour, using tools so small I could barely see them. Finally she loosened something beneath the face, and a dry seed fell onto the counter.

“An apology,” she said.

“His or mine?”

She slid it toward me.

“I can’t tell from here.”

I carried it home in my wallet. For three days I took it out whenever I paid for something, then tucked it behind a receipt.

On Sunday I called my father.

We discussed football, then his car, then the weather. I nearly hung up.

“I shouldn’t have said that at Christmas,” I told him.

“No,” he said.

I waited.

“Neither should I.”

After the call, I looked for the seed. It was still there. I planted it in a pot on the kitchen windowsill.

***

By autumn, the shop had become popular.

People queued with lamps, umbrellas, jammed drawers, music boxes. A man brought a door still attached to its frame. Two sisters arrived carrying opposite ends of a dining table.

There were complaints.

One customer wanted a refund because his repaired radio played only songs he had once loved. Another accused the woman of ruining a perfectly good mirror.

“What did you do to it?” I asked.

“Removed a flattering distortion.”

“Can you put it back?”

“Certainly.”

“Will you?”

“If she asks again.”

The woman never advertised. She closed for lunch. Sometimes she refused a job without explaining why.

***

In November, I found her packing.

The telescope was wrapped in newspaper. The empty frames were stacked by the door. She had finished the gray knitting; it was a scarf, much shorter than I expected.

“Are you leaving?”

“My sister has room for me.”

“What about the shop?”

“Someone will rent it.”

I stood there holding a toaster. It had been burning everything for a week.

She took it from me.

“This one really does need a new thermostat.”

“Oh.”

“I’ll order it before I go.”

Behind her, the window looked bare. Without the objects, I could see straight through to the street.

“I thought you might stay,” I said.

“I know.”

She wrote my name on a label and tied it to the cord.

***

A bakery opened there in February.

For a while, I resented it. Then one wet morning I went inside and bought two buns, still warm from the oven.

I took them to my father’s house.

We ate at the kitchen table. He wore his old cardigan, the one missing a button. I noticed it while he was telling me about a train journey.

This time I listened to the end.

Then I asked if he had a sewing kit.

The city opened the Office of Unused Time on a Tuesday, between the licensing bureau and a shop that repaired vacuum cleaners.

Nobody noticed for three weeks.

Then a retired teacher named Mrs. Vale came in carrying a biscuit tin.

“I believe,” she said, “these are yours.”

The clerk looked up. His name was Daniel, and until recently he had worked in parking enforcement. His new position came with no instructions beyond a rubber stamp, a ledger, and a brass sign:

**TIME CANNOT BE REFUNDED.**

Mrs. Vale placed the tin on his desk. Inside were buttons, a photograph of a dog, and eleven minutes.

Daniel knew they were eleven minutes in the way he knew the photograph was a photograph. They lay folded between the buttons, pale and slightly warm.

“What kind of minutes?” he asked.

“The ones before my husband came home. I used to finish making dinner early and wait in the kitchen. Sometimes I’d check the potatoes again.”

“How many years?”

“Forty-six.”

Daniel considered the tin.

“There should be more.”

“I expect I used most of them.”

He entered eleven minutes in the ledger.

“Will you be wanting a receipt?”

“What would I do with it?”

He stamped a receipt anyway.

By Friday, there was a queue.

People brought afternoons lost to delayed trains, hours spent pretending to understand instructions, the strange hollow seconds after someone said, *We need to talk.*

A man arrived with seven years in a suitcase.

Daniel declined to accept them.

“They weren’t unused,” he explained.

“You didn’t see my marriage.”

“That doesn’t mean you weren’t there.”

The man left the suitcase. Daniel spent the morning trying to lift it, then pushed it under the desk with his foot.

At first, unused time went into filing cabinets. Later, the city provided shelves. By winter, Daniel could barely reach his chair.

The time made a quiet sound. Not ticking. More like a room full of people turning pages.

He began to learn its habits.

Unused Saturdays smelled faintly of cut grass. Minutes saved by walking faster were thin and slippery. The time children spent waiting for adults was heavier than it looked.

There was very little unused sleep.

One afternoon, a girl of about seventeen came in without a coat.

“Can I withdraw something?”

“We receive deposits.”

“But you’ve got all this.”

She gestured at the shelves.

Daniel glanced at the brass sign.

“What would you need?”

“Twenty minutes.”

“For?”

“My mother gets home at six. I get home at six-twenty. She leaves for work again at six-fifteen.”

“Different shifts?”

The girl nodded.

“She leaves dinner in the microwave. I leave notes on the fridge.”

Daniel had a form for deposits. He turned it over and wrote WITHDRAWAL on the blank side.

“Name?”

“Mara.”

He found twenty minutes beneath a box of cancelled dental appointments. They were ordinary weekday minutes, clean and almost transparent.

He put them in an envelope.

“How do I use them?” Mara asked.

“I don’t know.”

She turned the envelope over.

“Do I swallow them?”

“I wouldn’t.”

She laughed. Daniel realized it was the first laugh he had heard in the office.

The next day, Mara returned.

“It worked.”

“What did you do?”

“I sat on the bus and held them.”

“And?”

“The bus got in early. Or I got off early. I’m not sure.” She paused. “We had tea.”

Daniel waited.

“She told me about a woman at work who keeps stealing her yogurt.”

“Was that worth twenty minutes?”

“Yes.”

After that, Daniel started issuing withdrawals.

Ten minutes to a baker who wanted to watch snow fall before beginning the ovens. An hour to two brothers who had been discussing their inheritance for eight months without mentioning their father. Three minutes to a man who needed to tell his doctor something he had denied at every appointment.

There were rules, though Daniel discovered them mostly by getting things wrong.

Time could not carry you backward.

It would not make someone answer the phone.

You could not stockpile it. A businessman requested six additional months, then returned furious because the envelope contained nothing but dust.

“What were you going to do with them?” Daniel asked.

“Keep my options open.”

Daniel noted this in the ledger.

One evening, Mrs. Vale returned with her biscuit tin.

“More minutes?” he asked.

“No. I wondered if you needed the buttons.”

He didn’t, but accepted them.

She looked around the office.

“You’ve given quite a lot away.”

“Yes.”

“What do people do with it?”

“Mostly ordinary things.”

“Good,” she said. “That’s mostly what there is.”

After she left, Daniel sat at his desk until the vacuum repairman locked up next door.

He had three messages from his sister.

He had been meaning to call her since September. There was never a suitable evening. She had children; he worked late; they were not particularly close.

He picked an envelope from the shelf.

Then he put it back.

His phone rang twice before she answered.

“Is everything all right?”

“Yes,” Daniel said.

“Oh.”

He could hear water running.

“Are you busy?”

“Just washing up.”

He pictured her kitchen, which he hadn’t visited in years. He still imagined the yellow cupboards from their childhood home.

“What colour are your cupboards?”

“What?”

“Your kitchen cupboards.”

“White. Why?”

“I don’t know. I was thinking they were yellow.”

She turned off the tap.

“You’re thinking of Mum’s.”

“Yes.”

For a while they talked about that kitchen: the broken drawer, the burn mark beside the stove, whether there had really been a mouse behind the freezer.

When they hung up, Daniel wrote nothing in the ledger.

He put on his coat, switched off the light, and stood outside looking for his keys.

He had left them on the desk.

For once, he did not mind going back.

The city had a department for lost minutes.

It occupied the third floor of a building nobody remembered entering. You could find it only when you were late for something important and had stopped, briefly, to look at the sky.

Most people arrived angry.

“I had it a moment ago,” they said, slapping the counter. “An entire afternoon. I was going to do something with it.”

The clerk would give them a form.

Name.
Approximate duration.
Last known location.
Was the time lost willingly?

That last question caused trouble.

People could remember an afternoon disappearing into a screen, or a summer collapsing into work, but they objected to the word *willingly*. It sounded like blame.

The clerk, whose name was Mara, had learned not to explain it.

She simply pointed to the boxes.

Yes.
No.
I don’t know.

Almost everyone chose the third.

Behind her were drawers containing moments recovered from across the city. Eleven seconds found beneath a dentist’s chair. A Sunday morning discovered in an unopened package of curtains. Forty-two minutes lifted from the space between a father saying, “We need to talk,” and his son answering, “Okay.”

The moments were not stored in clocks. Clocks were only containers for time that still belonged somewhere.

Lost time took other shapes.

A wasted hour resembled a pale, heavy pear. A minute of embarrassment looked like a tiny red bird and had to be handled with gloves. Time spent waiting for medical results collected as cold water. Mara kept it in sealed jars, although the water sometimes rose against the lids.

Happy time was difficult.

It became almost nothing: a feather, a warm coin, a smell that vanished when named.

For twenty-three years, Mara had sorted what people misplaced.

Then, one Thursday, a boy arrived carrying a shoebox.

He was perhaps nine. His coat was fastened incorrectly, giving him the air of someone assembled in a hurry.

“I found these,” he said.

Inside the box lay seven small stones, smooth and blue.

Mara put on her spectacles.

“Where?”

“In my mother’s room.”

“Is your mother missing them?”

“No,” said the boy. “She’s missing.”

Outside the window, a delivery van stopped in the rain.

Mara brought the box behind the counter and held one stone in her palm.

At once she was standing in a kitchen she had never seen. Someone was cutting an apple into slices. A child was explaining, with furious precision, that a whale was not a fish. The woman holding the knife nodded solemnly.

“Well,” she said, “I’m glad somebody told me.”

Then the kitchen disappeared.

Mara set the stone down.

“These aren’t lost minutes,” she said.

“What are they?”

“Kept ones.”

The boy looked relieved, as though this were an administrative distinction that might help.

“Can you get her back?”

Mara had forms for mistaken deliveries, damaged hours, and time recovered after the claimant had moved away. She had no form for this.

“No,” she said.

The boy nodded too quickly.

“But I can help you look at them.”

He sat beside her while she laid the stones on a square of felt. In one, his mother was asleep in a chair, a book open against her chest. In another, she was angry about a broken window. There was a bus ride, a birthday cake that leaned badly, a song sung without knowing most of the words.

The smallest stone contained no picture at all. Mara heard breathing, then the boy’s voice, much younger, asking whether she was awake.

She was.

They took a long time with that one.

“Will they wear out?” he asked afterward.

“I don’t think so.”

“What if I forget where I put them?”

“Keep the box somewhere you’ll find it.”

He considered this.

“I’ll need a bigger box.”

After he left, Mara went into the storeroom.

There, behind eleven years of neglected lunch breaks, was a drawer she had never opened.

Her own name was written on it.

She knew what it held. A telephone call she had delayed. An evening she had spent doing accounts because her father would still be there tomorrow.

Inside was a small grey cup.

She lifted it.

Her father’s kitchen appeared around her. There was the burn mark beside the stove, the calendar still showing the previous month. Through the window she could see him in the garden, reaching up to tie a branch to its support.

This was the hour she might have visited. He had made tea anyway.

Mara stood very still.

The cup warmed in her hand. She knew that if she tipped it toward her lips, she could remain until the hour was over. Perhaps she could go into the garden. Perhaps, though she had never advised anyone to try it, she could speak.

She put the cup back.

For a while she stayed on the floor beside the open drawer.

Then she went downstairs and used the telephone in the lobby.

Her sister answered on the sixth ring.

“Mara?”

“Yes.”

“Is something wrong?”

Mara looked through the glass doors. The rain had stopped. A man was unlocking his bicycle, holding a loaf of bread beneath one arm.

“No,” she said. “I wondered if you were home.”

“I’m home.”

“Could I come over?”

There was a pause, long enough for Mara to hear her sister move something away from the receiver.

“Of course,” she said. “Have you eaten?”

Mara hadn’t.

She went back upstairs for her coat. On the counter lay the boy’s discarded claim form. He had filled in his name, then crossed it out and written his mother’s.

Mara placed it in the drawer for unresolved cases.

For once, she left work before closing time.

samples.result:
The city installed a thirteenth hour on a Tuesday.

At first, nobody noticed. Tuesdays were already long.

The new hour appeared between 3:00 and 4:00 in the afternoon, when most people were too tired to argue with clocks. Wristwatches hesitated. Phones displayed a small gray circle. The clock above the railway station turned its hands backward, then forward, as though reconsidering an answer.

By evening, the mayor had issued a statement.

“This additional hour represents an exciting opportunity for increased productivity.”

By Wednesday, employers had claimed it.

By Thursday, parking meters had learned to charge for it.

Only the old clock repairer on Bell Street put a sign in his window:

**NO CHARGE FOR THE EXTRA HOUR.**

His name was Elias. He had been repairing clocks for forty-three years, although lately people brought him other things: a toaster, a mechanical bird, a lamp shaped like a lighthouse.

“Does it keep time?” he would ask.

“No.”

“Then I can’t promise anything.”

He usually fixed them anyway.

On the first Friday of the new hour, a girl came into his shop carrying a kitchen clock under one arm.

“It’s wrong,” she said.

Most customers said this.

“How wrong?”

“It doesn’t do the extra bit.”

She put it on the counter. It was yellow, with a painted lemon where the twelve should have been. At 3:00, its second hand continued obediently toward 4:00. Outside, every other clock in the city had entered the new hour.

Elias took off his glasses.

“Where did you get this?”

“Our kitchen.”

“Yes. Before that.”

“My mum bought it.”

“May I keep it overnight?”

The girl folded her arms.

“We need it.”

“For what?”

“To know when things happen.”

Elias considered this.

“Fair enough.”

He fetched a battered travel clock from the shelf behind him.

“A loan,” he said.

“Does that one do the extra bit?”

“Yes.”

She looked disappointed.

That night, Elias opened the yellow clock.

There was no strange mechanism inside. No hidden spring. No tiny door through which impossible afternoons might enter. Just a battery, a circuit, and a little dust.

He cleaned it. He checked the contacts. He sat with it through the extra hour the following afternoon.

The clock refused.

At 3:17, according to the yellow clock, Elias heard somebody laughing outside. Two boys were riding a shopping trolley down Bell Street. One stood inside with his arms out; the other pushed. They passed the bakery, which was closed, and the pharmacy, which was open, and disappeared around the corner.

At 3:42, a woman stopped beneath the tree opposite his shop. She put down two heavy bags and stood without doing anything at all.

Elias watched her.

He realized he had not seen anybody stand without doing anything for a very long time.

When the girl returned, he asked her name.

“June.”

“June, who lives in your house?”

“Me. My mum. Sometimes my uncle, but only when his boiler breaks.”

“And during the extra hour?”

“Mum works.”

“What do you do?”

“Wait.”

He looked at the yellow clock.

“Where?”

“School, mostly. They made another lesson. It’s called Independent Enrichment.”

“Do you like it?”

“We do worksheets.”

Elias wound the travel clock, although it did not need winding.

“Your clock is perfectly healthy,” he said.

“Then why’s it wrong?”

“I’m not sure it is.”

June took it home.

The following week, three people brought clocks that would not recognize the extra hour.

One belonged to a retired violin teacher. One had hung for twenty years in the back room of a café. The third was a watch worn by a nurse who came straight from a night shift, still carrying a packet of crackers in her coat pocket.

Elias inspected them all.

There was nothing wrong with any of them.

He began asking questions.

The violin teacher spent the extra hour playing badly, which she preferred to playing well for an audience.

The café owner closed his shutters and ate lunch with his brother.

The nurse slept.

By the end of the month, there were seventeen clocks on Elias’s shelves that kept the old time.

A reporter visited.

“Are these devices defective?”

“No.”

“Is this a protest?”

“I repair clocks.”

“Do you believe time should belong to the people?”

Elias looked annoyed.

“Whom else would it belong to?”

That sentence appeared in the newspaper above a photograph in which he looked like a man accused of stealing his own furniture.

More clocks arrived.

A bus driver brought his mother’s alarm clock. A solicitor brought a watch she had bought to celebrate making partner. June brought a friend whose clock still followed the new hour.

“What do I have to do?” the friend asked.

Elias had no answer.

“Can I stay here for a bit, then?”

He found her a stool.

She sat beside the counter and drew the clocks in a notebook. At half past three, she turned the page.

The mayor’s office sent a letter. The manufacturers sent a warning. His landlord reminded him that Bell Street was a commercial district.

Elias put all three envelopes beneath the short leg of his workbench.

By winter, there was usually someone sitting in the shop during the extra hour. June did her homework there, then complained about having done it. The nurse sometimes came to collect a repaired watch and fell asleep in the chair by the radiator.

Elias still charged for repairs. Batteries and rent had not become less expensive.

But between three and four, he made tea.

If a customer asked when their clock would be ready, he checked the workbench before answering. If someone stayed, he found another cup.

The city kept its lost things beneath the railway station.

Not just umbrellas and gloves. Those were upstairs, in plastic bins beside a man who ate oranges with a pocketknife.

The other things were downstairs.

You reached them by asking for a ticket to somewhere that no longer existed. The clerk would look at you for a moment, then slide a brass token under the glass.

Mara asked for a ticket to the house where she grew up.

“Single or return?” the clerk said.

She hadn’t expected that.

“Return.”

He gave her the token.

Below the station, the air smelled of dust and warm electrical wiring. A woman sat behind a desk, repairing a radio. Her gray hair was held back with two pencils.

“What have you lost?”

“My father’s voice.”

The woman set down her screwdriver.

“When?”

“Not when he died. Before that, I think. I can remember things he said, but when I try to hear him saying them, it’s my own voice.”

“People often come for that.” She pulled a drawer open. “Name?”

“His or mine?”

“His. Unless he was someone different with you.”

Mara gave both names.

The woman wrote them on a card and handed it to her.

“Aisle nine. You may hear things calling from other shelves. Don’t answer unless you’re certain they belong to you.”

Beyond the desk stood rows of shelves that disappeared into a darkness deeper than the room should have allowed. Each aisle had a hanging lamp. Under the lamps were boxes, bottles, envelopes, small wooden cabinets.

A jar labeled THE ABILITY TO SLEEP IN A MOVING CAR sat beside a shoebox marked CONFIDENCE, AGE ELEVEN.

Mara paused at an empty stretch of shelf.

“That’s for passwords,” the woman called. “They don’t stay long.”

In aisle four, something laughed behind a cabinet door. It was a boy’s laugh, breathless and delighted. She thought of a classmate whose name she had forgotten. She kept walking.

On a shelf in aisle seven lay a pair of blue mittens.

Her mother had knitted mittens just like them. Mara had lost one on a school trip, and her mother had made a third, slightly larger. For a winter she’d worn the mismatched pair. These were the same size.

She left them alone.

Aisle nine smelled faintly of coffee.

There were hundreds of voices. Some lived in seashells. Others were wound onto reels of tape or folded into paper birds. One came from a chipped cup: a woman saying, “Careful, it’s hot,” over and over.

Mara checked the names on the labels.

She found her father near the floor, between a tin of a grandfather’s whistling and an answering-machine cassette labeled DON’T WAIT UP.

His voice was in a plain brown envelope.

She crouched and held it.

Inside, he said, “Well, let’s have a look.”

She sat down on the floor.

He used to say that when she brought him broken things: a bicycle light, a school project, the little music box with a dancer who had stopped turning. Once, when she was seventeen, she’d brought him a letter she was afraid to send.

“Well, let’s have a look.”

The envelope was light enough to blow away.

She opened it.

“Hold this a second.”

“Where’s your mother?”

“No, the other screwdriver.”

“Oh, Mara.”

That last one hurt. She couldn’t place it. It might have been after she crashed the car, or when she arrived for a visit without warning. She tried to make him say it again, but now he was complaining about the price of pears.

She stayed on the floor until the lamp above her flickered.

Back at the desk, the woman had coaxed a weather forecast out of the radio. Rain was expected somewhere.

“Can I take it home?” Mara asked.

“Yes.”

“How do I keep it?”

“Listen occasionally. Don’t try to learn every word. And keep it away from magnets.”

“Might I lose it again?”

“You might.”

Mara looked down at the envelope. “What do I owe you?”

“Something you’re finished with.”

From beneath the desk, the woman brought out a shallow wooden tray.

“Not something you want to be finished with,” she added. “People offer grief all the time. It usually follows them out.”

Mara considered the small injuries she still carried. A friend who hadn’t called. Something cruel she’d said and never apologized for. The woman waited, working a thumb against a smear of solder on the desk.

Then Mara remembered a telephone number.

For years after leaving home, she could still dial it without thinking. It had belonged to the kitchen wall, to her mother shouting that dinner was ready, to her father taking messages on the backs of envelopes. The number had been disconnected long ago.

She spoke it into the tray.

Seven little clicks sounded against the wood.

The woman covered the tray with a cloth.

At the top of the stairs, Mara tried to remember the number. She knew the first digit had been a four, but couldn’t be sure of the rest.

Outside, rain darkened the pavement. She tucked the envelope inside her coat and hurried to the bus stop.

At home, she put the kettle on. Then she took the envelope out and set it on the kitchen table.

For a while it was quiet.

She found a mug, opened the cupboard, and discovered she was out of tea.

“Well,” her father said, “let’s have a look.”

Mara pulled up a chair.

The lost property office opened at six, although nothing was ever lost that early.

At six, people still believed the day would behave itself. Keys waited in bowls. Wallets occupied pockets. Names belonged to faces. The losses began after breakfast, once the buses started and the children were sent outside.

Nevertheless, Mara arrived at five forty-five and put the kettle on.

The office occupied a former railway station beside a line that no longer went anywhere. In summer, grass grew between the tracks. In winter, the rails held the frost until noon. The timetable remained nailed to the platform wall, promising arrivals that had not occurred for thirty-seven years.

Mara had tried to remove it once. By morning, it was back.

She no longer interfered with the timetable.

On her first day, nineteen years earlier, her predecessor had shown her the shelves.

“Umbrellas here. Gloves there. Things people are ashamed of losing go in the drawers.”

“What sort of things?”

“You’ll know.”

Then he gave her a ring of keys, took his hat from a peg, and left without telling her where the drawers were.

She found them eventually.

Most of the work was ordinary. Spectacles. Shopping bags. A brass door knocker. Single shoes, never pairs. But every few months someone brought in something less easily described: the courage to leave a husband; the taste of a grandmother’s soup; an afternoon that had disappeared between two Tuesdays.

Mara entered everything in the ledger.

She had discovered that naming a thing was often enough to keep it from getting lost again.

On a Wednesday in November, a boy arrived carrying a cardboard box with both hands.

He was perhaps ten. His coat had been buttoned incorrectly, leaving one corner longer than the other.

“I found this under the bridge,” he said.

Mara cleared a space on the counter.

Inside the box lay a small, dark object. It seemed to move when she looked away.

“Where under the bridge?”

“Near the shopping trolley.”

“Did you touch it?”

“Only with my sleeve.”

She fetched the thick gloves.

The object was warm. When she lifted it, she heard a woman laughing somewhere very far away.

“What is it?” the boy asked.

Mara turned it carefully in her hands.

A summer evening flickered across the window: yellow light on a kitchen wall, a dog asleep beneath a table. Then the glass showed the platform again.

“I think it’s someone’s future,” she said.

The boy frowned.

“Can you lose that?”

“Apparently.”

“Will they come for it?”

“We’ll put up a notice.”

She wrote:

**FOUND: ONE FUTURE.  
UNDER THE NORTH BRIDGE.  
OWNER MUST DESCRIBE.**

The boy read it twice.

“Can I wait?”

Mara looked at the clock. School had already started.

“You can wait until the kettle boils.”

He stayed all morning.

By lunchtime, eleven people had arrived to claim it.

A retired dentist described a villa overlooking the sea. A woman with ink on her fingers described three books she had not written. A young man described becoming so rich that nobody would ever interrupt him again.

The object remained quiet.

Mara asked each of them to leave an address, in case anything else turned up.

At two, the boy’s father arrived.

Mara knew him slightly. He repaired roofs and had once collected a bucket of nails left on the evening bus.

“There you are,” he said.

The boy looked down.

“I called the school,” his father continued. “Then I called your aunt. Then I called the school again.”

“I found something.”

“I can see that. Get your coat.”

Mara reached for the telephone to explain, but the father put a hand on the back of the boy’s chair.

“Please,” he said. “We need to go.”

At his voice, the thing in the box began to shine.

All three of them looked at it.

“That’s yours,” the boy whispered.

His father shook his head.

For a moment, nothing happened. Then the room smelled of fresh bread.

The station clock struck thirteen.

Outside, the bare trees became green.

Mara saw the father sitting at a kitchen table, older by twenty years. Across from him sat the boy, grown, telling a story so badly that neither could stop laughing. A third place had been set. Someone was coming down the stairs.

Then the leaves vanished. The clock resumed its ticking.

The father stood very still.

“My wife died in March,” he said.

Mara lowered her eyes.

“I’m sorry.”

He sat beside his son. For a long time he watched the box.

“I thought that was it,” he said at last.

The boy leaned against him, but he did not seem to notice until the boy took his hand.

“Is it hers?” he asked.

“No,” Mara said. “Yours.”

“But she wasn’t there.”

“No.”

He put his free hand into the box. The dark thing softened under his palm.

“How do I take it home?”

“Perhaps in the box.”

He nodded, grateful for instructions.

Before they left, Mara straightened the boy’s coat buttons. His father carried the future carefully, keeping the box level as they crossed the platform.

That evening, Mara closed the office late.

She checked the shelves, turned off the lamps, and stood beside the drawer she had never entered in the ledger.

Inside lay the sound of her sister saying her name.

She had found it in a dream eleven years ago and kept it wrapped in a clean handkerchief. Sometimes she opened the drawer merely to make sure it was still there.

Now she unwrapped it.

“Mara,” said her sister.

Nothing followed. Mara waited anyway.

At last she folded the handkerchief and put it back in the drawer. She left the drawer open while she washed her cup.

Outside, beyond the weeds and the rusted tracks, a train sounded its horn.

Mara took her coat from the peg, locked the office, and walked down to the platform to look.

samples.result:
The lost-property office was beneath the railway station, behind a door most people mistook for a cupboard. Mara had worked there for seventeen years. She had returned umbrellas, violins, dentures, a sack of onions, and once a sleeping boy whose mother had boarded the wrong train.

She had never received a Tuesday before.

It arrived in a cardboard box at 8:40 on a Thursday morning. The porter set it beside her tea.

“Platform six,” he said.

“What is it?”

He shrugged. “Still warm.”

Inside the box was a pale light, folded several times. It smelled of rain on pavement and toast left too long under a grill. Somewhere within it, a telephone rang three times and stopped.

Mara checked the label.

**TUESDAY, 14 OCTOBER.**  
**UNCLAIMED.**

She glanced at the calendar above her desk. Wednesday, 15 October. Someone had forgotten to turn the page.

Yesterday had been Wednesday. The day before—

She sat down.

The day before was Monday.

Outside, trains moved through the station with their usual tremendous indifference.

***

By noon, Mara had made seven telephone calls.

The railway supervisor told her to contact the council. The council told her to contact the observatory. The observatory asked whether the Tuesday had a visible tail.

Finally she called her sister.

“Do you remember what you did on Tuesday?”

“Which Tuesday?”

“This one.”

A pause.

“I suppose I went to work.”

“You suppose?”

Another pause, longer.

“Mara, I’m in the middle of something.”

Her sister hung up, which was what her sister did when frightened.

Mara opened the box again.

A bus sighed at a stop. Someone laughed with a mouthful of food. A dog barked once, decisively, as if settling an argument.

At the bottom lay a small blue mitten.

She did not touch it.

***

There were regulations for unclaimed property.

Perishables: dispose of after twenty-four hours.

Valuables: secure in the locked cabinet.

Ordinary articles: retain for ninety days.

The regulations said nothing about days themselves.

Mara put the box in the cabinet between a silver cigarette case and a trumpet. Then she went upstairs to buy a sandwich.

The station was full of people staring at clocks.

Near the departure board, a man in a grey coat was arguing with his phone.

“I sent it Tuesday,” he said. “I know I sent it Tuesday.”

A little girl beside him tugged his sleeve.

“Dad, when was my birthday?”

“Saturday.”

“No. My school birthday.”

He looked down at her.

Mara carried her sandwich back untouched.

***

At four o’clock, the first claimant appeared.

He was an elderly man wearing a tie patterned with tiny fish.

“I understand you have something,” he said.

“What have you lost?”

He took off his glasses and polished them.

“My wife died on Monday night.”

Mara waited.

“Wednesday morning, I woke up and knew she was dead. But I couldn’t remember the first day of knowing it.”

From inside the cabinet came the sound of water filling a kettle.

The man shut his eyes.

“I thought perhaps I’d been spared.”

Mara unlocked the door.

The box trembled when she placed it on the desk.

He leaned over it. The light rose to his face. For a moment Mara could see a kitchen reflected in his glasses: two cups on a shelf, a chair pulled back from the table.

Then he began to cry.

She fetched a clean handkerchief from the drawer where she kept things too personal to auction.

***

More people came.

A student who had passed an examination.

A woman who had kissed someone she should not have kissed.

A delivery driver who remembered reversing his van on Monday and receiving a complaint on Wednesday, but not breaking the ornamental gate between.

They stood together in the cramped office. Nobody was sure how to queue.

Mara asked each person to describe what they had lost.

The student remembered the examiner tapping a pencil against his teeth.

The woman remembered a loose button.

The driver remembered, after a while, the exact sound of the gate.

With each answer, the Tuesday brightened.

It began to unfold.

Mara moved the ledger and her tea. Then the telephone. Light spilled over the edge of the desk and pooled around their shoes.

The porter appeared in the doorway.

“Oh,” he said. “It’s got out.”

***

At six, the station manager came downstairs carrying a form.

“We’ll need everyone’s details.”

Nobody moved.

The old man with the fish tie was smiling now, exhausted.

“It can’t be returned individually,” Mara said.

“Why not?”

She looked at the box. Through its open sides, rain was falling across a thousand streets. A woman searched for a receipt. Someone peeled an orange. In a hospital room, a hand moved beneath a blanket.

The manager lowered his form.

“What do we do?”

Mara considered the office window. It was small and stiff, opening at pavement level. All summer she had meant to ask someone to fix it.

“Help me with this.”

***

They pushed together.

The frame gave with a crack, and cold evening air entered the room.

Tuesday rose slowly, catching on the filing cabinet and the porter’s sleeve. Mara freed it. For an instant it rested against her hands.

She remembered the bowl she had broken that morning.

Her mother’s bowl. Blue, with a white rim.

She had swept it up before work and stood over the bin, holding the largest piece. Then, because she was late, she had dropped it.

Now she remembered sitting down afterward.

Only for a minute.

Tuesday passed through the window.

Above them, conversations faltered. A suitcase fell over. Across the station, a hundred phones began to ring.

The people in the office left quietly.

Mara entered the date in her ledger. Under *Description*, she wrote: *One day.*

Under *Condition*: *Used.*

She waited for the ink to dry, then closed the book and went home.

samples.result:
The town had a lost-and-found office for things that could not be put in a drawer.

It stood between the bakery and the locksmith, in a building so narrow that two people entering together had to decide which of them was lonelier. Above the door, a painted sign read:

**LOST HOURS, UNFINISHED CONVERSATIONS, OTHER ITEMS**

Mara had worked there for thirty-one years.

Every morning, she unlocked the door, watered the fern, and checked the overnight box. Usually there was a misplaced afternoon or an apology that had arrived too late to be useful. Once, someone turned in the smell of a grandfather’s coat. It stayed in the office for six months, making everything faintly resemble rain and pipe tobacco.

The owner never came.

Mara kept it anyway.

There were rules. Lost things could not be manufactured. Found things could not be improved. Nothing could be returned to someone who only wanted it because another person had it.

People argued about that last one.

“But it was my happiness,” they would say.

“Was it?” Mara would ask, and usually they would look at the floor.

On a Tuesday in November, a boy arrived carrying a cardboard box.

He was perhaps twelve. His jacket sleeves stopped short of his wrists. He placed the box on the counter with both hands, carefully, as though something inside might wake.

“I found this in the park.”

Mara opened the flaps.

Inside was a summer evening.

The office filled with warm grass, distant lawn mowers, and the gold light that briefly makes even ugly buildings seem necessary. Somewhere, beyond sight, a screen door banged shut.

“That’s a good one,” Mara said.

“Can you find who lost it?”

“Sometimes.”

“What happens if you can’t?”

“We keep it safe.”

The boy nodded, but did not leave.

“Would you like a receipt?”

“No.”

“Then what is it?”

He studied the fern.

“Can someone lose something on purpose?”

Mara closed the box.

“Yes.”

“And then want it back?”

“That happens too.”

The boy pulled his sleeves down over his hands.

“My mother doesn’t laugh anymore.”

Mara waited.

“She smiles. At people. When she has to. But it’s different.”

“Do you think she lost her laugh?”

“I don’t know. I thought maybe you could check.”

Behind Mara, shelves climbed to the ceiling. There were jars of courage, envelopes of almost-forgotten names, and a large blue tin containing the particular satisfaction of taking your shoes off after a long walk.

There were laughs too.

But a laugh without its owner was difficult to recognize. Some sounded like coughs. Some looked like birds. One had been sitting on the filing cabinet since April, refusing to explain itself.

“What’s your mother’s name?”

“Eleanor Vale.”

Mara searched the ledger.

Nothing.

The boy watched her face.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

He nodded too quickly.

“That’s okay.”

People often said that when something was not okay at all.

After he left, Mara opened the cardboard box again.

The summer evening rose around her.

A woman stood in a garden, laughing so hard she had one hand against her ribs. A little boy was wearing an enormous straw hat. Someone had dropped a bowl of strawberries. Red fruit scattered through the grass.

Mara reached for the ledger.

Then she stopped.

You could not improve a found thing. You could not take it apart and distribute the pieces you believed someone needed.

A summer evening was not a laugh.

She shut the box.

For three days, she thought about Eleanor Vale.

On Friday, she broke a rule that was not written down: she went looking.

The Vales lived above a hardware shop. Eleanor opened the door wearing a gray sweater with a loose thread at the cuff.

“Has something happened to Ben?”

“No,” Mara said. “He brought something to my office.”

“Oh.”

Eleanor’s expression changed. Not relief exactly. Something heavier setting down its bags.

“He thinks I’ve lost my laugh.”

Mara said nothing.

“My husband died last year.”

From somewhere inside came the small click of a radiator cooling.

“I’m sorry.”

“He used to do ridiculous things,” Eleanor said. “Not big things. He would announce dinner like a railway departure. Put labels on the fruit bowl. *Emergency pears.* That sort of thing.”

She smiled.

Mara did not mistake it for laughter.

“Ben misses him,” Eleanor said.

“Yes.”

“So do I.”

“Yes.”

Eleanor looked past her, toward the stairs.

“Do you actually have it?”

“Your laugh? No.”

“Then I don’t know what you can do.”

“Neither do I.”

That seemed, unexpectedly, to help.

Eleanor invited her in.

They drank tea at a small kitchen table. Mara learned the husband’s name was Daniel. He had disliked olives, loved maps, and once spent an entire holiday trying to photograph a kingfisher.

“He never got the picture,” Eleanor said.

“Did he see one?”

“Several. Apparently that wasn’t the point.”

When Mara left, Eleanor was holding a cold cup between her palms.

The summer evening remained unclaimed.

Months passed. Mara put it on a shelf beside a perfect snow day and the feeling of being expected somewhere.

Then, in March, Ben returned.

“No box today?” she asked.

He shook his head.

“She laughed.”

Mara put down her pen.

“What happened?”

“I burned the toast.”

He considered this.

“Really badly.”

“Was she angry?”

“First.”

“And then?”

“I told her it was emergency toast.”

The boy grinned, and Mara laughed.

He glanced over her shoulder at the shelves.

“So you can lose things and get them back.”

“Sometimes.”

“Even if nobody finds them?”

Mara thought of Eleanor setting the burned toast on a plate, of Ben watching her, waiting to see what she would do.

“Apparently.”

After he left, she noticed her tea had gone cold. She drank it anyway, then moved the summer evening to a lower shelf. Whoever came to collect it would not need to wait for her to fetch the ladder.

The shop appeared between the pharmacy and the laundromat on a Tuesday, which was inconvenient, because I had walked that stretch of pavement every morning for eleven years and preferred not to discover that the world had been keeping spare rooms.

Its window contained a chair, a green apple, and a handwritten sign:

**MINOR LOSSES RECOVERED.**

Underneath, in smaller letters:

**No people. No pets. No exceptions.**

I went in because of a blue button.

It had fallen from my father’s coat the winter before he died. I remembered hearing it strike the kitchen floor, remembered thinking I would pick it up after I finished washing the cup in my hand. By the time I set down the cup, I had forgotten.

This was nineteen years ago. I had no practical use for the button. The coat was gone.

A woman behind the counter was repairing an umbrella with a needle threaded through rain.

“Keys?” she asked.

“A button.”

“Buttons are easy.”

“It’s been a long time.”

“That generally isn’t the difficulty.”

She put the umbrella aside. A few drops fell upward.

“Describe it.”

“Blue. Dark blue. Four holes. A scratch along one edge.”

“Material?”

“I don’t know.”

“Most people don’t.”

She opened a drawer and took out a small white dish. In it lay the button.

I recognized the scratch. For a moment, I also recognized the kitchen: the damp windows, the cup warming my fingers, my father at the table struggling out of his coat.

“What does it cost?”

“What were you doing when you lost it?”

“Washing a cup.”

“Then a cup will do.”

“There’s no cup here.”

“Bring one tomorrow.”

I took the button home.

It was lighter than I remembered.

***

The next morning I brought a yellow mug from the back of my cupboard. The woman turned it over, checked the base, and nodded.

I asked whether she could recover other things.

“Sometimes.”

“A conversation?”

“Words, occasionally. Not conversations.”

“An opportunity?”

“No.”

“A feeling?”

She looked up sharply.

“What feeling?”

I hadn’t expected to be asked. Outside, a bus sighed at the curb.

“Never mind.”

She took the mug to a shelf already crowded with cups. One had a broken handle; another was so small it might have belonged to a doll.

“People usually come back three times,” she said.

“What happens the third time?”

“They ask for something I can’t give them.”

***

On my second visit, I asked for six minutes.

“When?”

“June. About twenty years ago. Maybe twenty-one.”

“What happened?”

“Nothing.”

She waited.

I had been sitting on a wall behind a supermarket with a woman named Elise. We were sharing a carton of strawberries we hadn’t paid for yet. It was hot, and the bricks were warm through my shirt.

There had been six minutes—perhaps five, perhaps eight—when I was not thinking about what came next. Not work. Not whether Elise liked me as much as I liked her. Not the unopened envelope on the table at home.

A delivery truck was backing toward the loading dock. Elise had a strawberry seed stuck to her wrist. She was telling me about something her brother had done, and I was laughing too hard to hear the end.

The shopkeeper listened without touching anything.

“You can’t take those away with you,” she said.

“I don’t need to.”

She went through a curtain behind the counter and returned carrying a shallow wooden box.

“Sit down.”

The chair from the window was beside me now. I sat.

She opened the lid.

I had expected light, or a scent, or some other trick I could recognize as a trick.

Instead, my shoulders dropped. The chair was comfortable. There was no particular reason to speak.

The woman continued repairing her umbrella.

After a while, she closed the box.

“How long?” I asked.

“Six minutes.”

I rubbed my palms against my knees. I wanted her to open it again, but I was embarrassed to ask.

“What do I owe you?”

“An afternoon.”

“Which one?”

“One you haven’t made plans for.”

I agreed before asking how she would collect it.

***

On my third visit, I brought nothing.

The shopkeeper was eating the green apple.

“I wondered when you’d come,” she said.

“I want the last time I spoke to my father.”

“No people.”

“Not him. The call.”

“Tell me.”

He had called to ask whether I knew where his spare glasses were. I was at work. Someone stood beside my desk, waiting for me to finish.

I told him to check the drawer by the stove.

He asked how I was.

“Fine,” I said. “Busy.”

“All right. I’ll let you go.”

Those were his last words to me.

“I want to answer differently.”

“You can’t.”

“I could have talked for another minute.”

“Yes.”

I disliked her for agreeing.

She put the apple down.

“What did you say after that?”

“After what?”

“After he said he’d let you go.”

I tried to remember the phone in my hand, the person beside my desk. For years, I had stopped at my father’s words.

“I said, ‘Talk to you Sunday.’”

“And?”

“He said, ‘Right you are.’”

I sat down without being asked.

The woman gave me a clean handkerchief from beneath the counter. I didn’t use it, but held it until she needed to close.

***

The shop was gone the next morning.

Between the pharmacy and the laundromat stood a narrow brick wall, darkened near the pavement. I ran my fingers along the mortar.

That Saturday, I meant to clear out a cupboard. Instead, I fell asleep on the sofa after lunch and woke when it was nearly dark. I couldn’t account for the hours.

In my pocket was the blue button.

I keep it in the drawer by the stove. Sometimes, looking for batteries or a rubber band, I come across it. I turn it over, feel the scratch with my thumb, and put it back.

The city’s lost-property office occupied a room beneath the central station, between a locked electrical cupboard and a vending machine that sold only tomato soup.

Mara had worked there for eleven years.

People lost predictable things: umbrellas when the rain stopped, gloves when the weather improved, books they had been meaning to finish. They lost wallets reluctantly and wedding rings under circumstances Mara had learned not to investigate.

Every object received a numbered tag. Every claimant had to describe something that couldn’t be guessed.

“Blue umbrella” was insufficient.

“Blue umbrella with a broken spoke and a handle my daughter repaired with pink tape” was usually enough.

On a Tuesday in November, a man arrived carrying nothing.

“I’ve lost a Saturday,” he said.

Mara looked up from a box of spectacles.

“Which Saturday?”

“The one when my son was nine.”

Behind him, the soup machine dropped a paper cup. Neither of them turned.

Mara opened the bottom drawer of her desk.

This drawer was not mentioned in the training manual. Her predecessor had shown it to her on his final afternoon, after surrendering his keys.

“Sometimes,” he’d said, “people lose things that don’t fit on the shelves.”

Inside were several plain envelopes.

Mara took out the oldest.

“Tell me about it.”

The man sat down.

“I was supposed to take him fishing. I’d bought the rods. He slept with his beside the bed.”

“What happened?”

“A client called. Something urgent.”

“Was it?”

“I don’t remember.”

Mara waited.

“He stood in the doorway while I was on the phone. He had his coat on. After a while, he took it off.”

The envelope grew slightly heavier in her hand.

“Do you remember what you said?”

“Next weekend.”

She slid it across the desk.

He did not touch it.

“What’s inside?”

“Your Saturday.”

“Can I go back?”

“No.”

“Can I see it?”

“Yes.”

He opened the flap.

Mara looked away. She always did.

For several minutes there was no sound except the station above them: footsteps, announcements, the long metallic complaint of a departing train.

Then the man began to cry.

When he left, he took the envelope.

That evening, Mara called her brother.

They talked about his boiler, which was making a noise like someone shaking a tin of screws. Neither mentioned that it had been eight months since their last conversation.

Before hanging up, he said, “You should come Sunday.”

“All right,” she said, surprising them both.

***

After that, the unusual claims increased.

A woman came looking for the courage she had possessed at seventeen.

A retired teacher had misplaced the name of someone he once loved.

A child wanted yesterday’s dream, the one with the enormous white horse, because he had woken before learning where it was going.

The bottom drawer always contained the right envelope.

There were rules, though Mara had never been told them. She discovered them by making mistakes.

You could not retrieve something for another person.

You could not claim a thing merely because you regretted losing it.

And you had to be able to say what was missing.

“Everything,” one woman said.

Mara could offer her only a chair and a cup of tea.

They sat together until closing.

***

In December, a girl brought in a red mitten.

“Found this on platform four.”

“Thank you.”

The girl remained at the counter.

“Is this where you get things back?”

“Sometimes.”

“My dad lost his laugh.”

Mara glanced toward the drawer.

“He’s still got the little one,” the girl explained. “The one he uses when people visit. Not the proper one.”

“Does he know it’s missing?”

The girl considered this.

“I think he knows where it is.”

“Then he’ll have to come himself.”

“He won’t.”

Mara set the mitten on a clean patch of desk.

“People surprise us.”

The girl gave her a look that made the sentence feel cheap.

After she left, Mara put the mitten beside the envelopes instead of on the shelf.

She wasn’t sure why.

***

On the last working day before Christmas, Mara arrived to find her predecessor waiting outside the office.

He had become smaller since retiring. His coat seemed to have kept its original dimensions.

“Still getting the odd ones?” he asked.

“Yes.”

He nodded.

They went inside. Mara switched on the heater.

“I’ve come to make a claim,” he said.

She took her place behind the desk.

“What have you lost?”

He examined his hands.

“I don’t know.”

She waited.

“That’s the trouble. I keep thinking of things it might be. My wife. My health. The house we sold. But those are gone, not lost.”

Mara opened the drawer.

There was only one envelope inside.

It was empty.

He saw it and smiled without pleasure.

“I wondered.”

“What does it mean?”

“It means I haven’t come to the right place.”

She made tea anyway.

They drank it while commuters hurried overhead.

Before leaving, he touched the counter.

“You know you’re allowed to use it?”

“The drawer?”

“You work here. You’re not furniture.”

***

That night, Mara sat alone after closing.

For years she had believed she’d lost her mother’s voice.

But she could hear it perfectly: *Take the bread out before it burns.* *Ring when you get there.* Her mother’s voice had survived in instructions.

What Mara couldn’t remember was the last time they had enjoyed each other’s company.

Not a hospital visit. Not an argument softened by exhaustion. An ordinary afternoon.

She opened the drawer.

The envelope smelled faintly of oranges.

Inside was a grocery receipt, seventeen years old.

Reading it, Mara remembered her mother trying to balance a cabbage on the kitchen scales. It kept rolling off. They had laughed until her mother sat down.

Mara put the receipt in her pocket.

On Sunday, she went to her brother’s house carrying bread.

He opened the door before she knocked.

“You came.”

“Yes,” she said. “I said I would.”

samples.result:
The first thing the city forgot was how to pronounce the river.

For centuries, its name had passed easily from mouth to mouth. Children shouted it from bridges. Lovers whispered it into collars. Old women said it when predicting rain.

Then, one Tuesday, a bus driver paused halfway through announcing the next stop.

“River,” he said finally.

By evening, the maps had changed.

Nobody panicked. Cities lose things all the time: umbrellas, factories, entire neighborhoods beneath new names. The river kept moving. Its ducks displayed no concern.

But the following week, everyone forgot the little song people hummed while waiting for kettles to boil.

After that, the smell of the cinema lobby.

Then the reason a certain bench in the western park had always been painted blue.

That was when Mara began collecting.

She had worked for thirty-one years repairing clocks, although she disliked the phrase. Most clocks didn’t need repairing. They needed cleaning, patience, and someone willing to believe their small interior troubles mattered.

Her shop stood between a pharmacy and a building that had once been a pharmacy. In the window sat a clock with no hands.

“What does that one tell?” customers asked.

“Whether you’re looking,” Mara said.

She began with the bench.

Its blue paint was peeling. One leg rested on a brick. Mara sat beside a man eating an orange and asked if he remembered why it was blue.

“No.”

“Do you remember knowing?”

The man stopped peeling.

“Yes,” he said.

This distinction seemed important.

Mara wrote it down.

Soon she had seven notebooks filled with things the city had forgotten but still felt the shape of: a joke whose punch line had vanished; the location of a door everybody remembered knocking on; a woman who had sold flowers outside the station, though nobody could recall her face or what had happened to her.

People brought these absences to the clock shop.

“I miss something,” they would say.

“What?”

“That’s the trouble.”

Mara made tea. She asked them where the missing thing hurt.

One boy pointed to his teeth.

An elderly dancer touched the back of her knee.

A taxi driver held out both hands, as if whatever he had lost might still be resting there.

She wrote everything down.

At night, the notebooks made sounds.

Not words, exactly. More like a room full of people deciding whether to speak.

Mara wasn’t frightened. She had spent her life listening to mechanisms after everyone else declared them dead.

She placed the notebooks on her workbench and waited.

Eventually, one opened.

On the blank page at the back, a sentence appeared.

**You cannot keep what nobody uses.**

Mara considered this.

Then she wrote beneath it:

**I use these.**

The reply came slowly.

**You store them.**

Outside, a tram passed without ringing its bell. Mara realized she could no longer remember the sound.

She put down her pen.

“What would count?” she asked the room.

The pages lifted in a draft she couldn’t feel.

The next morning, Mara carried a kettle to the western park.

She set it on a camping stove beside the blue bench. A handwritten sign read:

**TEA. PAYMENT: SOMETHING YOU ALMOST REMEMBER.**

The man with the oranges returned first.

“My brother,” he said, “used to sing a song about a horse with a government job.”

“Sing what you can.”

“I can’t.”

“Then sing what you can’t.”

He gave her a suspicious look, but accepted a cup.

After a while, he sang three uncertain notes.

A woman walking a terrier stopped.

“That’s not right,” she said.

“Then help.”

She supplied two more notes, badly.

The terrier barked.

Somebody laughed, and the man began again.

By noon, twelve people were arguing about whether the horse had worked at the post office or collected taxes. Nobody settled it. But they sang the song six times, with increasing confidence and decreasing accuracy.

That evening, the first notebook grew quiet.

Mara kept going.

For the cinema lobby, they borrowed a popcorn machine and found an old red curtain in a school basement. They hung it between two trees. People stood beneath it, smelling butter and dust, describing films they had seen with people they no longer knew.

For the vanished joke, they held a competition for the worst possible punch line.

For the missing door, they built one.

It stood upright in the park, attached to nothing. People knocked. Other people answered.

Sometimes they said, “Come in.”

Sometimes, “Not today.”

One woman knocked, waited, and began to cry.

Nobody asked her why. Someone pulled the blue bench closer so she could sit down.

Weeks passed.

The city still forgot things. A staircase. A recipe. The particular silence after heavy snow.

Mara’s notebooks still filled.

But now people came to the shop carrying other things too: flour, photographs, trumpet cases, a jar of buttons, an unreasonable quantity of string.

They had ideas.

One afternoon, a little girl arrived with a cardboard box.

“What have you got?” Mara asked.

“A place for something.”

The box was empty except for a folded cloth.

“What thing?”

“I don’t know yet.”

Mara cleared a space on the counter.

That night, the notebooks spoke again.

**This is not preservation.**

“No,” Mara agreed.

**Some of it is wrong.**

“Yes.”

There was a long pause.

Then:

**The horse collected taxes.**

Mara smiled.

The next day, she added a verse.

Years later, when the clock shop belonged to someone else, people still met in the western park. The kettle had been replaced several times. The door had been repaired until none of its original wood remained.

Nobody could remember why the bench was blue.

They painted it blue anyway.

samples.result:
The first bench Daniel installed faced a brick wall.

He checked the work order twice. There was the address, the diagram, the small black arrow indicating the direction of the seat. Behind him stood a perfectly respectable park: plane trees, a pond, a statue of a man whose achievements had outlasted everybody’s interest in them. In front of him stood a wall.

He called his supervisor.

“Is there a reason?”

“There’s always a reason,” she said. “It’s not always on the form.”

So he drilled the holes.

By eleven, the bench was secured. He swept the dust into a neat gray pile and stood back. It looked like a punishment somebody had forgotten to administer.

An old man approached carrying two paper cups.

“You’ve finished.”

“Apparently.”

The man handed him a coffee.

“Was this your request?” Daniel asked.

“Yes.”

“You know it faces the wall.”

“I was quite specific about that.”

Daniel drank. The coffee was sweet enough to hurt his teeth.

The old man sat at the left end of the bench, leaving room beside him. He wore a brown suit with shining elbows and shoes that had been repaired more carefully than they had originally been made.

“What used to be here?” Daniel asked.

“A cinema.”

“Before my time.”

“Before most things.”

Across the street, a delivery driver argued with a parking meter. Somewhere in the park, a child was explaining the rules of a game to another child who had already decided not to follow them.

“My wife worked in the ticket booth,” the man said. “I used to wait outside until her shift finished.”

Daniel looked at the wall. There were pale rectangles where signs had once hung.

“Did you go to the films?”

“Not often. We were saving.”

“For what?”

The man considered this.

“At first, a washing machine.”

“And after that?”

“A better washing machine.”

Daniel laughed. The man smiled into his cup.

“People imagine their parents had grand ambitions. Sometimes we just wanted the sheets to come out less wet.”

That afternoon, Daniel installed three ordinary benches facing ordinary things.

He found himself annoyed by them.

***

The old man came every Thursday.

Daniel knew because Thursday was inspection day. He drove through the district with a clipboard, checking for loose bolts, splintered wood, graffiti. The work required him to sit briefly on every bench. His supervisor called this load testing. His brother called it the best job in the country.

At the wall, the old man always had two coffees.

His name was Arthur. His wife had been named June.

“She hated June,” he said one week.

“Her own name?”

“The month. Too many weddings. She said nobody should make promises while the weather was flattering them.”

Another Thursday, Arthur brought a photograph. June stood inside the ticket booth, one hand raised against the camera.

“She looks annoyed.”

“She was. I’d told her to smile.”

“Did she?”

“Not that afternoon.”

Daniel looked closely. Behind her was a board advertising a film he recognized from television.

“My mother loved that one.”

“Everyone loved that one. June said the ending was dishonest.”

“Was it?”

Arthur took the photograph back.

“I don’t remember the ending.”

***

In November, Arthur stopped coming.

Daniel arrived with his clipboard and found the bench wet, empty, and scattered with leaves. He checked the bolts. He sat down.

The following week, he brought two coffees, then felt foolish and drank both.

He thought about asking the council for Arthur’s address. He thought about whether that would be permitted. He thought about it long enough that it became the thing he had done instead of asking.

December arrived with early darkness.

Someone sprayed a silver crown on the wall. Someone else drew a door beneath it.

Daniel reported the graffiti. It was washed off within forty-eight hours.

He regretted reporting the door.

***

In January, a woman was sitting on the bench.

She had Arthur’s eyes and June’s expression from the photograph.

“You must be the bench man,” she said.

Daniel nodded.

“I’m his daughter.”

“I’m sorry.”

She rubbed a gloved hand along the armrest.

“He didn’t die.”

“Oh.”

“He fell. Then there was a hospital stay, and an argument about stairs. He’s living with me now.”

“That’s good.”

“It is, depending on which of us you ask.”

She handed Daniel an envelope.

Inside was a photograph of Arthur sitting in a kitchen, looking offended by a slice of cake. On the back, in uneven handwriting, he had written:

*The coffee here is terrible. Otherwise acceptable.*

Daniel laughed.

“He asked me to give you that,” she said. “And to tell you something about the cinema.”

“What?”

“She wasn’t my mother. June.”

He looked again at the wall.

“They were engaged before the war. It didn’t work out. He met my mother later.”

Daniel put the photograph back in its envelope.

“So why—”

“I asked him.” She pulled her scarf higher. “He said he waited here a lot.”

***

The bench remained.

On inspection days, Daniel tightened what needed tightening and picked litter from beneath the seat. Once, he found a bus ticket tucked between two slats. Once, a blue mitten no larger than a plum.

In March, somebody drew another door on the wall.

This one had a round handle, three hinges, and a little crooked mail slot. Daniel stood in front of it with the graffiti report open on his phone.

Then he closed the report.

He sat on the bench to complete the inspection. A woman walking past slowed, looked at the wall, and looked at him.

“What’s there?” she asked.

“Used to be a cinema.”

“Is that why the bench faces that way?”

Daniel shifted to check the last bolt.

“Somebody asked for it,” he said.

samples.result:
The city opened its Department of Lost Things on a Tuesday, because Mondays were already responsible for enough.

At first, the department occupied a narrow room behind the tax office. There were shelves for umbrellas, drawers for keys, and a refrigerator for lunches abandoned on buses. A clerk named Mara sat beneath a sign that read:

**IF YOU HAVE LOST SOMETHING, PLEASE DESCRIBE IT WITHOUT EXAGGERATION.**

This proved difficult.

“My wallet,” people said, “with my whole life in it.”

“My wedding ring. It means everything.”

“My phone. I’m literally dead without it.”

Mara would hand them a form.

“Just the object, please.”

For seven years, the work was ordinary. Gloves arrived singly. Earrings glittered in little envelopes. Someone misplaced a trombone, which remained unclaimed despite being difficult to forget.

Then, one rainy afternoon, an elderly man entered carrying nothing.

“I’ve lost the smell of my mother’s kitchen,” he said.

Mara looked up.

“Was it attached to anything?”

“No.”

“Did you lose it on public transport?”

“I don’t think so.”

He stood quietly while rain ticked against the window.

“She used to burn the butter a little,” he added. “Not badly. Just enough.”

Mara should have sent him away. Instead, she gave him a form.

Under *Description of Item*, he wrote: *Warm. Slightly bitter. Before anything bad happened.*

That evening, while locking the cabinet of watches, Mara smelled butter browning in a pan.

Behind the cabinet stood a small blue door.

It had not been there that morning.

Mara opened it.

Inside was a kitchen, though not exactly a kitchen. There were no walls, only the suggestion of wallpaper. A woman’s voice hummed beyond sight. On the stove, butter foamed in a blackened skillet.

Mara closed the door carefully.

The next day, she called the elderly man.

He stayed inside for eleven minutes.

When he came out, he was crying, but he looked less tired.

“Can I take it home?”

“I don’t know how you would.”

He nodded. Before leaving, he asked whether he might return sometime.

Word spread.

Soon people came looking for things no shelf could hold: the courage they had possessed at nineteen, a language they had stopped speaking, the feeling of being expected somewhere.

The department moved into an abandoned railway station.

New doors appeared nightly.

Behind one lay the summer before a brother died. Behind another, the precise silence following a snowfall in a village that no longer existed. One room contained nothing but the conviction that tomorrow would be better.

That room was always booked.

Mara hired assistants. They developed procedures.

No flame was allowed near recovered anger. Lost afternoons had to be stored flat. Childhood friendships were fragile and could not be exposed to fluorescent light.

Some items remained stubbornly missing.

Nobody found the right words for the last conversation.

Nobody recovered time in usable quantities.

People complained about this.

“I pay taxes,” one man said.

Mara agreed that he probably did.

There were dangers, too.

A woman found her first love and refused to leave the room. A violinist recovered his ambition, only to discover it no longer fit inside his life. A father asked for his daughter’s trust, but the department could locate only the moment he had broken it.

“We don’t manufacture things,” Mara told him.

He stayed sitting across from her long after she finished speaking.

Years passed. Mara’s hair silvered. The station filled with doors.

Every morning she checked the arrivals ledger. Every evening she walked the corridors, listening for leaks. Once, an unattended room spilled three hours of Sunday happiness into the main hall, and everyone missed their train without minding.

Mara herself filed no requests.

She considered this professionalism.

Her assistants considered it suspicious.

“You must have lost something,” said Ivo, the youngest.

“Of course.”

“Then why not look?”

She capped her pen.

“Someone has to keep the office open.”

One winter, a package appeared on her desk.

It was wrapped in brown paper and addressed in her own handwriting, though she did not remember writing it.

Inside lay a small brass key.

Attached was a note:

*You are allowed to miss what you chose to leave.*

Mara sat down.

Before the department, before the tax office, there had been a house near the sea. There had been a man who laughed with his whole face. There had been plans involving a garden, a dog, a table large enough for friends.

She had left.

The leaving had been necessary.

This had not made it painless.

For thirty years, she had confused regretting the loss with regretting the decision. Whenever a good memory surfaced, she rehearsed the reasons she had gone until it sank again.

At the end of the western corridor, a door waited.

The key turned easily.

Inside, the sea breathed against a shore of pale stones.

There was the house, its windows lit. There was the garden they had never planted. She could hear him laughing somewhere indoors.

Mara stood on the path.

She did not enter.

Instead, she sat on the low wall and watched the water darken.

For the first time in years, she remembered an ordinary happy evening without making herself account for it. They had eaten outside. He had dropped a fork between the boards of the deck. Neither of them had wanted to get up and fetch another.

She stayed until she was cold.

In the morning, Mara changed the sign above the front desk.

It now read:

**IF YOU HAVE LOST SOMETHING, YOU MAY DESCRIBE IT AS BEST YOU CAN.**

Below that, in smaller letters, she added:

**FINDING IT DOES NOT OBLIGE YOU TO TAKE IT BACK.**

Then she unlocked the station doors.

Outside, people waited in the cold, holding photographs, empty boxes, and one unremarkable umbrella.

Mara welcomed them in.

The city hired a man to repair the things nobody else could find.

His office was between a locksmith and a bakery, behind a blue door that appeared only when someone was walking slowly enough. Most people passed it for years without noticing. This was not magic, exactly. The city had discovered that a great many useful things could be accomplished by making people slow down.

On the door, in gold letters, it said:

**MINOR RESTORATIONS**  
*No miracles before noon.*

The man’s name was Ellis. He had a kettle, three good screwdrivers, and a drawer full of buttons that belonged to coats no longer in existence.

Every morning, he swept the pavement outside his office. Every afternoon, he repaired whatever arrived.

A woman brought him the last five minutes of a conversation with her father.

“I didn’t know they were the last,” she said.

Ellis examined the minutes beneath his desk lamp. They were ordinary-looking: a remark about the weather, a question about the car, a silence in which neither person had felt the need to speak.

“Nothing’s broken,” he told her gently.

“But I would have said something different.”

“Yes.”

“Can you change it?”

“No.”

She stood for a while, holding her bag with both hands.

“What can you do?”

Ellis found a small wooden box, lined it with soft cloth, and placed the minutes inside.

“I can make them easier to carry.”

She returned a week later with two oranges. Ellis ate one at his desk and left the other on the windowsill, where it glowed in the afternoon sun.

—

Some repairs were straightforward.

A boy had lost his ability to enjoy Saturdays. Ellis discovered a splinter of Monday lodged behind the boy’s left ear and removed it with tweezers.

A retired bus driver brought in a dream that had started making an unpleasant grinding noise. It needed oil.

A young couple arrived carrying a silence between them. They had wrapped it in a towel, but it kept leaking onto the floor.

“Is this the comfortable kind or the dangerous kind?” Ellis asked.

“We’re not sure.”

He listened to it.

“Neither,” he said. “This one’s hungry.”

He sent them away with instructions to feed it one honest sentence each evening. Nothing grand. *I’m afraid you’re bored with me.* Or: *I miss you even when you’re in the room.*

They asked how long the treatment would take.

“Until you stop counting,” he said.

—

Ellis was not especially wise. He forgot birthdays. He had once spent forty minutes looking for spectacles already on his face. He disliked admitting when he was wrong, though he generally managed it before bedtime.

He knew how to repair things because he had broken a great many of them.

In his twenties, he had broken a promise.

In his thirties, a friendship.

In his forties, the habit of expecting good news.

The city hired him at fifty-three, after finding him in a park trying to mend a paper kite that did not belong to him.

“Do you have experience?” asked the woman from the municipal office.

“Mostly on the other side of the transaction,” he said.

“That will do.”

—

One November afternoon, a girl came in carrying nothing.

Ellis waited.

She waited.

Outside, rain moved down the window in uneven lines.

“What needs repairing?” he asked.

“I don’t know.”

“How old are you?”

“Eleven.”

At eleven, Ellis had understood that adults were in charge of the world. At twelve, he had noticed how often they were frightened. He still remembered the awkward year between those discoveries.

“Would you like some tea?”

“No.”

“A biscuit?”

“Yes.”

She ate it carefully, catching the crumbs in her palm.

“I think,” she said, “there’s something wrong with wanting things.”

Ellis put down his screwdriver.

“What sort of things?”

“All sorts. When I get one, I want another. When I don’t get one, I’m miserable. My mother says I should be grateful.”

“Your mother may be tired.”

“She is.”

They considered this together.

Ellis took an empty jar from a shelf and handed it to her.

“What’s that for?”

“Tomorrow, find one thing you weren’t looking for.”

“Like money?”

“Possibly. A funny dog will do. Or a patch of sunlight. Or someone being kinder than necessary. Write it on a piece of paper and put it in the jar.”

“Will that make me stop wanting things?”

“No. Come back when it’s full, and tell me what you found.”

She inspected the jar.

“Can I decorate it?”

“I was hoping you would.”

—

Years passed.

The locksmith retired. The bakery changed hands. People began paying for bread with watches, which Ellis found unsettling.

The girl returned at twenty-six with a cracked blue jar and a baby asleep against her shoulder.

The boy who had lost Saturdays became a nurse.

The couple sent a postcard from a town by the sea. On the back, one had written, *Still feeding it.* The other had added, *It eats a lot.*

One morning, Ellis found that his own joy would not start.

He tapped it. Shook it. Held it up to the light.

Nothing.

For the first time in years, he left the blue door closed.

By noon, a small crowd had gathered outside: the nurse, the couple, the woman who once brought oranges, the locksmith leaning on a cane.

Nobody knew precisely what to do.

The woman put the kettle on.

The nurse opened the curtains.

The couple argued quietly over whether Ellis needed soup, then made some.

The locksmith tightened a loose hinge.

Ellis sat among them while sunlight spread across the floor. His joy still would not start, but when the soup was ready, he ate two bowls.
