The city had a department for everything, including things it preferred not to discuss.

There was a Department of Bridges, a Department of Sanitation, and a Department of Trees Whose Roots Had Become Everybody’s Problem. There was an office that issued permits for music after ten at night. There was another that collected the permits and denied having issued them.

In the basement of the municipal building, behind a door marked STORAGE, was the Department of Unfinished Things.

Mara found it on a Tuesday while looking for a bathroom.

Inside, a man in a cardigan sat beneath a clock with no minute hand. Behind him stood rows of shelves containing objects that seemed ordinary until she looked closely: a scarf ending in a knitting needle, a chessboard midgame, a letter with only “Dear” written at the top.

“Name?” the man asked.

“I’m just looking for—”

“Most people are.”

He opened a ledger.

“Mara Vale,” she said, although she couldn’t have explained why.

The man ran one finger down a page. “You have quite a collection.”

“I’m sorry?”

He stood, fetched a cardboard box from a shelf, and placed it on the counter. Her name was written on the lid in her own handwriting.

Inside was the blue notebook in which she had once intended to write a novel. Underneath lay a plane ticket to Lisbon, a packet of tomato seeds, and a photograph of her younger brother.

“That’s mine,” she said.

“Yes.”

“How did you get it?”

“Things arrive.”

The photograph had been taken beside a river. Her brother was seventeen, all elbows and certainty, squinting into the sun. Mara remembered the argument afterward. He had called her afraid of everything. She had told him fear was a reasonable response to knowing him.

That had been twelve years ago.

He was alive. That was somehow worse for the purposes of the box.

“I don’t understand.”

“Would you like the official explanation?”

“Would that help?”

“Rarely.”

He took the lid and set it beneath the box.

“We store what people leave unfinished. Not everything, obviously. Nobody has shelf space for every abandoned sandwich. Only the things that keep taking up room after they’re gone.”

Mara touched the notebook. She had last seen it in an apartment she no longer remembered fondly.

“Can I take them?”

“One at a time.”

“Why?”

“We tried allowing more. People became ambitious. It caused a backlog.”

She looked again at the photograph.

The man said nothing.

“What happens if I leave them here?”

“Nothing.”

“Forever?”

“We don’t use that word in municipal government.”

Mara almost laughed.

She chose the tomato seeds.

The clerk nodded without approval or disappointment. He stamped a form and handed her the packet.

Outside, rain had darkened the pavement. She stood under the municipal building’s stone awning and read the instructions.

Sow indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost.

It was September.

For the first time all afternoon, this struck her as genuinely inconvenient.

***

She returned the next Tuesday.

“I planted them,” she said.

The clerk looked up. “Good morning.”

“In pots. On the windowsill. I know it’s the wrong season.”

“Plants don’t read.”

“They’re going to die.”

“Possibly.”

She waited for something wiser.

He continued sharpening a pencil.

“I’d like the notebook.”

He brought down the box.

At home, Mara opened it to the first page. There was a title, crossed out three times. Then a sentence:

*When the sea disappeared, everybody blamed the mayor.*

She remembered writing it. She remembered being delighted.

On the next page were seventeen reasons the idea wouldn’t work.

She tore out that page.

Then she regretted tearing it out and put it back between the covers.

For an hour she wrote badly. The mayor acquired a wife, then lost her because Mara couldn’t decide what she wanted. A fisherman discovered his boat balanced on the roof of the aquarium. Someone stole all the salt from the supermarkets.

At midnight, she stopped.

The sea was still missing. Nobody had explained anything.

She slept better than she had in months.

***

On her third visit, the clerk wasn’t there.

A woman sat at the counter eating an orange.

“Where’s the man?”

“Dentist.”

Mara felt foolishly relieved.

“I’d like something from my box.”

The woman retrieved it, then turned back to peeling the orange.

The plane ticket was expired. The notebook was at home. The seeds had become six pale stems bending toward the window.

Only the photograph remained.

Mara picked it up.

“Do you have a phone?” she asked.

The woman pointed to one beside the ledger.

Her brother’s number had survived three phones and several declarations that she intended to delete it.

He answered on the fourth ring.

“Mara?”

She watched the woman place a curl of orange peel on a napkin.

“I found a picture of you,” she said.

“All right.”

“By the river.”

He was quiet.

“You looked ridiculous,” she said.

“You took it.”

“I know.”

Neither of them apologized. Not then.

He told her he had moved. She told him about the tomatoes.

“It’s September,” he said.

“I’m aware.”

He laughed, and she recognized it before she recognized how much she had missed it.

***

In December, the plants produced one tomato.

It was small, crooked, and mostly green. Mara put it on the kitchen table and called her brother to report the harvest.

He suggested frying it.

She said that seemed disrespectful.

“Of course,” he said. “Better to let it rot.”

She found a pan.

While the oil heated, she opened her notebook. The sea had returned during the night, filling the streets with cold water. She had no idea what happened next.

samples.result:
The city hired someone to listen to the bridge.

Not inspect it. Not measure its strain or test the bolts, though other people did those things. This job was to sit beneath the eastern span between midnight and five, wearing headphones connected to six microphones, and write down anything unusual.

The official title was Acoustic Infrastructure Monitor.

The woman who got the job was named Ada.

On her first night, she recorded:

**00:43 — Truck crossing. Loose panel, perhaps.**  
**01:16 — Rain begins.**  
**03:02 — Sound resembling a spoon dropped into a sink.**

At five, she handed the notebook to a man in an orange vest. He nodded without opening it.

“Anything serious?”

“I don’t know what serious sounds like yet.”

“You’ll learn.”

—

The bridge was forty-seven years old. It carried buses, delivery vans, ambulances, people who had argued at dinner, people going home to apologize. Underneath it, the river dragged leaves toward the sea.

Ada worked from a small concrete room that smelled of warm dust. There was a kettle, a desk, and a photograph of the bridge on opening day. In the photograph, everyone wore a hat.

She had taken the job because she was good at staying awake and needed money. Until recently, she had cared for her mother, whose sleep had become unpredictable. Some nights her mother had wanted breakfast at two. Some nights she had wanted to telephone someone who had died in 1986.

Ada had learned to listen from the next room.

The bridge was easier. Mostly.

—

In October, she began hearing a knocking sound.

Three knocks, then two.

It came after the last bus crossed, but before the first delivery truck.

She reported it.

An engineer visited with a tablet and very clean boots. He checked the microphones, looked at a diagram, and asked whether the noise might be coming from a boat.

“There isn’t a boat.”

“Expansion, then. Cooling steel.”

“Does cooling steel knock in a pattern?”

“People are good at hearing patterns.”

He was not unkind. He seemed tired. Before leaving, he adjusted the kettle’s plug, which had been hanging half out of the socket.

That night, Ada heard the knocks again.

Three, then two.

She waited.

“Hello?” she said, feeling foolish.

The bridge made a sound like a spoon dropped into a sink.

—

After that, Ada brought a wooden ruler to work.

When the knocks came, she tapped the desk.

Three, then two.

The reply arrived almost immediately.

Two, then three.

She sat very still.

In the notebook she wrote:

**02:11 — Possible structural movement. Follow-up required.**

Then, below it:

**Responds.**

She crossed that out so thoroughly the paper tore.

—

November was cold. Ada bought fingerless gloves and began taking soup in a flask.

The bridge, if it was the bridge, had no useful vocabulary. They developed a few signals. One knock meant yes. Two meant no. A low metallic groan meant either *I don’t understand* or *a heavy vehicle is crossing*.

Ada never managed to distinguish those.

“Are you in pain?”

Two knocks.

“Are you lonely?”

A long silence.

Then one.

Ada looked toward the photograph on the wall. A mayor with enormous scissors. Children holding paper flags. The river much wider than it seemed now.

“All those people go over you,” she said.

One knock.

“None of them stop.”

One knock.

She unscrewed her flask.

“That happens.”

—

She started reading aloud.

At first she read the newspaper. The bridge seemed uninterested in elections and strongly interested in the shipping forecast, although this might have been a loose support vibrating when the wind changed.

Then she brought novels.

Sometimes a lorry interrupted an important passage and she had to repeat it. Sometimes she fell asleep mid-sentence and woke to a small, reproachful ping.

She began leaving the bookmark on the desk during the day, as though someone might come in and continue without her.

—

In December, the city announced repairs.

A section of the eastern span would be replaced. New joints. New surfaces. A long list of improvements printed beneath an artist’s cheerful illustration.

Ada asked the engineer whether the bridge would still sound the same.

“Quieter, probably.”

He smiled.

“Better for you.”

That night she explained the work.

The bridge said nothing.

“They’re not taking you down. Just replacing some parts.”

Nothing.

“They replace parts of people too. Knees. Heart valves.”

At last, two knocks.

“No?”

Two knocks.

Ada waited, her hand resting on the notebook.

She had spent the previous year washing her mother’s hair in a basin, keeping water out of her ears. Afterward her mother would sometimes ask who she was. Ada had always answered.

“I don’t know,” she told the bridge.

The traffic passed overhead.

—

On the last night before construction, Ada brought no book.

She described her mother’s garden instead: runner beans leaning across the path, a cracked birdbath, the rosebush that caught everyone’s sleeves. She described the kitchen drawer full of rubber bands and the scissors nobody else could use.

Near five, the bridge knocked once.

“Yes,” Ada said.

She stayed until daylight.

—

The repairs took eleven weeks.

When Ada returned, the room had a new kettle. The photograph was gone. Somebody had painted over the damp patch beside the door.

She put on the headphones.

At 00:43, a truck crossed.

At 01:16, rain began.

She listened all night. There were tyre noises, water noises, a faint whistle she traced to the window seal.

At five, the man in the orange vest came for her notebook.

“Anything unusual?”

“Not tonight.”

She took her gloves from the desk. Then she put them back in the drawer, beside the ruler, ready for tomorrow.

samples.result:
The city employed one person to retrieve things that had fallen between the seconds.

Her name was Ada Vale, and her office was beneath the municipal swimming pool. All day, above her ceiling, people practiced not drowning. She found the sound reassuring.

Most losses were small.

A word someone had known until the instant they needed it. The last note of a song, clipped by a train entering a tunnel. The expression on a father’s face when his child, looking elsewhere, said something unexpectedly kind.

These arrived in the pipes.

Ada would hear a tapping, set down her tea, and open the brass valve beside her desk. Whatever had been lost slid into a shallow porcelain basin.

Words resembled fish bones. Musical notes were warm enough to hold against your cheek. Expressions appeared on thin, translucent leaves, which had to be stored flat or they curled into smiles that meant entirely different things.

She catalogued everything.

There were regulations.

Nothing could be returned without proof of ownership. Nothing could be retained for personal use. And no item recovered from between the seconds was to be confused with something deliberately thrown away.

This last rule caused the most arguments.

“Of course I didn’t mean it,” people would say.

Ada would turn the form toward them.

“Then you’ll need to explain what happened.”

One Tuesday, a man brought in an empty shoebox.

“I’ve lost a whole afternoon.”

Ada looked at him over her glasses.

“Have you checked your phone?”

“No. Not that kind.”

He was young enough to think grief had made him old. His coat was buttoned incorrectly, with one side hanging lower than the other. He placed the shoebox on her desk as though something sleeping lay inside.

“My mother’s kitchen,” he said. “Rain against the windows. She was making bread. I was doing homework. Nothing happened.”

“When?”

“Twenty-three years ago.”

“Why do you want it now?”

He looked down.

“She died on Sunday.”

Above them, a whistle blew. Someone shouted, “Again.”

Ada took out a form.

She disliked these cases. Not because they were difficult, although they were. She disliked the way people waited while she searched, watching her hands as if the right movement might undo everything.

“Was there anything distinctive about the afternoon?”

“She kept singing the wrong words.”

“To what?”

“I don’t remember.”

“What kind of bread?”

“I don’t remember.”

“Your homework?”

He shook his head.

Ada pushed the form aside.

“I’ll look.”

After he left, she opened the valve.

A copper taste filled the room. Then came a clatter of misplaced keys, three interrupted sneezes, and the courage a woman had gathered outside a courtroom but dropped before entering.

Ada caught the courage in a jar.

She waited.

The pipes hummed.

By evening, the basin held a chipped blue afternoon.

It was smaller than she expected, no larger than a bar of soap. She lifted it with both hands. Somewhere inside, rain moved down a window, and a boy erased an answer so vigorously that the paper tore.

She should have sealed it immediately.

Instead, she held it a little longer.

The kitchen opened around her.

There was flour on the mother’s sleeve. A radiator knocked under the window. The boy asked whether seven times eight was fifty-four.

“Nearly,” his mother said.

“That means no.”

“It does.”

He sighed and bent over his page.

She sang half a line about a sailor, substituting “cupboard” for a word Ada couldn’t hear. The boy laughed. His mother glanced at him, pleased, then returned to kneading.

That was all.

Ada set the afternoon in a padded envelope.

The man returned the next morning. He had corrected the buttons on his coat.

“I found it,” she said.

His face changed so quickly that she looked away to give him privacy.

“How do I—”

“Hold it. Somewhere quiet. It will last as long as it lasted.”

“Can I go back more than once?”

“No.”

“Can she hear me?”

“No.”

“Can I tell her—”

“No.”

He sat down.

For a while, neither spoke.

Then he asked, “Will it hurt?”

“I don’t know,” Ada said.

He nodded as though this was the first answer he trusted.

She gave him the envelope.

At the door, he stopped.

“Do people ever decide not to?”

“Yes.”

“What happens to those?”

“We keep them.”

“How long?”

Ada glanced toward the shelves behind her desk.

“Until they’re ready.”

That evening, after the swimmers had gone, she took a small parcel from the bottom drawer.

It had been there eleven years.

Inside was a morning at a railway station. Her brother stood beneath the departure board, carrying a green bag. They had argued in the car. When his train was called, she said, “Go, then.”

He went.

She had recovered the moment after the accident, intending to use it straightaway. Then she had learned that he would not hear anything she said. For eleven years, she had kept finding reasons not to open it.

Ada unwrapped the parcel.

The station was cold. Her brother shifted the bag onto his other shoulder.

“Go, then,” she heard herself say.

He looked at her. Tired, annoyed, alive.

Then he reached out and tucked the label of her coat back inside the collar.

“All right,” he said.

She had forgotten that.

The train doors opened.

Ada stayed until the morning ended.

samples.result:
The city hired a woman to listen to the bridge.

This was not the title of her job. On paper, she was a structural maintenance technician, grade four, with a pension that would become meaningful if she lived long enough. But every Tuesday and Friday, before traffic grew heavy, she walked beneath the eastern span with a thermos, a clipboard, and a small brass hammer.

She tapped the bolts. She listened.

There were sounds that meant everything was fine, sounds that meant something needed tightening, and one sound she had been told she would recognize immediately, though she had never heard it.

“What does it sound like?” she had asked during training.

Her supervisor considered the question.

“Like you should stop tapping.”

Now, seventeen years later, she thought this was the most useful instruction anyone had ever given her.

Her name was Mara. She was fifty-three. At home, she had a lemon tree that refused to fruit and a son who called from another time zone. Each offered occasional signs of progress. A blossom. A message saying, *Sorry, busy week.*

The bridge was more forthcoming.

In winter, its joints clicked. In summer, its cables gave a low humming complaint. Rain made every surface articulate. Mara knew where water collected, where pigeons nested, which repairs had lasted, and which contractors had put their faith in paint.

One Friday in October, she found a blue glove beside pier seven.

It was a child’s glove, the fingers short and stiff with cold. She placed it on a dry ledge where its owner might see it.

The following Tuesday, there were two gloves.

Not a pair. A red gardening glove had appeared beside the blue one.

By Friday, somebody had added a knitted hat.

Mara stood looking at the little arrangement.

People crossed the bridge carrying things. Sometimes they dropped them. That was all.

She tapped a bolt.

It rang cleanly.

Over the next month, the ledge accumulated a scarf, three keys on a ring, a spectacle case, and a photograph of a dog standing proudly beside a hole.

Mara could not imagine how the photograph had escaped its owner. It was not something you took out to use in the cold. On the back, in faded ink, someone had written: *He did this himself.*

She bought a transparent storage box and set it beneath the ledge. On its lid she wrote:

**FOUND HERE. TAKE WHAT IS YOURS.**

The next week, the blue glove was gone.

For some reason, this pleased her all morning.

People began leaving notes.

*Black umbrella, curved wooden handle?*

*Missing silver earring. Sentimental value only.*

*Has anyone found a brown wallet? You can keep the money. I need the license.*

Mara pinned the notes to a piece of corkboard, which she attached to the pier using an approved exterior adhesive. She was particular about that. Nothing drilled into concrete without authorization.

Then someone left a note that said:

*I miss my brother.*

She read it twice.

There was no name and nothing on the back. She put it on the board beside the note about the umbrella, though she wondered afterward whether she should have moved it somewhere less exposed.

On Tuesday, beneath it, another person had written:

*Me too.*

Mara stopped taking photographs of the board for the maintenance log.

By December, people were leaving things that were not lost.

A packet of biscuits. A paperback with a cracked spine. A jar containing seven coins and a folded note: *Bus fare if you need it.*

She worried about this. Food attracted rats. Glass broke. A box meant for gloves was becoming something she had no procedure for.

She removed the biscuits before the rain could reach them. She took the coins to the station kiosk and exchanged them for two transit cards. She left the cards in an envelope.

At Christmas, her son called while she was making soup.

They spoke about his work, the weather, whether she had arranged the problem with the kitchen window.

“Someone should fix that,” he said.

“Yes.”

“I mean properly.”

“Yes.”

After a while he asked, “Anything interesting happening?”

Mara looked at the spoon in her hand.

She could have told him about the box, or the dog photograph, which had finally disappeared after six weeks. Instead, she said, “Not really.”

When the call ended, she ate standing at the counter, then washed the pot before the soup could dry on it.

The next morning, though it was Thursday, she went to the bridge.

The box was nearly empty. The corkboard was crowded with damp paper.

Near the center, someone had written:

*I don’t know how to talk to my daughter anymore.*

Mara read it, then took a pencil from her coat.

She stood there long enough for her fingers to become cold. At last she wrote:

*You could tell her that. If you’re not expecting her to fix it.*

She did not sign her name.

In January, the city sent a young engineer to inspect her route. He had bright boots and a tablet in a waterproof case.

“What’s all this?” he asked.

“Lost property.”

He read several notes.

“Some of it doesn’t appear to be property.”

“No.”

“Is it authorized?”

Mara looked up at the bridge. Traffic passed overhead, each vehicle making a brief sound at the expansion joint.

“Not yet,” she said.

He made a note on his tablet, and she showed him a drainage channel that needed clearing.

That Friday, Mara arrived early. She checked the bolts along the eastern span, working steadily toward pier seven. There was nothing new in the box except a black umbrella with a curved wooden handle.

She dried it with an old rag and placed it where it could be seen.

The city had a department for things that almost happened.

It occupied the third floor of a building whose directory listed only a dentist and an accountant. You reached it by pressing the elevator button twice, then waiting until you remembered something you wished you had said.

Most people found it by accident.

Mara arrived carrying a bag of oranges.

She had meant to visit her father in the hospital. At the station, she had watched the doors close on the train she needed. Then she had walked aimlessly through the rain until she found a building with an unlocked door.

Behind the desk sat a woman knitting a gray sock.

“Name?” the woman asked.

“Mara.”

“Which one?”

Mara considered this.

“The one who missed the train.”

“That narrows it down.”

The woman placed the knitting in a drawer and brought out a folder. Its cover bore a date from twenty-three years earlier.

“I don’t understand,” Mara said.

“You’re not required to. Would you like a receipt?”

“For what?”

“Whatever you leave.”

Behind the woman, shelves stretched into a distance the building could not possibly contain. There were shoeboxes, glass jars, bundles of letters tied with string. A bicycle leaned against a cabinet labeled APOLOGIES: TOO LATE / STILL POSSIBLE.

Somewhere, a telephone rang once.

“I haven’t brought anything,” Mara said.

The woman glanced at the oranges.

“Those are for my father.”

“Yes.”

“He likes them.”

“Yes.”

“He’s in the hospital.”

The woman waited.

Mara put the bag on the counter. One orange rolled free and stopped against the folder.

“What is this place?”

“We keep the consequences of choices nobody made.”

“Why?”

“For a while, people find them useful.”

The woman opened the folder.

Inside was a photograph of a kitchen Mara recognized. Her childhood kitchen. Her father stood at the sink, younger than she remembered him ever being. A little girl sat at the table with a red plastic cup.

Mara touched the photograph.

“That’s me.”

“It would have been.”

“What does that mean?”

“In this version, he came home early.”

She remembered the day.

Her mother had been gone three weeks. Mara had waited at the kitchen table until it grew dark, drinking water from that red cup. When her father finally arrived, she had pretended to be asleep.

She had kept pretending for years.

“What happens in the picture?”

The woman slid it closer.

In the kitchen, the man dried his hands. He sat beside the girl. Neither spoke at first.

Then he said, “I don’t know how to do this.”

The girl looked at him.

“Neither do I.”

They ate toast for dinner.

Mara withdrew her hand.

The photograph became still.

“He never said that.”

“No.”

“He said we’d be fine.”

“Yes.”

“We weren’t.”

The woman picked up the knitting again.

“People often say that when they have no other sentence ready.”

Mara looked down the aisles.

“Is there a version where my mother stays?”

“There are several.”

“Can I see them?”

“You can.”

“Can I take one?”

“No.”

“Then what’s the point?”

The woman set down her needles.

“Some visitors need to stop wondering. Others discover they prefer what actually happened. Occasionally someone sees a thing they could still do.”

Mara thought of her father’s hospital room: the paper cup beside his bed, the television showing a cooking program neither of them watched. The last time she had visited, he had asked whether her apartment was warm enough.

She had said yes.

He had said good.

Twenty minutes later, she had left.

“What else is in my folder?”

“A degree you almost finished. A friendship you mistook for inconvenience. Three dogs. A very bad marriage. A garden.”

“A bad marriage?”

“You’re not the only person relieved you didn’t make that choice.”

Mara almost smiled.

The woman turned a page.

Here was a small apartment with yellow curtains. Here was Mara at forty, kneeling beside a dog. Here was a letter she had written and deleted, its opening line visible beneath her hand:

*I think I have been angry long enough.*

“Was that to him?”

The woman nodded.

“What did he say?”

“You never sent it.”

“But here—”

“Here, you sent it. I don’t have his answer in your folder.”

For the first time, Mara noticed the clock above the desk. It had ordinary hands, and they were moving.

“What time is it?”

“Twenty past six.”

“Visiting hours end at seven.”

“There’s another train.”

She gathered the oranges. The loose one had left a damp crescent on the counter.

“Can I have the photograph?”

The woman shook her head, then took a blank card from beneath the desk.

“I can write down what he said.”

Mara watched her print the words in blue ink.

*I don’t know how to do this.*

Outside, the rain had weakened to a mist. At the station, Mara held the card while the train approached. She had imagined the hospital conversation so many times that it always ended before she entered the room.

This time she boarded.

Her father was awake when she arrived. He looked at the bag.

“Oranges,” he said.

She sat beside him and began peeling one. The rind came away in small pieces; she couldn’t manage the unbroken spiral he used to make for her.

“Is your apartment warm enough?”

She nodded.

He waited for her to ask about the doctors.

Instead she placed half the orange on his napkin.

“I’m frightened,” she said.

He stopped reaching for it.

For a moment she thought he would tell her not to be. Then he rested his hand beside hers on the bed.

“So am I,” he said.

Mara took the card from her pocket. She looked at it once, then turned it over and put it away.

They ate the orange slowly.

The city hired a man to repair its silences.

His name was Emil, and before this he had worked on elevators. He understood the kinds of trouble that came from leaving a thing suspended too long.

The notice appeared between an advertisement for piano lessons and a warning about counterfeit parking permits.

**MUNICIPAL POSITION AVAILABLE.  
EXPERIENCE WITH DELICATE SYSTEMS PREFERRED.  
MUST BE COMFORTABLE WORKING ALONE.**

At the interview, a woman in a green suit asked him what he knew about silence.

“Usually,” he said, “it means something’s stuck.”

She wrote this down.

He started on Monday.

***

Not all silences required repair.

There were good ones: the silence after snow, the silence of someone reading beside someone else, the little hush inside a bakery before the first customers arrived.

Those were marked blue on his map.

The damaged ones were marked red.

His first assignment was a kitchen on the fourth floor of a building near the river. A mother and her adult daughter had eaten breakfast there every Sunday for eleven years. Then, one morning, the daughter had said something about moving away, and the mother had said something about gratitude, and both had discovered how many years could fit inside a sentence.

Now the kitchen was silent even when nobody was in it.

The refrigerator motor turned, but made no sound. A spoon dropped onto the floor landed without ringing. Rain struck the window invisibly.

Emil opened his toolbox.

It contained felt, copper wire, a tuning fork, three small glass jars, and an envelope labeled:

**FOR USE WHEN THERE IS NOTHING TO FIX.**

He had been told not to open the envelope until necessary.

He placed the tuning fork against the kitchen table and struck it gently.

Nothing.

He tried the refrigerator door.

Nothing.

Finally he touched it to the empty chair nearest the window.

A faint note traveled through the room.

Emil sat in that chair for forty minutes. He did not think about the daughter or the mother. He watched a ferry cross the river and watched the ferry’s wake catch up with the shore.

When he stood, the refrigerator hummed.

On his report he wrote: **Chair bearing excess weight. Relieved temporarily. Follow-up recommended.**

***

By winter, he had become good at the work.

He repaired the silence in a classroom after a teacher accidentally called a boy stupid.

He repaired the silence around a hospital vending machine where a family had waited all night and then left without buying anything.

He could recognize the brittle silence of shame and the padded silence of exhaustion. He learned not to mistake quiet people for broken people.

Some jobs could not be completed.

In a basement laundry room, he found a silence so old that the building had settled around it. He worked for three days, then closed his toolbox and recommended that the room be converted into storage.

Sometimes containment was the best available repair.

The woman in the green suit approved his report.

***

In February, an address appeared on his map that he knew.

His own.

He turned the map over, as though another address might be printed on the back.

Then he went home.

His apartment contained an armchair, two lamps, a table, and a shelf of books he mostly intended to read. The window faced a brick wall. On the kitchen counter stood a mug with a hairline crack.

His wife had bought the mug years ago at a roadside shop.

She had not died. This was important.

She lived somewhere else.

People often assumed death when he said, “She isn’t here anymore,” and he rarely corrected them. Death was easier for strangers to understand than the slow departure of a person who had been sitting beside you throughout it.

He tested the apartment.

The kettle whistled. The floorboards creaked. A bus sighed at the stop below.

Then he opened the cupboard where he kept the second mug.

Nothing.

He touched the tuning fork to it.

Nothing.

He wrapped copper wire around the handle. He placed a jar upside down on the shelf. He adjusted the hinges.

By midnight, every tool was laid out on the table.

Only the envelope remained.

Inside was a single sheet of paper.

**A silence cannot be repaired while it is being used as shelter.**

He read it twice.

Then he was angry.

This seemed an unreasonable thing for a municipal department to say to an employee.

***

In the morning, Emil called in sick.

He took the second mug from the cupboard and washed it, although it was clean.

Then he called his wife.

When she answered, he had nothing prepared.

“Hello,” he said.

“Hello.”

He looked at the damp mug in his hand.

“I think I’ve been letting people believe you died.”

There was a pause.

“That’s rather dramatic of you.”

“Yes.”

“Have you?”

“Yes.”

Outside, the bus arrived. Its brakes squealed.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

She was quiet long enough that he began to worry she had hung up.

“I didn’t know what to tell people either,” she said eventually.

He put the mug down.

They talked for twelve minutes. She asked about his work, and he told her about the classroom. He asked about her sister. Neither mentioned coming home.

Afterward, Emil opened the cupboard again.

The hinge squeaked.

He wrote **Initial repair successful** on his report, then crossed it out.

He sat at the table a while longer before writing:

**Sound restored. Cause unresolved.**

***

On Monday, he returned to work.

There was a new apprentice waiting outside his office, holding a toolbox with both hands.

“What’s the hardest part?” she asked.

Emil considered the question.

“Knowing when to leave,” he said.

He took his map from the desk. Three red marks had appeared over the weekend, one of them at the railway station.

“Bring a scarf,” he told her. “The platforms are cold.”

The city had a department for everything, including things that had stopped existing.

There was an Office of Removed Trees, where the clerks kept rings of old trunks pressed between glass. There was a Bureau of Interrupted Songs, staffed mostly by people who hummed while eating. And beneath the courthouse, down a stairway that smelled of wet wool, was the Department of Lost Mornings.

Mara found it on a Thursday, though the morning she had lost belonged to a Tuesday seventeen years earlier.

She had been nine. Her father had promised to teach her how to whistle with a blade of grass. That was all she remembered: his hands held close to her face, the green strip between his thumbs, his instruction to blow harder.

Then came the telephone call.

After that, whenever she recalled the day, it began with the call. Her father answering it. His shoulders settling into a shape she had never seen before. The drive to the hospital. Her mother’s coat folded over a chair.

The grass was still there somewhere. She was certain of it.

At the department’s front desk, an elderly man was repairing a stapler.

“I’m looking for a morning,” she said.

“Aren’t we all.”

He did not look up.

“I mean a particular one.”

“That narrows it considerably.”

He gave her a form with seven boxes.

Date. Approximate duration. Weather. Persons present. Reason for loss. Intended use upon recovery. Signature.

Under *Reason for loss*, Mara wrote: *Something happened afterward.*

The clerk read this and nodded.

“Most common cause.”

He led her through a door into a room much larger than the building above it. Shelves rose into dimness. On them stood thousands of glass jars, each holding a small quantity of light.

Some were pale and gray. Others burned gold. One contained a furious pink flicker.

“Sunrise over a laundromat,” the clerk said, noticing her glance. “Unexpectedly popular.”

“People lose that?”

“People lose everything.”

They stopped at a shelf marked with the year she had given.

The clerk ran one finger along the labels.

“Tuesday. Nine years old. Grass instruction. Here.”

The jar was smaller than she expected. About the size of one used for mustard.

Inside, the light was green.

“What do I do?”

“Open it.”

“Here?”

“Unless you’d prefer to take it home. But there is one thing.”

She waited.

“It won’t change anything that happened later.”

“I know.”

“Most people say that.”

“I do know.”

He handed her the jar and withdrew to his desk.

Mara sat on a wooden stool. The lid resisted, then gave with a soft click.

There was no flash.

She was simply in the garden.

The grass was damp through her trousers. Her father sat cross-legged beside her in the old blue shirt with a missing button. There was soil beneath one of his fingernails. A fly landed on his knee and departed.

“No, like this,” he said.

He stretched the blade between his thumbs. Blew. A thin, rude shriek cut through the air.

Mara laughed.

The sound startled her more than the garden had.

For seventeen years she had remembered herself as a child waiting unknowingly for disaster. Here she was merely laughing at a ridiculous noise.

Her father selected another blade.

“Your turn.”

“I can’t.”

“You haven’t tried.”

“I did.”

“You breathed on it. That’s different.”

She pressed her thumbs together. The blade slipped.

He waited while she tried again.

From inside the house came the clatter of a spoon dropped on the kitchen tiles.

Her mother.

Not a coat over a chair. Not the pale rectangle of a hospital pillow. Her mother, mildly annoyed with a spoon.

Mara turned toward the open back door.

“Don’t go wandering,” her father said. “You’ve nearly got it.”

She wanted to stand. To run inside. To say something immense and impossible.

Instead she stayed.

The grass squealed between her hands.

“There,” he said, smiling. “See?”

The morning ended.

She was back on the stool, holding an empty jar.

For a long time she listened to the clerk working on his stapler. Metal clicked against metal. Somewhere among the shelves, someone sneezed.

Finally she stood.

“Can I come again?”

“Of course.”

“For the same morning?”

The clerk shook his head.

“Once returned, they don’t belong to us.”

She looked into the jar. A drop of moisture clung to the bottom.

“Will I remember it?”

“Not perfectly.”

That seemed unfair. Then it seemed ordinary.

At the door, she asked, “Why are they in jars?”

The clerk tested the stapler on a scrap of paper.

“What would you put them in?”

Outside, the city was having an unremarkable afternoon. A delivery cyclist argued with a taxi driver. Rain gathered in the seams of the pavement. Someone had left a chair beside a rubbish bin, though the chair appeared perfectly good.

Mara walked to the little park behind the library.

For years she had told the story of her mother’s death beginning with the telephone. She had gone back over the words her father used, trying to remember which came first, as though the right order might make them easier to hear.

Now she could also remember the missing button on his shirt.

At the edge of the path, she found a long blade of grass.

She wiped it on her sleeve and placed it between her thumbs. She blew until her head felt light. Nothing happened.

A boy passing with his grandmother stopped to watch.

“You’re doing it wrong,” he said.

“I know.”

“You have to make a little hole.”

She adjusted her hands.

The grass gave a sharp, embarrassing cry.

The boy grinned. His grandmother pulled gently on his hand, and they continued down the path.

Mara chose another blade.
